THE GRAY FATHER. A tiny girl went singing Among the meadow flowers; Her father watched her, bringing Eler happy thoughtless hours. She never ssw his features, She never knew his face, Of all unconscious creatures She had the joy and grace. ' Years passed !—her father brought her A jewel for her brow; She thought !—and while she thought;her Gray father she saw now. But she was not so mirthful -; That father now she knew; Of grief she found old earth full, ' And she was older too. The father of that maiden, He is old Father Time, • A parent heavy laden With more of prose than rhyme. No more you hear her laughter The flowering fields among; Her words for ever after . Are rather said than sung. —Temple Bar. KENINGALE COOL

- - - Always behind—The hansom driver. A babe in the house is a well-spring of pleasure' but twins—twins are a deluge. Why are balloons in the air like vagabonds ?—Because they have no visible means of support. A tear in the eye of a woman is ten times more per- suasive than a rolling-pin in her hands. George Selwyn once said, "The only happy pairs I have ever known are those of the House of Commons." Customer: "Are yon sure this bread is fresh, baker?" Baker: "Fresh! Well, I should say so—it's to-morrow's." Advice, like snow, the softee it falls the longer it dwells upon, and the deeper it sinks into the mind.—Coleridge. Purity is freedom from foreign substances, internally; cleanness, externally—in man as in metals. Are you pure, or only clean? The paths of virtue, though very seldom!, those of 'worldly greatness are always those of pleasantness and peace.—Sir W. Seca. When the savages of Louisiana wish to have fruit, they cut the tree at the bottom, and gather the fruit. That is exactly like a despotic government. "If small girls are waifs, are large 'cines wailers ?" .asked a college student of his sister. "Certainly," she replied; at any rate, the boys are in the tiabit of applying them to their lips in sealing their vows." Little Johnny one day surprised his father with: "Pa, I love grandma, and I want to marry her." "You silly boy, that would be impossible." "Why, pa ?" "Because —because she is my mother." "Well, pa, didn't you marry my mother." Pa collapses. At a dinner give.n to celebrate the completion of a country church the builder was toasted. Thereupon ' be rather queerly replied that he was " more fitted for the scaffold than for public speaking." A beautiful Oriental proverb runs thus:—" With time and patience the mulberry leaf becomes satin." How encouraging is this lesson to the impatient and despond- ing; and what difficulty is there that man should quail at, when a worm can accomplish so much from a leaf of the mulberry? The weakest living creature, by concentrating his powers on a single object, can accomplish something; the strongest, by dispersing his over many, may fail to- accomplish anything. The droo by continued falline bores its passage through the hardest rock—the hasty torrent rushes over it with a hideous uproar, and leaves no trace behind. Once on a time it happened that a poor wight married. a shrew, who led him a piteous life. She fell ill, the doctor was called in, and the anxious, affectionate, Hus- band inquired of him how his dear spouse was. Galen shook his head, and told him to prepare for the worst. "What," said he," is she likely to get over it?" Lamb was one of the kindliest of men, and his humour had the smallest possible infusion of ill-feeling; and yet even Lamb must have sacrificed a friend to a joke pretty often. When he replied to Coleedge's question, " Did you ever hear me preach?" "I never heard you do anything else.' we may be pretty sure that the re- mark 'did not strike Coleridge as altogether pleasant. MADE SURE Or IT.-4n Austin, Texas. it is.' impossible to ascertain when any particular train leaves, without going to the depot and inquiring of the agent how many hours behind time the train is. Colonel Yerger wished to go to San Antonio on the 11 o'clock train, so he said to his coloured servant—" Sam, go down to the depOt, and see what time the 11 o'clock train leaves." It was about three o'clock when Sam returned. "Well, when does the train leave?" "tilt's done let', boss. Bit leff at hal pas' two, sah." "What?" "I did jess what yes- tole me. Yer tole me ter see when de train leff, an' I watched till it was plain outer sight on de udder side ob de Colorado ribber." When Carter. the Lion King, was exhibiting with Du. crow, a manager egith whom Carter had made a broken engagement. issued a writ against him. The bailiffs came to the stage door, and asked for Carter. "Show the gentlemen upstairs," said Ducrow. When they reached the stage, there sat Carter composedly in the great cage, with an enormous lion on each side of him. "There's Mr. Carter waiting for you, gentlemen," said Ducrow, "Go in and take him. Carter, my boy open the door." Carter proceeded to obey, at the same time eliciting, by private signal, a tremendous roar from his companions. The bailiffs staggered back in terror, and rolled over each other as they rushed downstairs. , BRAN Homes APYV.AaANCIL—When I first saw him he was in the prime of life, although his hair was turning grey; he was inclining to be stout, and promised to be stouter. When I last saw him his hair and whiskers were snowy white, and his features more decidedly marked. he was, indeed, very fond of commenting on what he called e his ugliness," and after seeing the frontispiece to the Life, one can appreciate a store he used to tell of himself. how one day he noticed a little girl looking very earnestly up in his face. "Well, my dear, I don't think you've seen me before." "Oh, yes, bee." "Why, ;where?" "I saw you the other day climbing up a pole, and I gave you a bun." Another little girl was told to go and kiss Dr. Hook. She hesi- tated, shrugged her shoulders, and exclaimed, "Tell mamma to go and kiss him first."—Tentple Bar. A NOVEL POsT-OFFIcE.—AS we walked from one of the Sixth Avenue stations to the restaurant where I was to have my first "square American meal," I noticed how different the letter-boxes are from the purple-red pillars of Englend, reminding one of Tommy Atkins on guard at street corners. They are dark-green and small, and are fastened to street lamp-posts. They are so insignifi- cant that I probable should net have noticed them but for the marvellous ornaments they each and all wore. These were ornaments in a true sense of the word, being proofs of the trustworthiness of the community those boxes served. They were bundles of papers, pamphlets, and even books, too bulky to be forced into the aperture for letters, therefore left there on the top of the box, in full view and open exposure to every passer-by, till the postman should make his next round. This is a common practice* all over America; that is, in cities. Every Christmes-time since then I have been amazed to see how thoroughly the American public is trusted. Every Christmas—often at .other times—the letter-boxes are filled high with packages of all sizes and shapes, await- ing the postman. Every one of them had a Christmas look, and even the postage-stamps on them would tempt dozens of street arabs, one would think. If any are stolen, I never hear of it, and the practice is 80 general as to receeye no attention. Once at the corner of Sixth Avenue and Twentieth-street I sew a sudden gust of wind send half-a-dozen of these packages flying. Every passer-by put himself in pursuit, but he who caught the most of them was the pea-nut vendor whose stand is at' that corner.—Caseell's Family Magazine. CDARLEs DiCKENS.—THE BEGINNING AND THE END.— We have more than once glanced at the frequent men- tion of Rochester, chatham, and the neighbourhood in the writings of Charles Dickens. This is no wonder. It was the scene of his happiest days of childhood; in th'e vicinity—at Gadshill—was the home of his later years. Be was not, indeed, born in Kent, but his father catne to Chathatn when Charles was a tiny boy of four years old, and lived near St. Mary's Church. Here for five years he passed a thoroughly happy life—a quaint, old- fashioned child, weak in body but precocious in mind: a devourer mt novels, and noted even then for his powers as a story-teller and an actor. During the last two years he was placed at a school in the town, and played, as he tells us, in the hay-fields now covered by the South- Earern Railway Station. Thence he went to London, leaving the old ruin, the gray cathedral, the quaint town, the great river, the gardens and orchards of Kent, with playmates, bgy and girl, to all which he was fondly attached, for dingy, smoky streets, and many sorrows more than childish. Here his Alicawber-like fatner fell into difficulties, and thaeperiod of his life commenced of which he has given us so sad a picture in an episode of the boyhood of David Copperfield. When be had risen to fame he pur- chased the house at Gadshill. which as a boy he had thought "the most beautiful he had ever seen " ; and there, one peaceful June evening in the year 1870, the end suddenly came, and the word finis was written all too soon on the pages of his last work, and on the record of his busy, overstrained life; almost. the latest words in the uncompleted manuscript being a picture of the morning rays of a summer sun illuminating the haunts of his childhood. "Its antiquities and ruins" (thus he wrote of Rochester under the name of Cloisterham), "are surpassingly beautiful, with the lusty ivy gleam- ing in the sun, and the rich trees waving in the balmy air. . Changes of glorious light from moving boughs, Bongs of birds, scents from gardens, woods, and fields— or, rather from the one great garden of the whole culti- vated island in its yielding time—penetrate into the cathedral, subdue its earthy odour, and preach the Resurrection and the Life."—Our Own Country for October.

On Monday, before his Honour Judge Collier, at the Liverpool County Court, Messrs. Agnew and Sons, art publishers, of Manchester, made an appli- cation for a new trial in the case of Agnew and Sons v. Steele. which was decided in the defendant's favour a week or so ago. Mr. Stewart (instructed by Mr. H. C. Reynolds) appeared for the applicants, and Mr. M•Conkey (instructed by Mr. J. C. Clarke) appeared to oppose. The facts on the original hearing were, shortly, as follows :—The defendant (Dr. Steele) gave an order in October, 1885, for an etching of Munkacsy's great picture, "Christ on Calvary," which at that time was being exhibited in Liverpool. The etching, however, was not tendered until July in the present year. and when so tendered was refused by the defendant ; and on the tria the plaintiff sought to recover the price from the defen- dant, but his Honour held that there had been unreasonable delay in the tendering of the etching, and also that as plaintiffs would only have been entitled to damages if they had proved loss, but which they -had failed to prove, he must give judgment for the defendant.—On the heiring on Monday of the application for a new trial Mr. Stewart argued at length, but without calling on Mr. M'Conkey to reply. his Honour refused the application on both the grounds (as stated above) with costs.

LOCAL REVISION COURTS. GRAPPENHALL. On Wednesday Mr. C E. Lloyd, revising barrister, sat at the Barry Arms Inn, Grappenhall, for the purpose of revising the voting lists forthe townships of Appleton, Grappenhall, and Latchford, in the Knutsford Division of Cheshire. Mr. Lance Bentley (Knutsford), and Mr. H. J. Longton (Watrington) appeared for the Conservatives, and the Liberals were represented by Mr. Joseph Steel (Alderley.) No public interest was taken in the Proceedings, the business being of a routine eharacter.—The list for Appleton was first gone through, but, as there were no party objections, it was soon finished. In one , ease the Revising Barrister drew attention to the names, of two gentlemen lodging at one house, one of whom already had a vote; and one of whom desired to have ote. He pointed out •that from the statements of qualification it appeared as though the two paid £l6 a year between them for lodgings. inslructions for the I claims had been taken by Mr. Longton, who said that he I was under the distinct impression that each of the claimants paid £l6 a year. Both held good positions at the brewery. The Revising Barrister, however, said that he did not think he had sufficient informa- tion. He should only allow a vo.e in the case where it had been held before. When the Appleton list was finished, the Revising Barrister said that he was glad to see that the list was a decided improvement on, the one for Appleton that he had to revise last year.— The list for Grappenhall was taken next, but nothing of importance transpired. On a lodger claim, that was allowed, being considered, it wasstated that fiveshillings a week was paid for bedroom and sitting room, which I led the Revising Barrister to remark that in that neighbourhood lodgings were very cheap. When read- ing over the list his Honour referred to one entry, re- marking that it hardly looked like a qualifying property when a man was described as of "New England.' An Assistant-Overseer: There is an Australia about hero, (Laughter.)—During the revision of the list for Latchford a discussion took place in regard to people who lived in the Parliamentary borough of Warrington. —Mr. Bentley: These are those v,oters who come on for the first time this Year, who live within the Parlia- mentary boundary of year, but not. within the borough boundary. They will vote for the County Council of Cheshire. The municipal boundary Is not co- extensive ivith the county boundary. There has been an agitation in Warrington to throw this township, and also Grappenhall township,into Warrington —The Bevis- I ing Barrister: It has been left in t.a county of Chester.— Mr. Bentley: Yes.—The,Revising Barrister said that the names were entered in division 1, and if he signed it he should be putting them on the list for a parliamentary division of Chester.—Mr. Bentley said that seeing that these persons were Outside the Warrington municipal area, and had no municipal vote for Warrington, they , might be allowed to vote for the County Council of Ches- ter. They resided in the County —The Revising Barris- ter said that it appeared to him that it was the only way in which they could record a County Council or munic- ipal vote. He would allow the claims to that ex- tent, and alter to division ,3. He supposed that there were very few boroughs so situated.—Mr. Bentley said that the township had given a lot of trouble in past years.—Mr. Longton: In Warrington we have no diffi- culty, because we have municipal and parliamentary lists.—The Revising Barrister: I should think this is one of the most peculiar townships in the kingdom. I shall change division 1, to division 3, and give these persons a County vote.—This was all the business

div.p: DARESBURY.

On Thursday Mr. Clement E. Lloyd held a court at Daresbury to revise the lists of the Daresbury and Whitley polling districts of the Knutsford division. The Liberals were represented by Mr. Joseph Steele, of Alder- ley Edge, and the Conservatives by Mr. L. Bentley. The assistant overseers of the different townships were in attendance, but the general public was scarcely repre- sented. The business was formal.

THE ROMANCE OF THE SEVERN TUNNEL.

The history of the Severn Tunnel is something like an engineering romance. In Mr. Walker's recently- published work, "The Severn Tunnel, its Construction and its Difficulties," which has just been added to the Preston Free Library, the indefatigable contractor for the Prestcn Dock Works, the Manchester Ship Canal, and other great undertakings, tell' in a popular and unprofessionel style the story of the Severn Tunnel, the construction of which was entrusted to him in 1879 by Sir John Hawkshaw. Mr. Walker, in the preface to the book, gives a choice little piece of auto- biography which is worth reproducing. Not being one of thoseiTortnnate individuals," he proceeds, "who are said to be born with a silver spoon in their month. I was forced to undertake responsible work in the year of the railway mania (1845) before I reached the age of 17, after a very briefecourse of instruction at King's College. Both in that year and 1846 I did consider- able work on Parliamentary surveys. In 1847, Mr. Braseey was good enough to give me a position on the North Staffordshire Railway, and I remained upon Ida ' staff for seven years, the last two being spent upon his great contract for the Grand Trunk Rail- way of Oanada. For a slirther seven years I remained in Canada, constructing railways for the Govern- ment of the Lower Provinces, and I returned home after an absence of. nine years, in 1861. In 1863 I made some extensive surveys for railways in Russia. In 1864 and 1865. further surveys and explorations in Egypt and the Soudan, passing as far south as Me- tammeh, 100 miles north of Khartoum! On my return to England, in the spring of 1865, I was offered and accepted the management of the construction ef the Metropolitan and Metropolitan District Railways for the three firms who had jointly nndertaken the con- tract, namely, Messrs. Peto and Betts, John Hilk, and Waring Bros. The construction of these lines, from Edgware-road to the Mansion House, I carried out successfully, and they were completed on the let of July. 1871., Shortly after this, I, in partnership with my brother, the late Mr. Chas. Walker, undertook the contract for the extension of the East London Rail- way from the end of Brunel's Thames Tunnel under the London Docks. through Wapping, Shadwell, and Whitechapel. Sir John Hawkshaw was the engineer- in-chief of this work. and I was fortunate in gaining his good opinion, and carried out the works, I believe, to his complete satisfaction, and it AMR owing to the confi- dence he reposed in me that he afterwards entrusted to me the still more difficult work of constructing the Severn Tunnel." The Severn Tunnel may be regarded so far as Mr. Walker's rnagnus opus. The construction of sub-aqueous tunnels is not to be entered upon lightly end without grave consideration. To be. threatened with floods from above and floods from below is not a plea- sant exnerience. "One such experience at the Severn Tunpel,". remarks Mr. Walker, "with its ever-varvins and strangely-contorted strata, and the dancers from floods above aria floods below, has been sufficient for me. One selorigneone tunnel is quite enough for a lifetime." When Mr. Walker's first tender for the con- struction of the Seyern Tunnel wag considered by the directors of the Great Western Railway Company, it was thought that too vent an amount had been esti- mated for contingencies, and they deeirled not to let the contract until they had driven e. heading through the whole length of the tunnel. On the 18th of October, 1879, the whale of the workings were flooded, and the men not without great difficulty escaped with their lives. "It was," remarks Mr. 'Walker. "a melancholy result of nearly seven years' work, and no doubt those in authority no longer undervalued the contingencies of such a work, which they had thought had been over-estimated by the contractors two years before." Sir John Hawk- shave, whe had hitherto been the consulting engineer, was then asked to take full charge of the works us chief engineer, and to carry them on as he thought best himself. Sir John Hawkshaw sent for Mr. Walker, and he was induced to undertake the contract, the works being handed over to.him'on the 18th December, 1879. Then commenced a weary struggle extending over years; difficulties innumerable cropped up; pumps broke, doing tremendous dainafee ; panics occurred. Divers were engaged to undertake perilous j6wrneys. eropine in total darkness'over the debris which strewed he bottoni of the hemlines. One accident tank nearly ‘welve months to repair, the whole of the time beim' spent in battling with the most gigantic difficulties and resorting to every ingenuity that engineering science' eonld devise. The year ending in 1800 seemed to have been one long struggle. Mr. Walker states that it 'was well for them that they had not known all the difficulties they were to encounter when they entered on, the work, almost with a light heart, on the Jannerv- previous. The great snowstorm of January, 1881, stopned their supplies of coal, and they were rednced to all kinds cf expedients, begging and borrowing nil ; the coal they could in th. neighbourhood, cud finally rutting up timber to keep the pumnipz engines going. Then some of the hands, dissatisfied with the method of' the shifts, struck. "We want the eight hour ' shifts," said one of the men. "My good man," , replied Mr. Walker, " yen will never get that , if von stop here for a bemired years. There is a 'rain at two o'clock, and if you den% make haste •:.nd get your money von will lose your train. You had eteer get your money as soon as you can end go." Anil so Mr. Walker weeded out the had characters, mil a good feeling henceforth reigned between em- !doyers arid employed. In December. 1882, the mission -oom which Mr. Walker had erected for the men was hurnt to the eround ;, eix days later a man came to him hi teeny., exclaiming "The river is in; the tunnel ie • in !" He hurried to the top of the shaft, and there found between 300 and 400 men evidently in tie) greatest 'of terror. Herdly one of them could sneak from exhaustion, and they were anxiously await- ing the arrival of the large cage which was bringing up a further batch of men. Mr. 'Walker descendea the sheet, and, on errivine at the bottom, they found it, , rerfectiv dry. There was no danger, and the panic had been caused by some one alarmed at a trivial oc- intrrencf;, and, mistaking its nature, crying out. " F,scape for your lives, boys! the river's in !" "A they ran towards the shaft" the narrative continues, the men in the other break-ups joined in the panic, ' coil at last the whole stream of the men—three or fonr hundred in number—ran for their lives to the winding 'aft at Seabrook. When passing through lengths of finished tunnel, they spread out in a Cisorderly ”rowil. running perhaps 20 feet, wide; then they would come to a short length between two break-up., where there was only a seven feet heading. Here they threw each other down, trampled upon each other, shout- ing and screaming, and then, to add to the disorder. llie ponies in the various break-ups took the alarm, ena galloped down in the direction of the winding shaft, trampling on the prostrate bodies of the men. The principal foreman afterwarda asked one of the men why he had thrown,away his clothes. 'To swim, zur,' he said. I fear he would have made_ a bad hand at swimming in a 71t. heading, if any large volume ef water from the river hat) really entered the works." Mr. Walker is far from blaming the men for cowardice: indeed, he is never tired of paying tribute to their hardihood and bravery, both individually and col- lectively. He says, "To understand how easily a panic spreads, nnder the circumstances, it would be necessary one's self to be under the river, a mile away from the shaft, confined in a narrow space, with rocks dripping or running with water all round, with only the light of a stray candle here and there, and he most extra- ordinary sounds that ever greeted the ears of mortal man; first from the east, and then from the wett. heave tiriebers thrown down suddenly, with a noise that re-echoes through the whole of the works; then astray shot fired in one direction, then a complete salvo of 50 or 60 shots from the other—every sound totally differ- ent from the sounds in the open air—all the surroundings such as must produce a feeling of awe and tension of' the nerves; and then, when men Following their dangerous employment heard others run- ning by them below, shouting to them to escape for their lives for the river was in, would any man pause to consider, when he thought his life could only he saved by the rapidity of his flight from an enemy against which he could not contend." On the 9th Febrii• cry, 1883, four men were killed by the fall of an iron skip; the same'year a great tidal wave burst over the whole of the low-lying ground between the shaft and the river, coming in like a solid wall of-water five or six feet high. It entered all the houses, most of which were only one storey, and rose above the bed in which the children were asleep. The children were saved by being placed 'on high tables and shelves. The wave reached the boilers that worked the winding and pump- ing engines and flawed dawn the pit with a fall of 100 feet. Eighty-three men were imprisoned in the tunnel at the botto'm of the shaft; one trying to escape up a ladder was thrown back by the force of waterand killed the other men were eventually rescued. Mr. Walker describes in a very concise and interesting manner the main events that occurred up till the completion of the tunnel, which • wa-s finally opened' for pas. senger traffic on the Ist December, 1886, nearly 14 years from the time the Great Western Company had first commenced their works, ,and as nearly as possible seven years from the time they had let the contract to Mr. Walker. The line of the Severn Tunnel Railway was 8 miles 26 chains long; the top of the ,tunnel was about 145 feet tinder the level of high-water spring tide, and about 50 feet under the bed of the river at its deepest point. The greatest number of men at work at one time was 3,628; and the amount paid in wages to day-work men in the largest pay, on Dec. 21st, 1884, was £4,372 13s. 9d. No less than 76,400,000 bricks were used in the construction of the tunnel and bridges. For more than a year the average

LORD ROSRBERY r LIKEDS.—Lord Rosebery, speaking at Leeds on Tuesday night, reviewed the recent speeches of Mr. Balfour. He said Mr. Balfour's recapitulation of Mr. Mandeville's doings prior to his death was in itself sufficient condemnation of the Irish Government, for it revealed a system of espionage that would do credit to any autocracy. Of Lord Hartington he observed that to condemn. the Liberal party because it had associated with the Nationalists was to fly in the face of Liberal tradition, which always advocated in national questions listening to national representatives. Lord Hartington described himself as a Whig, but he really discarded the principles of the old Whigs, who fought against the Treaty of Union to the death. Referring to Mr. Cham- berlain's speech, he said the demand that Mr. Gladstone should state his policy savoured a little of hypocrisy. It was already well known.—Lord Rosebery, replying to an address from the Leeds Chamber of Commerce ou Wednesday, expressed the opinion that the Foreign ' Secretary should be non-political, and should speak with the united voice of England. We should retain our I colonies, and give them a larger share in the voice of England abroad. On Wednesday evening Lord Rosebery, as president of the Leeds Junior Liberal Association, addressed a crowded meeting on the Irish qnestion. He showed that in 1885 he condemned the Tory- Nationalist alliance because the Tories entered into it with the object of gaining place and power, and that he was not inconsistent in favouring the Liberal-Nationalist alliance, because it was based on a principle. When that principle was conceded the association might be regarded as At an end. In order to give some idea ot this immense quantity of water, Mr. Walker adds, "It is sufficient to supply a town about the size of Liverpool or Manchester, and is about one-sixth of the quantity daily consumed in London. In elm year it would form a lake about 1,000 acres in extent, ad 10 yards deep. div.head: LATE SERGEAN T-MAJOR HUGHES,
div.p: THE LATE SERGEAN T-MAJOR HUGHES,

OF NEWTON. There has just been erected in the churchyard of St. Peter's, Newton, a handsome monument to the memory of the late Sergeant-Major Hughes, of the C troop of the Lancashire Hussars, who died on the 30th April last, from injuries accidentally sustained by falling from his horse, under circumstances that have previously been reported in our columns. The late Sergeant-Major Hughes, who for many years was in the employ of Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division, was very highly respected. Soon after his lamented death Messrs. Essenhigh Bros., of Manchester-rd., Warrington,were instructed to erect to his memory a massive marble monument. That work has now been completed in a manner that gives the most entire satisfaction to the friends and comrades of the deceased gentleman. On the monument, in imperishable red letters, is the follow- ing inscription : Sacred to the memory of Thomas Hughes, Sergeant-major, C. Troop, Lancashire Hussars. Born 30th April, 1837. Died 30th April, 1888:' At•the loot of the monument is the text "In the raidst of life we arein death." Round the curb- stone there is the inscription—" Erected by the 'officers and comrades of his regiment, and the clergy, choir, and friends of St. Peter's Church." The monument is of white Sicilian marble, and a panel in the head of it bears a representation of the accoutrements of the deceased, sculptured in first- class style. The accoutrements represented are a busby, cross-swords, carbine, spurs, and bit. A photograph of the monument has been taken by Mr. T. Birtles. of Sankey-st., Warrington.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. SOFT BOBBY AN' TH' PARSON. Soft Bobby wur one o' thoose chaps at's co'd " leet," For th' nayburs o thowt as he worn'd gradely reet. It's true he wur simple, an' harmless enuff, But his heart wur th' reet shop, an' med o' good stuff. At runnin' a errand, or tacklin' a job For buttercakes, nooan wur mooar willln' than Bob. 'rho' nobry wi' conshunse wod see Bobby clam, Nooan else thowt so weel o' th' poor lad as his mam. An' dud Bobby like her? Aye, better than owt ! He'd do wod koo wanted, an' grumble at nowt. Neaw Bobby, for o held a slate or two bee, An' shaped a bit daft-like, wur sometimes too fawse For them as looked wiser—who'd set him a trap— But fun eawt, too late, they wur wearin' his cap Some lads plagued him oft, an' thowt id a rare do To thow lieaw a softty avur th' butt ov a foo; But, Bobby, who relished a good hearty jooak In his way, wur deod sat ageon extra sharp fooak. An' wheer he wur once treated shabby or meon, 'Twin' odds as he'd never be sin theer ageon. Ther's a tale aw've-heeard o'er him at's put me o' th'

grin, To think heaw a foo tg)ok a wiseacre in; Wheer Bobby lived, th' parson wur ore o' th' owd sooart, As preyched a good sermon, an' looked after spooart. When fte dud thad he took care to ged eawt o' th' gate, An' he'd ramble deawn t' river, a way off, on t' quate, Just cloctas to a pub" wur a rare shop for perch; lie could fish, spree, an' sleep, an' land nicely for t' Church. One Setterday, t' parson sect wi' th' intent 0' spendiu' thad day, as a deol mooar he'd spent; But when he reached t' place, wheer his rod wur hid by, He stared, an' he coifed, an' he heaved a big sigh; Theer Bobby wur stood an' owd rod an' line, An' th' fish as he'd catched med owd parson's een shine. it wur th' best spot on t' river, thad fact he weal knew, But heaw to ged shut o' Bob? wed mut he do? He'd nod fish while he stopped, he mut blab a tale, If he see him ishin' bi th' pub, suppin' ale. So he put a bowd face on, an' lookin' severe, Bed sternly "Why Bob, what are you doing here 2" " Aw'm fishini" Bob anserd, as solid as lead, "More shame, then," sed th' parson, "and your mother dead!" "Wad, my mother deed 2" Bobby sobbed, "Yes, Indeed !" Bob, wi' thad, took his fish, an' soyled off at full speed; When he'd gotten away, t' parson fished theer hisser, An' smookin', he lafft, " Ah, I managed that well !" When Bobby reyched hooam, welly gaspin' for wind, He'd nowt but fond thowts ov his mom on his mind; He dashed into th' heawse, an' t' fost thing ak he see Wur his mother as lively an' reet as could be. "Hey, warn, are yo' wick ?" he axed, strokin' her heyd ; " Aw in so fain, for th' parson yon said as yo'd deed !" " Dorn'd heed 'em, ml lad, that tale's nobbut a sham, An' t' parson's bin stuffin' thee up, just for gam !" Well, Bob, after he'd bed some baggin' an' rest, Went to th' heawse o' th' °wit parson, an' axed for his best Sunda' suit. Knowin' Bobby, th' housemaid, in a crack Gi' id him, thinkin' th' parson wur needin' t' best black. Sunda' morning coom on, an' th' bell co'd fooak to

church, As t' parson reyched hooatn, fro' his breakfast o' perch, No best suit could he find, so he looked at hissel'. Pood his watca eawt, an' fun he'd to scatter, pell ; He thowt, as tort church he peyled fast, wi long stride, As t' surplice wod screen t' shabtiy suit i' th' inside; When he'd getten to t' gateway o' th' churchyard, he

stopt, If he hedn'd ha' leyned on a stooan, he'd ha' dropt. For theer, stood afooar him, i' cloth, hat, an' tie, Wur Bobby, who dismally gave a long sigh. 'Twur bis suit, th' parson knew, bi th' peculiar cut 0' th' collar, an' sherply this question he put, "Where did you get these? Come, now, tell me at once! What a clothes rack you are, 0, you poor foolish duncer "0, parson," Bob answered, "yo' shouldn't mek bother— Aw've nobbut gone into deep black for nri nt,ther!" JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER
div.p: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.

. • CHAPTER XIV. RAYMOND IS ASSAULTED. The gods, as Socrates said, sell all things at a price, and if the fortune left to Ursula involved the shifting of all responsibility on her young shoulders, it was possible.that the crushing weight might prove toe serious for her. The doctor remembered this when he ventured to remind her that Mrs. Maclurchan had probably not intended her young brother to be supplied so plenti- fully with money. "I am kept daintily enough myself," she said im- patiently, "though I was not used to it, and don't care about it in the least, and how can I refuse Ray when he comes to ask me for what he wants?" _

"That is just the point of it. You must refuse him and you must do your best to influence him.". She thought he ' spoke harshly, and looked at him with large eyes full of reproach. Ray was weak, l she knew, but she had hardly'realised how weak till she found how much he depended even on her. He had always been used to depend on other people, and she had not realised it sufficiently till the warning she had received.

--He-Was---down late the following morning—it was astonishing how, when she came to think of it, she had not attached more importance to his always being late. Time was when she could twist him round her little finger, and after her conversation with Dr. Havard she began unconsciously to assume again that grave, kind, motherly manner which she had always adopted to him more or less, but which had never been so marked as now. "If a woman could influence him it would be all very well," she said to herself, for the first time distrusting her own powers, as she watched him languidly attempting to eat his breakfast; "but I must recollect that there are women and women, ' and it seems to me too iifficult a task for me. ' There were still dainty and sheltered nooks in the garden of St. Agatha4s—smoking-rooms, Raymond called them; they were called kiosks orsummer-houses by other people—where a young fellow who was fond of the dolce far niente might resign himself to dreamy languor, if the day happened to be a fine one. And after breakfast Ursula, following him, noticed that he sat silently in one of these retreats smoking his pipe, with his hat thrown back, and the light full on his raven head. His features had grown more defined than before, and there was a sharp line drawn here and there on his boyish face. "What do you say to going somewhere now at the fall of the leaf? The doctor says a Scotch moor, and that I am to thrn you out to shoot." "The doctor is always jawing," he said, with that odd assumption of English slang, which was more grotesque in his case than even in his sister's. From the recesses pf his cosy nook his voice came with a languid drawl—he was already opening a yellow-back. To please Ursula he had pretended to read a little Latin, and less Greek, but the pretence was a very shallow one. It was useless to try to stir him up to greater manliness, or to make him exert himself more than he liked. And the doctor became morennd more an- noyed when reports reached him that not oily had young Campion taken with unusual quickness to the English fashion of flirting—with the full understand- ing that he could make love to girls of his own posi- tion in society without any explicit intention on either side—but that, in the absence of greater at- tractions, he had been ready to amuse himself with pretty girls in the village. There had been no real harm in the matter, as the young man was able to explain, magnani- mously abstainint, from triumphing, when Havard apologised for the fierceness of his indignation. , It was one of the provoking, things about ,Raymond that he was ready enough to talk in a depre- ,cating way about himself. The ardour of his satis- faction with himself had perceptibly cooled and he was willing enough to listen to disparaging remarks. It was a way he had—of flinging himself on the pity of other people, and he seemed to be confiden- tial even to the plain-spoken doctor. He was apt to talk to the last woman he met as if he had chosen her for a mother or sister-confessor, and if he did not flirt with pretty girls the fear was lest he should find a counter-attraction in the ale-house. What motive could Ursula give him for keeping straight? Being good for the sake of goodness did not much commend itself to him.,

" Ono wouldthink the whole duty of man was to all- stain from drinking too much wine," he said to her irritably one day. "England has made you priggish , —you a:re different to what you were. Time was when you used to smoke with me yourself." "You know that I never 'interfered with your ' smoking. On the contrary, I think tobacco has a ' soothing influence, and if—if I thou ht it would keep you from that horrible champagne, would smoke with you again." He saw how the colour flooded her face, and sus- pected her of caring, after all, more for convention- , ality and old-fashioned insular ways than he had sup- posed before. "It is partly your own fault; you should- have Hubert Allston to see him," said the doctor one day, j goaded into direct speech. There was a trifle of sensi- bility in the old md,n's composition which made him shrink from her appealing -look, as she twisted her hands together, and answered— " I will —if you think—it--necessary." Hubert Allston came. He was nothing loth. It gave him opportunities of which he spoke to no one. He had his reasons for taking a .particular interest In Miss Campion's brother. But in spite of an in- different hunting season, interrupted during the winter by long periods of frost and snow—in spite , of the horrid state of the roads and the difficulty of training Raymond to ride with proper courage on I the one hand, and to avoid pressing his horses I when his tremors took the form of desperation on the other—Sir Thomas and his son (lid their best to teach the youth to conquer his timidity. The exercise M the open air was the hest thing in the world for him. And as to Ursula—to see her brother clothed in the pink, with hunting-boots and spurs, pleased her fancy as it would have pleased the imagination of Hawthorn, on account of its old English associations. She would have liked to follow the hounds I herself, and was conscious of a bonyant sense , of exhilaration even in riding to the meets. But Miss Havard's objection—the old lady's softer feelings 'which might be somewhat archaic, being backed up by the doctor—acted as a check. Ursula was be- ginning to have a strange new tenderness for the ! older lady's prejudices. In her new anxiety about Raymond, she valued her kindly sympathy. It was [ Margaret's dislike to the worry Of stirring up I small-talk which alone kept Ursula from "step- ping," as that lady would have said, "out of her position" to inquire why the villagers passed her with incivility. The spirit of opposition amongst the cottager s whom she had tried to befriend seemed I to her at this timestrangelyuncalled for. Indeference to Miss Havant, she kept from 'interfering too much with her keepers—such interference having failed in a previous crisis, and Miss Havard declaring that it was utterly unbecoming. And though Ursula said, "I can't agree with you, these are really my affairs," she had . always refrained from answering the doctor's sister with irritation. As November passed into December, and December into January, Raymond aniusing himself with riding ' —heavy demands were made on-Ursula who resented the fact that she was expected to sparkle and chatter 'just to please the. Abbeyford folk, and that Miss ' Haver& would have liked to cast all her lady friends into one uniform social mould. ' It is astonishing how some of these maiden ladies who have never had anything tragic in their own lives, never ex- periencing any great sensations, any of the joys [ of motherhood, or the cares of wives, like j to live a vicarious life in the story of another. , Margaret Havard was vexed whenever contro- versial questions were brought uppermost in the conversation of sensible people. It seemed to her that no one could be expected to solve such ques- , tions, and that they were better left out of the talk of reasonable folk. Yet it was characteristic of her not to let Ursula alone, but to expect her to give in her adherence to all sorts of social formulas. I She could not understand the girl, and did not 'pretend to understand her. Ursula laughed to herself in a way that Miss Havard did not like, the corners of her mouth dimpling when the latter informed her one day that she was beginning to be the subject of 'remark again, in altogether another way—she was considered to be one of the beauties of Abbeyford. , "Then they must be hard up for beauties," said the girl, laughing. "I think nothinr, of their taste." 'Whether she thought much of their taste or not, it is certain that for a time she was the subject of a good deal of speculation and dismission, not always unAindly, among the gossips of Abbeyford. To be seen with her, to talk with her, and still more to dance with her, became the ambition of some of the swells, who, as the other girls said, coveted Miss Campion's

Money bags. She grew so heartily sick of it, tis much to prefer the quiet evenings when the doctor and a few of his old "fogey friends " dropped in for whist and coffee. She was pretty enough for the men to bear with her, though she played most abominably, and was often accused of holding splendid hands which she did not know how to manage any more than a baby. Any amount of whist was preferable to the dreadful phalanx of arguments with which Miss Havard tried to urge upon her the importance of every girl making a suitable "settle- ment "in life.

The lady did not mean to infringe on affairs which did not concern her, but she had been nervous and worried ever since Mrs. Wilson acknowledged to her in confidence that letters directed in a masculine handwriting with French itortmarks upon them were constantly arriving at the Manor-house. One such happened to be delivered when Miss Havard was spending a day at St. Agatha's. At the first moment when the girl had opened it, she had held out the letter with her usual frankness of manner, not feeling as if there was anything to hide, but at the next she caught it back and said, with a little break in her voice—

" You and your brother have been very kind, and there are many things I would do to please you, but tell my private affairs, I cannot." The speech was reported to the doctor, who gave his sister to understand once and for all that Ursula liked her liberty, wanted to look after her brother, and that it was of no use to speak to her about any amount of fitting and appropriate marriages. After that it seemed more humiliating to the girl than ever to angle for any sort of admiration. She found refuge in her plain-spoken ways, and took to politics with an alarming seriousness, which filled Sir Thomas Allston with horror. There were dull weeks during a reign of frost and snow, which commenced early in January,when it was impossible for horses or hounds to go overthe frost-hardenedground,and when they had to be maintained in idleness. During those days Hubert and Raymond "loafed "a good deal, often lounging in the streets of Abbeyford and find- ing a resource for a few days in skating before the snow had fallen too thickly. t tUrsula enjoyed the skating as much as anybody, but could not help being thankful when the frost broke up, though after accompanying her brother to the meets, she had many hours of dulness, listening to the feeble little trickle of Mrs. Wilson's conver- sation. There were still occasions when she frightened the old lady by discussing social wrongs with a scorn which ;was passionate, and when poor Mrs. Wilson shivered at her words—occasions when she felt as if she must find out some fresh secret of happiness, and refuse to have her life cramped and maimed as it was. But her devotion to Raymond's interests kept her, from making lament. If he complained when he Came home of the horrid state of the roads or of a slip made by his "high-stepper ;" if the groom told her one day that he could see by certain signs the animal had been down, Ursula ofily laughed. She knew that she did not need to preach the advantages of caution to Raymond, mid that if the casualties of past seasons were to be examined into, it would be found that the smallest proportion of them had befallen the most fearless riders.,

Mrs. Wilson WM not often garrulous except on the subject of misfortune. But with a love for funerals and catastrophes which is characteristic of many women of her age, her tongue began to wag directly the men had disappeared. • She had a number of wonderful tales to tell of those who had dashed at fences :without troubling about their height; of ardent sportsmen who had. lau,ghed at advice, and had refused to listen to the, presentiments of their friends. Mrs. Wilson was rather great at presentiments, and 'VW sure that something would happen before the season was over.' Either it would be Sir Thomas, who, forgetting that it was time for his cross-country days to 'she over, would probably attempt a jump for which his eye would not be sufficiently keen or his hand sufficiently steady ; or it would be Raymond, who, owing to the rawness of his youth and his want of practice in riding, would certainly lose this nerve, when confronted with actual danger. Ursula triedlo persuade herself that her brother had plenty of pluck. It was not, however, reassuring to find that on one of the days when Mrs. Wilson's com- plaints had been more hard to combat than usual, there was no sign of Raymond, although the twilight had set in. It had been really a wretched day. Raymond's horse had cast a shoe. There was no blacksmith near, and, as a matter of necessity, the lad had been left in the rear. At one time he had been obliged to dismount and lead his hunter. -le was going very slowly, splashed with mud from ' to foot, for Ray was a hit of a dandy, and din _.. like to find iiimaelf in a disreputable condition. He had to pull up the collar of his great coat to protect his neck from the bitter wind, which tore at his hair, his hat, and otherwise mauled his person. After all it did not so very much matter; the i hounds had lost their scentearly n the day. The fox had escaped to its covert. He had not much cared for the flashy appearance and bumptious. manner of some of the other men, many of whom were sons of • tradesmen. He, who was easily argued over to new political views,- was beginning to think with Sir Thomas, that .an ill turn was coming in the affairs of the country., The chill wind, the dark, leafless trees, and the toil of plodding through the muddy lanes, were all condu- cive to a tired dreamy state of body and mind very different from the doggedness of an ordinary young Englishman. He started from his reverie, when an old woman, tramping along with a bundle under her arm, suddenly accosted him, speaking in a low hurried voice. At first he could not understanci what she said, and was only able to make out— " The young missus ha' been guile to me. I'm riskin' summat to warn ye." "What about?' responded Raymond, a little nervously, in spite of his attempt at boldness. " sure I ought to be much obliged, to you." "I don't want to mek no to-do," said the woman sulkily, taking no notice of the sneer, "but I ain't come here for nothin.' If the chap thinks it worth carrying out his words—" "What words?" • "Can't you guess? No; you gov' it up clean?" The insolent interfering old harridan, as he called her swearing a little under his breath-- began to offend him as she laughed a cackling laugh. He tried to spur on his horse, but she stood in his ' path, so Mira he could not go on without knock- ing her down. " To'peimy ale is not what gents like you is 'sposed to favour," she cackled. "You don't go to the public to split a quart with other fellatis, and chink mugs for nothin , 808 he. And then he sipped hisself jest to draw 'ee on, and heard 'ee toast his own darter. " Well, what of that ,7" Raymond answered, look- ing impatiently at the Obstacle in his path. He knew well enough about the story to which she was alluding, and again saW a picture of a girl, slight and graceful as a lily, standing amongst the scarlet runners and rougher blossoms in her father's garden. And he remembered how when he had surveyed her with a critical glance slowly inciting into admiration, the father instead of being complimented, had muttered, "Damn him! I wish he'd-let the wenches be!" What if he had gone more than once to that house? He had done no harm, even if his glance ' dwelt lingeringly on a pretty face—the man himself had a head like a bulldog! Agleam of light fell on the beldame's features. The were very pale and her eyes were gleaming. y , "If they knew as I were a comin' to warn you o' the oath he swore on the big Bible—tthat if it were twenty wild Campions stead o' one he'd break every bone in their bodies and— flush, I hear 'em cornin' ! A fine sperrit that man has !" she added with dianity. "And there's a Ted bearded fellah as is namea Jean Brown, as has hounded him on—achap from Lunnon. Keep under they trees. Tek a bit o' advice." By this time Raymond was terribly frightened, and tried to hide his panic with bluster. "Why in the name of all that's confounded," he cried, turning his horse on one side, to get out of her way, "do you keep me here listening to all this rigmarole? It's a trick to get money out ef me. Let go !" She had caught his bridle, but broke away from him with a sudden cry. At the same instant Raymond heard a muttered oath and saw a heavy figure, short of 'stature, with a shock of thick hair, just discernible in the twilight, creeping in the shade of the, trees. In another moment a couple of men were aipon him. Never among the bravest of hie' sex under the best of circumstances, a cold sweat of terror stood on the .poor boy's face. He saw that his assailants held sticks in their hands. He could just hear the woman's voice pleading, "It wall be &Coward way to do it, when times is hard, and the young leddy good to us,"—just realise that he had his hunting stock in his hand when it was wrenched away from bin,, and he fell a victim to a shower or blows too dazed to understand the full vengeance of the encounter. (To be continued.)

TEE BLACK MOUNTAIN EXIIMITION.

Cancrrra, SUNDAY—The chief fighting in the Agror tiVedition so far has been done by Charmer's brigade. 44 captured the village of Kotkai after a smart engage- 'eat, and 200 of the enemy were killed. On our side., losses were slight. In addition to the casualties announced one man of the Royal Irish and threa were wounded. The Royal Irish received the of the fanatical Ghazis, and killed them all. ;::',-:-.- Crookshank has been seriously wounded in thd 'T. During the reconnaissance, three men of the ausse,.. lAnd two of the 14th Sikhs were wounded. The who). the columns are now advancing against the enemy. Rrame, MONDAY.—General Mc.Queen, retiring with the third column from the western slope of Black Mountain Urived yesterday on the ridge at Black Mountain, hotly followed by the enemy. Three sepoys were killed and two wounded. A reconnoitering party found a new ..to'llte, which is now being mended. While thus engaged 'may were under a In avy Ere from the enemy, by which three men were killed and one wounded. The second Ind third column are now joined in one camp. Saila, THURSDAY.—Detachments from the first and second columns of General M•Queen's expedition , .have burnt, foil'. native villages including Beerum, the ichabitants of which began the attack on the late Major nattye last June. The fourth column is now engaged in iMproving the road, and has been reinforced by two IPanies of the Seaforth Highlanders, THE LOSS OF ENGLISH TOURISTS. .tzmis, SUNDAY.—lntelligence received here announces at Mr. W. F. Donkin and Mr. Fox, the missing English I Jurists, were lost, with their two guides, on the glaciers Of Mount Kaschtanta, but that nothing positive is known ' aS to their fate. Mr. Quinton Dent, another tourist, has arrived here to organise a search for the missing party. SEVERE FIGHTING AT SUAKIM. The rebels around Suakim are believed to have saftered severely at the hands of a force from the garri- °On, which at dawn on Monday made a reconnaisanee to the left of the enemy, with the twofold object of .'rawing them under the fire of the forts and ships, and to dis- Cover their number. As,the Arabs? kept their trenches, the Egyptian force a.dv a nced to within 600 yards of their Position and then opened fire, a heavy fire at the same time being kept up from the forts and ships. After the Object of the reconnaisance had been attained, the troops retired. The casualties: on the Egyptian side were two. killed and 25 wounded. THE EMPEROR FREDERICK'S DIARY. BERLIN, SUNDAY.—The Post states on the authority of an obscure print that Prof ensor Ceffken obtained a copy of the Emperor Frederick's Diary from England, whither the original manuscripts were at the time of Queen Vic- toria's last visit to Berlin. These manuscripts theEnglisli Court declined to give up, although :requested to do so by General Von Winterfeld when that officer went tp England as the special envoy of the German Court. keanwhile it is stated that the manuscripts had been Copied several times. The Prince of Wales is said to have had a copy at Gmunden which lie showed to several People. This is explahied as the reason why he left Vienna for Hungary before, the Emperor William's arrivai St the latter place. FOREIGNERS IN FRANCE.

PARIS, MONDAY NIGIIT.--The prefect of police has de- cided that single lady foreigners are to be registered. Our charge ci'affaires, Mr. Egerton, who called on M. Eloquet about the decree yesterday, put him in great Perplexity by the apparently innocent question whether foreigners spending the win-ter on the Riviera are amen- able to the decree. The Premier, under pain of ruining Nice, had to say they were not, for which several papers that had stood by him tax him to-day with inconsistency. The League of French Workmen, whatever that body i!bay be, has sent an address of congratulation to the Government in its decree against foreigners, and urged that the different bills to tax foreigners should be intro- ducedby the Government early in \the session. The workmen are really in too great a hurry. M. Floquet cannot well put a tax on foreigners without first know- ling their names and whereabouts. :WAR BETWEEN PORTUGAL AND MOROCCO . THREATENED. Hostilities between Portugal and Morocco are threat- Pried. The Moorish Government has been requested to , salute the Portuguese flag as reparation for an insult thereto at Port f,araiche, and it has refused to comply. ,It is understood that the demand will he enforced by War ships. i r DBASTER IN ILLINMS.-500 PERSONS INJURED. •r, A Central News telegram from New York states that • the llooPlo of Quincy, Illinois, were yesterday celebrat- ; , ‘ag their town's anniversary, some 6,000 persons being &as, embled. During the progress of the celebration a Ja,..,rge temporary structure, erected to accomodate , '..,..aightseers,_ suddenly collapsed, hurling the occupants to ."'" ground. Five hundred persons were injured, many ' 116. f them seriously, and one person was killed. -
WARRINGTON FARMERS CLUB.

A meeting of the Committee of this Club was held at the Farnsers' Stores, Warrington. on Wednesday •,,evening, under the presidency of Mr. George Percival. There was but a small attendance of Members. THE Annursesrmx or Cmass.—The Secretary (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) reported that he had sent to each Sanitary Authority in the district the following resolution, which Was passed at a recent meeting, viz :—" That the atten- tion of the 4uthorities be respectfully called to the Consular reports recently issued by the Agricultural department of the Privy Council, shewing the extensive sale in this country, as • pure cheese; of mixtures of tallow, grease, cotton-seed oil, and other fats with the Product of milk in the manufacture of American Cheese, With the object of prosecutions being instituted by them for the purpose of exposing this fraud. And that a copy *4 it& resolution be forwarded to the Mayor and Nuisance Inspector of each Authority in the district." Ete had received several replies to the circular, amongst them communications from Corporations that were taking proceedings with regard to the sale of adulterated Cheese . The Town ch-rx of Birkenhead wrote triat the circular had boo" referred to the Medical Officer of ilealth for report, and the Town Clerk of Liverpool had replied that the matter had been referred to the Inspector Of Nuisances. Mr. Charles Estcourt, city analyst for Manchester, and analyst for several Lancashire boroughs, ilad written saying that he was making investigations into the matter, and would feel obliged if the Secretary S f the club would forward any informatibn he might have in his possession. If the club had come acros4 a Ifood specimen of adulterated cheese he should feel ebliged if about half a pound was sent to him. Con- tinuing, the Secretary said that a Macclesfield cheese factor, referring to the action taken by the club in regard to adulterated American cheese, affirmed that it was all a myth. Gentlemen who were instrumental in induc- ing Mr. McLaren M.P. o ask the Government to obtain a report from the American Consuls with regard to the adulteration of American cheese, who had seen the report, would be aware that nearly all the cheese sent from the North-Western States of America was adulter- ated. The report in question stated that a large quantity of this cheese, nearly one half of the whole, „ Was composed of tallow, grease, cotton-seed oil, and ' other fats. The cheese factor he had referred to was as Muck interested in the adulterated American cheese as Were the wholesale butter dealers in the introduction of hutterine.—The Chairman said that he had seen cheese ' that was unfit for food for pigs.—Mr. John Marsh remarked thathe believed that adultera ion was as much Practised in the manufacture of cheese as in the osanufacture of butter. An Act to prevent such adulteration would have very beneficial results. —The Secretary said that he knew that three-quarters Of the whole importation of American cheese was adulterated in the manner desCribed in the Consul's rol)ort. From all the North Western States of America Cheese was sent to England that the people there would not eat. It was manufactured especially for expor- tation.—Mr. John Derbyshire said that if the club per- severed in the action they were taking the Government would be bound to notice the matter, and good results Would come from it. It they continued .heir opposition to the unwholesome trade the day *ould not be far distant when their wishes would be complied with, and they would have been the means of assisting in bringing • about a great boon to consumers.—lt was then resolved, ers the motion of Mr. John Derbyshire, seconded by Mr. • John marsh, " that the Secretary forward the thanks of the Warrington Farmer's Club to the Birkenhead and Liverpool Corporations, for the steps they are taking . With regard to exposing the sale of adulterated cheese." MIsCILLANHous.—The meeting adopted a vote of thanks to the analyst (Mr. Estcourt) who recently. exposed a defect in the Margarine Act which was dis- _Covered in connection with a prosecution taken at wigan.—A short discussion followed on the question of the fraudalent sale of foreign killed meat, the Secretary' stating that the club's action had met with the approba- tion of established butchers. Those butchers who corn- Plained of a desire on the part of the club to injure them Were not the leading ones. Butchers' Associations were raking the matter up on the same lines, and the Man- Chester and Salford District Master Butchers' Association had been very energetic in bringing the matter under tile at.ention of Government.—After a little further discussion the subject droppedt
