div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

On Saturday, the Bull of the Iloly See reached Dub- lin, appointing the Very Rev. Michael Comerford, Monaster-Evan, Coadjutor Bishop of Kildare and Leitrim. Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P.. has written a letter to Mr. Man- ning, secretary of the Waterford branch of the National League, in which he speaks of the resistance offered to the evictions on the estate of Count De la Poer as being precisely what is required this winter in every parish in Ireland to smash the landlords and the coercionists its their last ditch. _

A report from Fermoy states that a desperate fight took place there, on Sunday night, between a number of soldiers of the Bedfordshire Regiment and the residents in the district known as Cork Hill. The affray, which had its origin in a difficulty between the drummers of the regiment and a portion nf the civilian youth of the locality, resulted in broken heads on both sides, an 3 the police, acting on the promptings of duty, got the Pre- verbial reward of those who interpose in quarrels.

About ten o'clock on Monday morning, a large tene- ment house, occupied by nearly a dozen families, fell in cusoberland-street, Dublin. burying a woman and two. children in the ruins. The pre brigade was summoned. and an attempt immediately commenced to extricate them. One child was dead and the wolnan badly injured when found. The second child marvellously escaped. Most of the other tenants were away at work at the time, and several women who noticed the tack wall giving way succeeded in escaping. . Upwards of 2,000 persons assembled at IDMinor Churchyard, on Sunday. to unveil a monument erected to the memory of John Kinsella, an evicted tenant, who was shot dead at Craghan, near Coolg,reany, by a body of eo3erstency men on Sept. 28 last year. The monu- ment, which is Ilft, high, is shaped like a cross. Sir Thomas Esmonde, M.P., Mr. J. J. Clancy, M.P., and Father Family addressed the meeting, strongly con- demning the circumstances attending Kinsella's death, and advised the people to continue the Plan of Cam- paign which they had adopted, assuring them that vic- tory would follow. The inquest on the body of Jane Beetmore, who was murdered at Birtley on the 22nd ult., was resumed at Birtley op Tuesday. The accused man, Waddle, was pre- sent in custody. The medical evidence showed that the deceased had been stabbed in various parts of the body, but the fatal wound was in the abdomen. There had been no attempt to mutilate the body, as had been re- ported.—Susannah Robson deposed to leaving the de- ceased in Waddle's company on the night of the murder. Other witnesses having been called with the object of proving that the deceased woman and Waddle were together on the night of the murder, the inquiry was ad- journed until the 24th inst. GREAT MEETING AT TIPPERARY.—LETTER FROM
GENERAL NEWS.

The Parnell indemnity fund amounts to £6,730, in- cluding subscription" from the Catholic clergy, Madras. The wrought nail manufa,...urers in Staffordshire, on Saturday, advanced the wages of the workpeople 10 per cent. _ _ _

A severe snowstorm burst over North Wales on Satur- day. The Berwyn mountains are enveloped in snow for many miles. The Empress of Austria has signified her intention of again visiting England this winter. She will stay some time at Bournemouth about Chri, tmas. There is a movement on foot in favour of reviving the meetings in Trafalgar-square, the concentration of he nolice in the East End affording a favourable oppor- tunity. A new steamer, the Peninsular, has been launched from Messrs. Caird and Co.'s yard at Glasgow, for the Penin- sular and Oriental Steamship Company. She is 5,500 tons register. The Belfast steamer, Baltic, was on Monday night being loaded in the Clarence. Dock, Liverpool, when she gradually settled, and sank. A port, or valve, had been left open. Another body of a woman, unknown, was found in the Thames, on Monday, near Waterloo Bridge. The de- ceased, who appeared about 30 y-cars of age, had met her death by drowning about ten (Jays ago. A party of twelve, from the Normal College for the blind at Norwood, started from London, on Monday, for a cycling trip to Derby. Two machines, accommodating eight and four respectively, were used, each steerea by a seeing man, the other riders being blind. •

, Row Disiteste is Spa—The Wolverharopton magis- trates have sentenced a hairdresser, named Lloyarch, to one month's imprisonment for permitting his daugh- ter whilst suffering from scarlet fever to associate with other children. The defendant had refused to allow the child to be taken to the borough hosoital. The Local Government Board have informed the Guardians at the Stockport Union that they will not offer any objection to the arrangement proposed for sending the workhouse children, excent the infants, to public elementary schools, broviding satisfactory arrangements are made for the supervision of the chil- dren out of school hours.

A special meeting of the Salford Town Council was held on Monday, and, after a long discussion, Mr. Samuel Brown, solicitor, of Stockport, was unanimously elected Town Clerk and solicitor to the Corporation, at a salary of £l.OOO per annum. The salary paid to Mr. Graves, who lately absconded, and whose post is now filled by Mr. Brown, was £1,500. A Midland goods train, while running between' Derby and Leicester, on Monday, knocked down John Wood- ford, a platelayer, who, being drawn under the wheels, had both his legs cut off. He was otherwise frightfully in- jured, and he was removed to the Leicester Infirmary in a dying condition. It is stated that Woodford got core fused between two trains.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT AN IRONWORICS: ONE MAN KILLED AND 'Firvn Iturnm.—On Monday, an accident occurred at Parkgate Ironworks, Rotherham, one man being killed and five iniur-d. An extension of tho works is taking place, and while an old shed was in pro- cess of removal a travelling crane which had been used in the girder shed struck the gable, and Caused the shed to fall in upon the men. DR. PARR STABBED IN KIREDALE GAOL. -- Dr. Barr, who gave evidence at the Mandeville inquest, and who is surgeon at Kirkdale Prison. Liverpool, was attending a negro prisoner who had complained of ill- ness, when the negro and another convict quarrelled. The negro drew a knife which he had concealed about him, and tried to stab the other convict; but he was seized by Dr. Barr, who, in the 'struggle, was somewhat seriously stabbed in the hand and wrist.

THE YORKSHIRE COAL TRADE CRISIS.—The movement among the colliers for an advance of 10 per cent in wages is spreading,. The applications to the Yorkshire Miners' Association for notices to leave are being re- ceived in a manner which shows that the men in that 'part of the country are more unanimous in this move- ment than they have been in taking any step in the same direction during many years. A meeting of the Shrop- shire miners was held on Monday, at which it was resolved to join in the general demand for an advance.

A DISHONEST LOCAL PREACHER.—John Jones, goods foreman in the employment of the London and North-, WesterrNailway Company, pleaded guilty at the Liver. pool Police Court, on Monday, to a charge of stealing a large quantity of tin, the property of the company, and was sentenced to four months' hard labour.. It was stated that he was a local preacher, a S-anday school teacher, and the treasurer to the Welsh Chapel. His wages were 265. weekly, and he was engaged in building operations in Colwyn Bay. When arrested he had £l6 108. in his possession. THE Quasrmy or LOCAL OPIION.—The third annual festival of the Hulme, Chorlton, and District Band of Hope Union was held in the Hulme Town Hall on Satur- day night. The Bishop of Salford, in the course of a brief address, expressed the opinion that the members of the House of Commons were becoming persuaded that+ within a very short time local option must be granted for the country. Another campaign or two, a fetv more battles, and that which had been the cry of the United Kingdom Alliance for so many years would be accepted 'the country- .

div.head: MR. JOHN DILLON.
div.p: MR. JOHN DILLON.

A magnificent meeting was held at Tipperary, on Sun- day, at which not less than 10,000 people assembled. Contingents assembled from parts of the counties a Cork, Limerick, Waterford, and Wexford, and a promi- nent feature was the presence of a number of the Gaelic Athletie Associations, dressed in costume and on horse- back. A force of nearly 100 police were present, but were stationed at a distance from the meeting, this arrangement having been arrived at with the promoters of the meeting on condition that a place should be afforded a Government note-taker on the platform. The following members of Parliament were present :---Messrs. John O'Connor, T. J. Condon, T. Mayne. P. O'Brien, and Dr. Tanner. The Veryßev. Canon Cahill, P.P., Tipperary, presided. Mr. John Dillon was expected to be present, but he sent a letter stating that, although he had gained strength rapidly since his release, he had been strongly advised to take some weeks' rest before going on active service again. He regretted this, because in his opinion it would be impossible to conceive a more.critical mo- ment than the present. There was no hope for the Irish tenants except in some method which would convince landlords that it would not pay to treat them in an in- sulting and unreasoning spirit. This winter was sure to be one of fierce struggle. It was precisely the same struggle in which they fought together in 1875 and 1876, when John Mitchell was elected for Tipperary. It was the cause of Irish freedom, and the struggle of the winter might be final. Resolutions were passed denouncing the Coercion Act, condemning evictions, and denouncing land-grabbing as a heartless and vicious system, opposed to the Irish tenant in his holding; calling for the restoration of an Irish Parliament as the sole means of remedying the wrongs of the Irish people, and pledging themselves not to cease their efforts until it was obtained: expressing confidence in Mr. Parnell and the Irish, and denouncing the attacks to tarnish his reputation; and expressing iieartfelt recognition of the invaluable services of Mr. oladstone and the Liberal party in breaking down the harriers of English prejudice towards Ireland.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

It was announced in Edinburgh on Monday that the Lord Advocate has been appointed Lord Justice Clerk, and the present Solicitor-General becomes Lord Advo- cate. Seats for Edinburgh and St: Andrew's Univer- sities thus become vacant. _

Sir James Ftergusson, M.P., speaking on Saturday night at a Sick and Burial Society's meeting at Newton Heath, referred with much satisfaction to the decrease pauperism which has taken place, notwithstanding the depressed state of trade, during the last TO years. He attributed the improvement to the better habits of the People, the spread of temperance and thrift, and the operations of such excellent institutions as friendly societies and sayings banks. He condemned extravagant expenditure upon funerals as being neither wise nor justifiable in a moral or religious sense. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, addressing his constituents in West Leeds, on Saturday night, predicted that a good time was coming for advanced Liberalism. After the victory bad been won the Gladstonians Were not going tn be burdened with the Liberal Unionists, who would not he allowed to be an obstruction in the way of great measures of home politics for Ireland. ,Referring to Mr. Balfour, lie said the right lion. gentleman preach?d very well on rnristianity in Manchester, but he practised it very badly in Ireland. Inquiries had been made into the Mitchelstown business, and before long Mr. Balfour would he brought to book and floored in the House of Commons.

ANOTHER ACTION AGAINST THE TINES. Mr. George Lewis, on behalf of Mr. Flenry Campbell. M.P., the private secretary of Mr. Parnell, has commenced an action against The Times newspaper for libel, the libel consisting in the statement that Mr. Campbell was the writer of the alleged forged letters. The LonclonderrN ,Centinel says :—We learn on good authority from London that it is very probable that two or three of the clynamiters recently convicted are to be released, and will give evidence against the Parnellite:s of a very incriminating character. We have this infor- mation from a private sourco of unquestionable and re- liable authority.

SITOCIONG DEATN OF A YOUNG WOMAN.—About seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, Sarah Agnes Ogle- thorpe, 29, daughter of Mrs. Oglethorpe, butcher, Lan- caster-road, Preston, was cleaning one of the front win- dows above the shop, and, in order to do so, got out on the shop cornice. It is supposed that she must have missed her footing, as she fell to the ground below alight- ing on her head. She was picked up and carried into the house and died in a few minutes. Dr. Broughton, North-road, was called in, but when he arrived the un- fortunate young woman had expired.

FAILERE OF THE SIBERIAN EXPEDlTlON.—lnformation was received in Newcastle on Saturday that the Wiggins expedition that went out from the Tyne in July last with a view of opening up a trade between this country and Siberia has been a failure. The Labrador reached Vardoe early in August, and proceeded on her journey through the Kara Sea. It seems, however, that this year there has been an unusual quantity of ice in the straits, and a telegram dated October 3 states that the Labrador returned to Vardoe on Wednesday without having reached Yenesei., bringing with her four shipwrecked crews from the Kara sea. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT: Two MEN 131ITHEO AmvE.—On Monday morning, about eight o'clock, a shocking accident occurred at Rockingham Colliery, near Barnsley, belonging to Messrs. Newton, Chambers, and Co., two men being buried alive. A miner, named James Dickinson, 32 years of age, living at Hovland, and a trammer, named Solomon Rigby, 18' years of age. of Worsborough, were working together' when about eight o'clock a deputy discovered that a large fall had taken place. Sloth mon were found dead, the bodies being buried in the debris. - - -
ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY OTJTRAGE.-.OnMonday after- noon an extraordinary outrage was committed at Cardiff. A man who is well known in the neighbour- hood as a hawker of lace knocked at 45, Adam-street.

pparently knowing that the only occupant was a ser- vant girl, he proceeded to tie her to tho banisters, and on her calling out he stabbed her several times in the left arm. Having locked all the doors he went upstairs and ransacked the rooms, stealing a silver watch and other articles. On completing his search he again abbed the girl and then ran down the street. He has not yet been discovered. ELECTRICAL BOATS ON VIE THAMES.—The first public i4easure boat to be driven by electrical power on the river Thames was launched on Monday. It is 65ift. long, 10ft. beam, and is designed to carry 80 passengers, with a mean draught of 221 n., 14 tons displacement, at SiS miles an hour. as regulated by the conservancy by-law. The electrical machinery and storage being rlaced below the deck fore and aft leaves a clear run the length of the boat for passengers. In the middle is a handsomely fitted cabin with lavatories, dining table, &c. The elec- tricity isstored 111 200 'accuniulators, and is converted into power by two motors of 72-horse power each driv- ing twin three-bladed propellers.

s' ATTEMPT TO MURDER A WOMAN.—An attempt to murder was made in Newcastle-on-Tyne, on Saturday afternoon, by a man named Dunnell. a plumber, who formerly lived with Margaret Cooper, a single woman. Dunnell wished to renew the intimacy, and went to the woman's house on Saturday. While he was there screams were heard, and he was seen to leave the house by the win- dow. The door, which was locked, having been forced, Cooper was found on the floor with her throat cut. A bloodstained table knife was lying near. The woman lies at the infirmary in a dangerous state. Dunnell was apprehended late on Saturday night in a public-house not far from the scene of the crime.

PETTIT GROWERS' CONFERENSE.—LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE. Another conference, convened by the National Fruit Growers' League, was held at St. Albans, on Tuesday. A letter from Mr. Gladstone wig read, in which the right hon. gentleman said, in testimony of his deep sympathy with the declared pnrpose of the League, be need only point to his local action at ilawarden, and his constant endeavours by public de- clarations to aid in stirring up the public mind, so that, it might come to appreciate the very great National im- portance of the question jointly embraced in the current phrase, "small culture." Fruit growing was un- doubtedly one of the most important questions to • growers, to consumers, and to our rural population, whose numbers it should increase, and -whose wages it should sustain or improve. SHOCK/NG FATALITY AT SCARBOROUGM.—Late on Satur- day night a cab proprietor, Amos Jackson, whose estab= lishment is in North Marine-road, Scarborough, commu- nicated to the police the fact that "something" had fallen into his back yard, and upon two officers investigating the matter, they discovered the dead body of a girl, clad only in A nightdress, the skull being frac- tured and the right arm broken. Subsequent inquiries showed that the body was that of Annie Watson, nine years of age, the daughter of John Watson, 'a joiner, who keeps a lodging-house nine houses away. The girl, with other children, slept in the attic, and it is clear that while asleep she obtained access to the roof, walked along the tiles over the distance of the intervening houses, and fell into Jackson's yard, which belongs to the last tenement of the row. The fall was forty feet.

MR. JOHN MORLEY IN WALES. Mr. John Morley visited Newtown (Wales), on Monday to address a series a meetings arranged by the Welsh National Council. Arriving in the afternoon, be ad- dressed an open-air meeting, and received an enthtie siastic welcome from what one of the speaker; styled the cream of Welsh Liberalism. Thanking them for his cordial reception. Mr. Morley said he did not hesitate to characterise the Liberals of Wales as the cream of the cream, for they had returned an almost solid vote for Mr. Gladstone and his policy. Indeed, the political com- pass of the Principality always pointed due north. In the evening, a public meeting was held, at which Mr. Morley was received with enthusiasm. Mr. Stuart Bendel!, M.P., presided, and said Mr. Morley was always right, and first to be right. He had been right with re- gard to Egypt and also in respect to Ireland, and now he was right about Wales. (Cheers.) Mr. Montan' said The limes asked what business he had there—he was not a 'Welshman. That was a stupid remark, for, while claiming to be an Englishman, and lie was proud of it. did not wish to see all Welshmen, Scotch- men, and Irishmen turned into Englishmen—(cheers)— and he held that it was only vulgar prejudice on the part of those who did wish to see such a transformation. Criticising Lord Hartington's speech, he said his lord- ship admitted that the Irish party,was now supported by a great and powerful party in England mimberine not much less than half the voting power at Great Britain. The Gladstonian Liberals vrere no Icfnger the rump of a broken party. Lord Hartington also said that Ireland, In some parts was not far removed from civil war, Which showed that firm and resolute government had not accomplished its work. His Lordship also admitted that, as things stood, an alternative policy on the part of the Unionists wina almost an impossibility. They had here the most com- plete confession of failure, of impotence, of helplessness, of hopelessness, that was ever made by a party leader. (Cheers.) The policy of the Unionists had brought the country to a deadlock, for there was going to be no re- venal on the part of Liberals. It was no use Unionists going about the country with a catechism in one hand nod a birch rod in the other. (Cheers and laughter.) The result of the policy which had been pursued during the past two years was that the Unionist party was doomed. Lord Hartington had compared the country to a weathercock and himself to the fixed points of the compass. Well, for his own part he did net believe that they could navigate the Ship of State through tronbled waters it they drove a nail through the compass so that it should always point in one direc- tion, and the Liberal party was not going to drive the Whig nail through their compass. (Cheers.) One of the questions in which Wales was interested was inter- mediate „education. There was not one and a half millions of people in Western Europe so fitted by natural gifts to profit by such education as the people of Wales, and yet who were so badly off for it? Mr. Mundella brought„ in several bills in different years. A Tory Government promised support, but refused to grant a committee, so that seven years after the report at 1880 was made the question was exactly where it was before. Could they wonder then that ther- was growing up a: Welsh question? (Cries of Then there was the land. The Richmond Com- mission appointed. in 1879 to inquire into the land question undoubtedly dealt with Wales in a manner that had proved unsatisfactory and insufficient. 'nit English land system was not a very brilliant success at home, where it depended upon unity of feeling and in- terest between the lan Ilord and the tenant. In Wales the Welsh members showed everybody that the English system could not be successfully applied in the face of differences of language, of form, of creed, and of politics. There was, therefore, a strong and irresistible case for inquiry, hut the Tory Government, being a Government. of landlords, left the Welsh farmer, than whom there was no harder worker, to struggle with enormous difficulties. Then with regard to the Church, that was another ques- tion which would have to be faced. He had no inclina- tion tiTi treat the Church question except as a purely political question. (Cheers.) English Liberals were now examining the case, and evens staunch Liberal Unionist like Lord Derby admitted that Weiss had a very- strong claim to be separately dealt with. (Cheers.'; Therefore they saw it was not the Separatists only who said it Was equitable in the interests of peace to listen to the demands of the Welsh people in respect to the Welsh Church. (Cheere.) Coming to the question of local government, their opponents had their eyes upon them. Lord Hartiugton said, "If you grant Home Rule to Ireland, then you must make the same concession to Wales. and England." He declined to ac- cept his definition of legitimate conclusions from Lord Ilartington. The secret of the success of the Goverment of this great Empire was that our statesmen had always prescribed special remedies to particular evils. Therefore ' because they insisted upon meeting the demand •,f Ireland it was fair that they must meet the demands of Wales, hut it was a question of machinery What they had to do was •to see that in Wales as in Scotland and in Ireland machinery was provided for carrying out, so far as was consistent with justice, . to the interests of the realm as a whole the 'wishes and the interests of the„population. He never had expected, and lie had Yet to 1:)Zh convinced, that it was necessare to exPecaidentity of machinery where the difficulties to be Past with were not identical. He advised them to de all in their power to make the County Councils as powerful as possible. But atter all the first question was.the Irish question. Nothing could be done until that was disposed of, but when it was out or the way then they could deal with °there. (Hear, hear.) Mean while those other questions were ripening, and when the next general election came the Liberal party would take a great step forward in securing a Parliament which should represent their principles and which should once more govern the country with justice, with wisdom, and with power. (Cheers.) A resolution was adopted welcoming him to Wales. and looking forward with confidence to the day whe6 the return of the Liberal party to power would allow him to take his full share in securing for Wales her national demands. On Tursday, Mr. John Morley visited the meeting of ihe Welsh National Council, at Newton. He said they all regarded the Irieh question alike, all over the king- as corning first and foremost. Until the present Coalition Government gave them an opportunity of testing' the feeling of the country, they must be content In go on thus. Tiresome as it was, they must argue the (reds question until they succeeded by the force of con- viction. Resolutions in favour of s ' elf-ouvernment for Wales, and urging the formation of adistinct Welsh National party, were oarried.

div.head: WORK FOR PARLIAMENT.
div.p: WORK FOR PARLIAMENT.

Mr. W. IL Smith addressed a meeting at Gloucester, on Monday. He sketched the work of the Parliamentary session, alluding to the Amended Rules of Procedure, the National Debt Conversion Scheme., the Railway Rates Bill, the Local Government Act, and the Imperial Defences Act. As to the Fisheries dispute between Canada and the United States, he expressed the belief that after the Presidential election in America was over, the matter would be settled. He denied the truth pf the recent rumour that Bechuanaland was to be banded over to the Cape Government. Her Ma- jesty's Government had no intention to recede from their obligations to the chiefs and natives of Bechuana- land. He acknowledged the great assistance which the Conservatives obtained froin their Liberal Unionist allies in all their labours, but more especially in resisting the attempts to break up the Constitution. He expressed great astonishment at Mr. Gladstone's method of reply to Mr. Balfour's detailed account of Mr. Mandeville's proceedings subsequent to his release. He denounced the language employed by the Parnellite party in carry- ing on their agitation in Ireland, drawing from i the conclusion that they aimed at total separation, and that their Liberal friends were deluding themselves. The Government were determined to enforce the law. •
TERRIBLE BALLOON ACCIDENT.
FALL OF 1,000 FEET.

News from Canada states that at the Central Canada Exhibition, at Ottawa, one of the attractions was a bal- loon ascent, in which Professor Williams, after reaching the height of 1,000 feet, was to descend by mans of a, parachute. Fully 5,000 persons were on the exhibition grounds to watch the performance and assist the profes- sor. Many willing hands stood around holding on to the aerial monster until it should be inflated and the words "Let go" given. Among the crowd was a young man, named Wensley, who had secured a good hold on the rope running around the bottom of the balloon. All was ready and the professor shouted " Let go," when, to the surprise of every one, Wensley still maintained his hold on the rope, deaf to all the cries of the crowd to drop. After he had reached about 50 feet in the air he shouted twice, appearing to have recovered his senses on realising, the perilous situation he was now in, but it was too late, and, with the balloon rapidly going upwards, he kept his grasp, endeavouring to raise his leg through the rope to give him a hold. Aftcr he had reached a height of about I,oooft. he was seen by the breathless crowd below to draw himself up as a last effort to save himself, and then his hold relaxed, and with lightningspeed he com- menced his descent towards the earth. At this point the excitement among the witnesses was beyond descrip- tion. Women fainted, and a panic was but narrowly averted. When the first part of the fall was commenced he came feet foremost, but suddenly he turned a somersault, and with outstretched arms and legs he struck the earth, The body fell to the ground about 300 yards from where the balloon started. A rush was made for the spot where the lifeless mass of humanity lay disfigured almost beyond recognition. Neck, arm, and legs were broken. Life must have been ended before the ground was reached. Professor Williams, ignorant of the terrible tragedy, cUt adrift from his balloon to commence his descent, about 20 seconds after poor Wemsley had started downward, and when he learned of the terrible accident he was completely prostrated. „,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.
SHOCKING DEATH AT ORFORD BARRACKS.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the coroner for South-west Lancashire, investigated a painful affair that has occurred at Orford Barracks, Warrington. On Saturday evening John Winskill, a sergeant in the South Lancashire regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, went with some friends to the H•op Pole Inn, Horsemarket-st., and fell down a flight of steps leading to the cellar in that house. He was taken back to Barracks in a cab, carried to bed, and was on Sunday morning found dead, under circumstances that were detailed in evidence at the inquiry, which was held in a room of the hospital at the Barracks. The first witness called was Benjamin Winskill, of 52, Burton-st., London, N.V4 .; who stated that the deceased sergeant was his brother. Deceased was about 37 years of age. Witness last saw him alive a fortnight or three weeks ago, when he left him at Willesden Station. Deceased enjoyed splendid health, and witness never knew him to require medical assistance.

Hannah Shrives, wife of Lance-Sergeant Joseph Shrives, who lives in Sharpe-street, said that be- tween seven and eight o'clock on Saturday evening she, with her husband, Sergeant Gordon, and the deceased, went together to a public-house in War- rington, where they had drink's. Deceased bad a glass of rum. They then went to the Hop Pole Inn, where they had more drink. She saw the deceased have two small glasses of rum. They were in the singing room. At about ten o'clock the deceased took off his belt and left the room. In her tiresence he had only had the glasses that she men- tioned, but when she first saw him on Saturday evening he looked the worse for drink. He did not return to the singing room, and witness and her companions searched for him. At about a quarter past ten she saw deceased in the passage. Some one gave him some water. She was told that he had fallen down the cellar steps. He seemed to be insensible. Some soldiers and civilians who were with him took him into the singing room, where his face was washed. He was then carried 1 to a cab, in which witness, her husband, and Sergeant Gordon, went with him to the barracks. Sergeant Gordon and witness's husband were the worse for drink. The deceased did not speak on the way, but snored very much. He was laid down in the cab, with his head on witness's lap. They arrived ,1 at the barrack gates at a quarter to eleven o'clock. 1 Sergeant Gordon got out of the cab, and fetched two soldiers to take the deceased out of the cab. He heard Gordon tell them to take the deceased to his bed,but she did not hear him say that deceased had been hurt. Gor- don then got into the cab again, and, with witness and her husband drove to their house in Sharp-st., where he was accommodated with a bed. Corporal Green and a mess waiter named Mahoney were the men called by Gordon, and Mahoney carried deceased on his back, while the corporal carried his side arms and stick. The deceased had no cross words with anyone at the Hop Pole Inn, and left the singing room by himself .—Police- sergeant Barnes:. Did you hear the landlord request the two sergeants to take the man in a cab to a doctor ? Witness: No ; I asked the waiter to let him have a glass of brandy and water, but he would not let him have it. He would not let him have any drink at all.— By a Juror: Deceased must have been about half-an- hour in the cellar, so far as she could understand. William Hesketh, porter, 42, School-brew, said that

fter leaving work on Saturday evening, at ten o'clock, he went to the Hop Pole. AS he was passing the cellar door he noticed that it was open, and saw a man lying with his lees on the steps, and his head at the bottom. The gas in the cellar was lighted. The man appeared to be insensible. Witness, the landlord, and a • private soldiert got the man into the passage. There was some blood at the place where he found the man. Witness heard 'he landlady say, "Take the man to a doctor, and I'll pay the expense," or something to that effect. One of the sergeants replied that he (the deceased) was ' all right, and they would take charge of him.—Police- sergeant Barnes: Was the woman sober P—Witness She did not look drunk, although I have no doubt she ' had had some. She had plenty to say about it.—The Coroner: It is not always a sign of drunkenness when women talk a great deal.—ln answer to further ques- tions, witness said that Mrs. Shrives tapped the deceased on the face and said he was all right, or something to the effect that the deceased had been worse before. Witness thought deceased was hurt because he had a "deathly snore." On the ground where witness had found him, there was clotted blood about the size of a small saucer. Thomas Halliwell, landlord of the Hop Pole Inn', said that after deceased had been found he gave him some water to drink. He said—" Take him to a doctor in a. cab, and I'll pay expenses" The other sergeants took deceased away. Sergeants Gordon and Shrives were neither drunk nor sober. Witness thought the deceased must be hurt, as he had lost so much blood. The steps were very awkward, and he had himself fallen down them, with a bucket of hot water. Thomas Kirkpatrick, a cabman, deposed to being called to drive the party to the Barracks. He thought that deceased was drunk, but‘that the others were sober. Private Richard McGlue, Sou.h Lancashire Regiment, said that he assisted to lift deceased from the cellar lo the passage of the Hop Pole. Sergeants Gordon and Shrives were a little intoxicated.—Police Sergeant Barnes: Did either of them say anything to you ? Witness: One of them said he would make me a prisoner, but I do not know which one it was.—Police Sergeant Barnes: He ordered you away like a dog, and said he would make a prisoner of you ?—Witness :Yes. Con- tinuing his evidence, witness said at the time that if he was made a prisoner it would mean fourteen days for him. He thought that the deceased was in a danger- ous state because he did not speak, and the water would not go down his throat. Sergeant Joseph Shrives, South Lancashire Regiment, said that on Saturday night the deceased was perfectly sober,as was also witness. He did not after the accident think thpt deceased was dangerously ill, or he should have taken him to the hospital. He thought he was in a stupor, as though he might have had a blow. He thought that after deceased left the singing room he might have had some more drink, and that the drink and the fall had made him stupid. When deceased was taken into the cab, he muttered "I'll be all right ; let me alone" or something to that effect. When witness left the'public house, he was capable of doing any military duty. He had had two glasses of beer, and two half glasses of rum hot. Gordon also was capable of per- forming any duty. Witness now perceived that it was his duty to have called a doctor, but at the time he did not think that deceased required medical aid. He did not think therewas anything serious the matter with him. Corporal McMahon, South Lancashire regiment, said that at-about 6.30 on Sunday morning he went to the deceased's room to call him for duty. Receiving aio answer, he went inside and found that the deceased was dead. He was lying on his back, and was dressed in his uniform, but his boots were off. Brigade-Surgeon McFall said that on examining the body of the deceased, he found that he had evidently been dead for several hours. There was a clot of blood on the right side of his moustache and on his cheek, which had issued from the right nostril. There was an abrasion on the left temple. There was also a small cut across the nose, and an incised wound about an inch in extent on the left side of the head. There was a good deal of blood on the left sleeve of the tunic of the deceased. In his opinion death was due to concussion of the brain, caused by the fall. He did not think that he could have done anything had he been called in on Satur- day night. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the death was accidental, and made a presentment to the effect that an alteration shoutd be made at the Hop Pole that would prevent the possibility of such an accident again occurring.

div.head: LONDO-N MURDERS.
div.p: THE LONDO-N MURDERS.
THE BLOODHOUND AS A DETECTIVE.

Sir Charles Warren has, it is stated, given instructions to the metropolitan police that, in the event of a similar murder to the Whitechapel tragedies again being dis, covered, bloodhounds are to be obtained frbm a certain veterinary surgeon, and placed on the scent before the body is removed. Of course, if Sir Charles Warren's intimation that elaborate and, it seems to us (Observer), costly arrange- ments have been made by Scotland Yard to set blood• t.ouns after the Whitechapel murderer be meant to quiet a panic-stricken public, we might let it pass. But there are not wanting signs that Sir Charles has some belief in the efficacy of the bloodhound as an amateur detective. If this be so, it will only nrove that the Chief Commissioner is singularly ignorant of even the most rudimentary facts in the natural history of our domeb- ic animals. One of these facts is that the bloodhound Is now a sham. He is, perhaps, the most useless and stupid beast that walks about in the semblance of eaninitv. Long years 'of neglect and disuse have blunted his perceptions. He has been bred not for the qualities that made him a good hound, but for those that made him a fashionable show dog— not for no, but for long ears, drooping chaps, and hideously voluminous wrinkles of loose skin. At the Warwick Dog Show two years ago the man-hunt by ,rack bloodhounds was a ludicrous failure. Only one dog displayed even fourth-rate gifts as an amateur detective. The beast that tracked Fish, the Blackburn murderer, was not a bloodhound, as is popularly sup- posed, but a mongrel—probably a bull-mastiff, with perhaps a trace of bloodhound in him. In plain truth the bloodbound is now so degenerate that in following a trail he is a poor feckless creature compared with the otterhonnd, the dog whose scent is now the keenest or all the hounds. Moreover, even were it not so—even were our bloodhound equal to the otterhound or the Cuban bloodhound of the past—his work would be dis- appointing. Ile is generally a failure if he be not set on what in the slang of venery is called an " unfoiled ~cent." In Wbitechapel we need not say that ten minutes after a dead body is discovered in the streets the scent is " foiled " by cross-trails La all directions. A POLICE SERGEANT STABBED.

At Clerkenwell Police Court, on TueAday, James Phil- lips, 37, and William Jarvis, 40, cab washers, were charged with being concerned together in cutting and wounding P.S. Robinson, at Phoenix-place, Clerkenwell, and, further, with cutting and wounding Henry Don- caster, at the same time and place. Beth prisoners had blood-stained bandages on their heads, and Robinson had cuts on the nose and forehead. P.S. Robinson detailed the circumstances under which he followed a suspected man into the cahyard in Phcenix-place. Witness was dressed in a woman's hat and mantle. The prisoners entered the yard, and he explained his presence there, whereupon Jarvis drew a pocket-knife and stabbed him in the face, end the other prisoner kicked him. He used his staff in self-defence. Henry Doncaster, who had his hand bandaged, said he also was watching a suspected person in the cabvard. He pursued Jarvis after the latter had stabbed Robinson. and Jarvis attacked him with Some weapon. Both prisoners said they were protecting their master's property. Dr. Muller described the wounds received, and said those on Robinson and Doncaster could not have been caused by a sharp instrument. They might have been caused by the blunt handle of the knife. The prisoners were remanded for a week. Bail was asked for, but the magistrate declined to grant it.

div.head: "JACK THE RIPI'ER'S" EPISTLES.
div.p: "JACK THE RIPI'ER'S" EPISTLES.

The f6llOOring postal telegram was -received by the Metropolitan police, at five minutes to twelve on Friday night It was handed in at an office in the Eastern district, at 8 p.m. :—"Charles Warren, Head of the Police Force, Central Office.—Dear Boss,—lf willing, enough to catch me, I am now in the City-road, lodging; but where, you will have to fi,nd out; and I mean to do another murder to-night in Whitechapel.—Yours, • Jack the Ripper." A letter was also received at the Commercial-street Police Station, by first post on Saturday, addressed, " Commercial-street Police Station," in black lead pencil; and the contents, which were also written in pencil, were couched in ridiculous language. The police believe that it is the work of a lunatic. It was signed, "Jack, :he Ripper," and said lie was "going to work" in Whitechapel that night He added that he was going to commit another murdei in Goswell-road that night; spoke of having "several bottles of blood underground in Epping Forest," and frequently referred to "'Jack the Ripper' underground." - A startling fact has come to light, in reference to the murders, which goes somewhat towards clearing up the !nystery with which the crimes have been surrounded. After killing Eddowes, in Mitre-seuare, tho murderer, it is now known, walked to Goulstone-street, where he threw away the piece of the deceased woman's apeon, On which he had wiped his hands and knife. Within a few feet of this spot, he had written upon the wall, "The Jews shall not be blamed for nothing." Most unfortu- nately, one of the potice officers gave orders for this writing to be immediately sponged out—probably with a view to bhecking the morbid curiosity which it would certainly have aroused. But in so doing, a very im- portant link was destroyed; fer, had the writing been photographed, a certain clue would have been in the hands of the authorities. The witnesses who saw the writing, however, state that it was similar in character to the handwriting ic the communication forwarded to the Central News, and signed "Jack the Ripper," and though it would have been far better to have clearly demonstrated this by photography, there is now every reason to believe that the writer of the letter and postcard sent to the Central News ( fac-similes of which are now to be seep outside every police station) is fhe actual murderer. The police, consequently, are very anxious that any person who can idehtify the hand- writing should. without delay, communicate with the authorities.

The Whitechapel Vigilance Committee have received the faowing letter from the Rome Secretary:— Whitehall, October 6.—The Secretary of State "for the Home Orpartment has Wilt the honour to lay before the Queen the petition signed by von, praying that a reward may be offered by the Government for the discovery of the perpetrator of the recent murders in Whitechapel, and he desires me to inform von that, though he has given directions that no effort or ex- oense should be spared in endeavouring to discover the person 'runty of the murders, he has not been able to advise her Majesty that in his belief the ends of justice would be pro- moted by a departure from the direction already announced with regard to the proposal that a reward should be offered by the Government.—/ am, &e.. E. Lama Pasmaarea.

div.head: _LETTER FROM THE HOME OFFICE.
div.p: _LETTER FROM THE HOME OFFICE.
INQUEST ON THE MITRE-SQUIRE VICTIM,

The inquest into the circumstances attending the death of Catherine Eddowes, the victim of the Mitre-square murder, was resumed on Thursday.—Dr. Sequeira, the first doctor summoned, expressed the opinion that the murderer had no design on any particular organ, and that no anatomical skill was displayed.—Dr. Saunders corroborated.—Annie Phillips identified the remains as those of her mother, Catherine Eddowes.—Detective Mitchell said he had ascertained that the deceased's husband was named Conway, not Eddowes ; he belonged to the 18th Royal Irish.—Detective Hunt said he had con- fronted Conway with two of the deceased's sisters, but they failed to recognize him.—Evidence was given to the effect that the deceased was arrested on the night of the murder for drunkenness, and discharged.—Mr. Lawende said he saw a man and woman near the scene of the murder. He was not allowed by the city solicitor to describe the man. ANOTHER ARREST.

An individual who sought admission to the casual ward at Elham Union, Kent, was detained by the master as resembling the description of the supposed White- chapel murderer. Blood was found on his trousers and shirt. He was detained while the London police were communicated with.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Work-house on Wednesday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. Greening, T. Houghton, Kilshall, F. Jones, Blackhurst, Strange, W. Houghton, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Eckersley, D. Jones, Owen, Darbyshire, Bonnell, Balharry, Swinton, Isherwood. Hibbert, Wright, Jolley, Harrison ; J. C. Sutton (clerk) ; S. Sutton (assistant clerk) ;C. H. Ward (Workhouse master),; H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools.)

div.head: , EOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: , EOUSE COMMITTEE.

Thig Committee reported that they had selected the following three applicants for the situation of nurse to appear before the Board that day, viz.:—Miss Daniels, Thirsk Union: Miss Maggie Dunne, Belfast Union; and Miss M. A. Birchemough, Chorlton Union Hospital.— The Chairman said that one of these candidates •would not appear before the Board as she had in the meanwhile accepted another position. The applicants from Thirsk and Belfast would appear before he Board. He wished to mention something which he had been told since he had come into the room, and to make a suggestion which they might accept or not. He had been told that /another nurse Intended resigning, though she had not yet done so, and he thought it possible they might save the expense of advertising again, by holding out some prospect to the second candidate of obtaining this other position.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: SCHOOL COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. Abel and Pickavance for leather during the March half-year be accepted. Miss Morris had given notice of her intention to leave the Board's employ, and it was accepted subject to a month's notice. Applications for increase of salary were received from Mrs. Ann Fairhurst, porteress ; and Miss • Hannah Blakemore, mother of No. 4 Home. The Committee could not entertain Miss Blakemore's request, but recommended that is. ed. per week more be paid Mrs. Fairhurst. A letter was received from Mr. Thomas Pemberton, treasurer of the Warrington Football Club, enclosing a cheque for £2 10s., as a donation for the purchase of the cricketing materials for the .boys in the School. It was reommended that the best thanks of the Board be sent to the members of the Club. The doctor reported that the general kealth of the children was very good:—Mr. DARBYBEIRE spoke in favourable terms of the manner in which Mrs. Fairhurst had performed her duties, and he moved that her salary be increased by 2s. instead of ls, Bd.—Mr. ISHERWOOD seconded this proposal, but it was decided that the consideration of this proposal ' should be left over till the next meeting.—The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: SCIIGOL FEES.
div.p: SCIIGOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 32 cases, 25 of which were old and 7 new cases.—Mr. BLACERITRST, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he was very glad to see that the applicants for fees were not so numerous as they had had them, and the committee's expenses were considerably lower than they were—£2o lower than last quarter. In fact, there were very few people applying for these fees but those who were really entitled to them.—Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes, which we agreed to.

LADIES AS GT/ARDIANS. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE referred to a meeting which he had attended at Manchester the previous day, and at which the Emestion of electing ladies as members of Boards of Guardians had been considered. From what he had heard he was quite in favour of some portion of a Board consisting of ladies. For going round the female side of the House and the hospital, looking after the children. and taking part in investigating the house and schools, he thought ladies would be a very great acquisition to a Board of Guardians, and especially to that Board, and he hoped some one would be found capable and willing to act as guardians in Warrington, and who would be able to discharge the duties of the office in a manner satisfactory both to the paupers and the ratepayers. These lady members would be able to assist the mothers of homes at Padgate schools, and other female officers, in a way that could not be done by male Guardians. He thought that any one who read the report of the meeting held the previous night would see at once that it would not be an improper thing for ladies to be members of Boards of Guardians to a certain extent, say four or six. Warrington was not represented on that Board to the extent that it ought to be, as it had the same number of representatives now as in 1845, although he dare say the population had almost doubled since then. He was of opinion that when the time came round it would be a very proper thing toask for an increase in the number of Guardians to represent Warrington, say, from the ten as at present to fourteen, and these four extra ones to be female guardians. He did net know whether such a proposal could be carried out, but he thought it would work beneficially.—The Chairman said they had that matter discussed in London at the general meeting of the Poor- law Conference. It seemed that in some instances ladies had proved very useful indeed, but . there was a strong feeling that it was important that the ladies should understand what were the duties they were undertaking; there were ladies and ladies. He thought the carrying out of Mr. Darbyshire's suggestion rested entirley with the electors.—Mr. Harrison said that if the ratepayers chose to nominate ladies they were entitled to do so.—The Chairman did not think the Board could come to any resolution on the matter. Their thanks were, however, due to Mr. Darbyshire for his kindness in putting before them what had taken place at the meet- ing in Manchester.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF NURSES.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF NURSES.

The business of appointing a nurse for the male side of the Workhouse Hospital was then proceeded with, Miss Dunne, of Belfast, and Miss Daniels, of Thirsk, both being called before the Board. It was decided, on the motion of Mr. GREENING, seconded by Mr. BONNEL, that Miss Dunne be appointed In the course of the discus- sion the fact that the nurse on the female side of the hospital had expressed her intention to leave was men- tioned and Mr. Greening, Chairman of the House Com- mittee, and the Workhouse master, were deputed to see the nurse as to her intention in this respect. On return- ing Mr. Greening said the nurse intended to send in her resignation at once, and it was thereupon decidedto appoint Miss Daniels, the other applicant, to the post which would be rendered vacant by this resignation.

THE NEWTON RELIEVING OFFICERSHIP. The Clerk said there had been 22 applications received for the post of relieving officer of the Newton district, made vacant by the death of the late Mr. Caldwell The applicants, whose testimonials were read, were the fol- lowing :—Alf red Cooper, vaccination officer, Earles- town; D. Davies, ironmoulder, Earlestown; N. P. Powlson, book-keeper, Winwick • Charles Allen, book- keeper, Warrington; Thos Mullock, builder, South- port; George Howarth, dairyman, Earlestown; John Fairclough, jun., farmer, Burtonwood ; John Manners, gentleitan's servant, Newton; John Wm. Caldwell, acting relieving officer, Newton; Edward Spencer, police constable, Newton; Thomas Latimer, assurance agent, Earlestown; George R. Thompson, book-keeper, Newton; Reuben Young, railway clerk, Newton; M. Roberts, shoemaker, Earlestown ; Joseph Williams, clerk and time keeper, Wargrave ; George Wright, black- smith, Earlestown; James Wm. Slingsby, police con- stable, Penketh ; J. H. Graham clerk, Earlestown ; Mathew McDuff, time keeper, Nev;ton ; Thos. Speakman, compositor, • Newton ; E. J. Mitchell; club manager, Warringten ; Robert Wilson, accountant, Southport.—lt was decided that six of these candidates should be selected to appear before the Board at its next meeting. The "weeding out" process was carried out first by nomination and then by voting. Eight of the candidates were nominated by Guardians present, namely, Messrs. Davies, Powlson, Allen, Fairclough, Spencer, Caldwell, Graham, and Mitchell. On these being put to the vote Davies and Spencer received the smallest number of votes—six and three respectively:—and they were con- sequently disqualified. The other six will be invited to attend the next meeting of the Board. APPLICATIONS FOR INCREASE OF SALARY. The following letter to the 'Chairman was read from Dr. C. N. Spinks :—" As this is the month of October,• when officers of this Union who are not satisfied with their remuneration must apply for an increase thereto, I now take the liberty to address the Board through you for an increase to my salary for the following reasons ; I First, because I have been deprived of certain extras

that I have received for the last thirty-four years, one without asking my consent to the breach of my contract, by the Guardians engaging a midwife to attend all cases of confinement, and the other by an Act of Parliament, depriving all workhouse medical officers of coroner's fees for post-mortem operations and giving evidence at inquests. Now by these alterations I consider lam a loser of from £l5 to £2O a year, as the following return will show. (Dr. Spinks•then quoted statistics to show that he had attended 18 births in 1882, 18 in 1883, 11 in 11884, 14 in 1885, 14 in 1886, 17 in 1887, and none in 1888). The numberof inquests I cannot give as I did not keep an account of them, but they averaged from four to six a year at £2 2s. each. Then, again, the pop- ulation of Warrington has increased, with a consequent increase of patients, particularly in the winter and spring the hospital was not large enough to accomodate the demands upon it. From the above I hope the Guardians will consider that I am in justice entitled to some compensation for my extra services, and when they remember that I have now well and faithfully served thig Union for 35 years."—The Workhouse master and matron (Mr. and Mrs. Ward) also applied for an increase of salary in the following letter : —"I and my wife have held office as master and matron of your workhouse a year and a half, and during that time we have done our utmost to merit your approval, and I have every reason to believe we have not failed. It is therefore with some confidence we now approach the subject of our salaries, which, at the time of appoint- ment, had been considerably reduced, viz :—master from £l2O to £BO ; matron £OO to £4O. At the same time the needle mistress was done away with, she having received £25 per annum, such sums showing a saving to the Union on our wages of something like £155 in that time. Permit me to call your attention to one or two further financial facts. During the last year and a half, I have collected and paid to the Treasurer on your account the sum of £1,057 4s. 2d. without receiving any commission for collecting; also the total amount of expenditure of the workhouse, as per day book, shews reduction: for instance, take the half-year just ended, September 29, 1888. £1,556 Bs. 3d.; the corresponding half-year of 1886 is £1,847 4s. 9d., a reduction Of £290 16s. 6d. Or,again,take the year and a half during which I have been master, £5,297 9s Bd., and the year and a half immediately preceding that £5,948 13s. 3d.; a reduction of £651 3s. 7d. ; and the house and appurten- ances in much better repair, the whole of the hospital wards and passages, a great portion of the. body of the House, and the bedsteads, having been repainted by indoor labour. I could mention many other things, but think I have said sufficient to cause you to look upon this application with favour, 'and to grant a substantial increase in our salaries as some encouragement to still further efforts."—Mr. JOLLEY proposed that Mr. and Mrs. Ward each have an increase of £lO a year, but this proposal was not discussed, as it was decided that the applications should be referred to the House Committee for consideration. The relief cases were then taken.
THE DECEASED WIF N'S SISTER BILL. NONCONFORM isr nucLARATIoN.

The following declaration has been signed by the Presidents and ex4'residents of I he Baptists, Calvinistic Methodists, Congregationalists, New Connexion Metho-, .lists, Primitive Methodiats, Unitarians. United Methodist it'reo Churches, and Wesleyan's. Sixteen prominent Quakers (among whom there exists no presidential :Ace) also subscribed to the dociiment :—" Five rears ago a petition to Parliament in favour of permitting marriage vrifh a deceased wife's sister was signed by 8,000 Nonconformist ministers of England and Wales. In the present year the leading bodies of Dissenters have, besides, passed resolutions strongly con- demning the restrictiop on such marrines; and within the past few weeks a measur, supported on miny former occasions in the House of Commons and reßttroduced with the object of removing this restriction, has again • been carried, receiving a much greater vote than on any previous occasion during a I 'onservative Government The undersigned, therefore, deem the present a suitable opportunity for reaffirming their adherence to principles which have always governed the attitwie of the Noncon- formist Churches of England and Wales in relation to this question, and for recording a further protest against the continuance of the existing law.'

div.head: TERRIBLE DISASTER IN SOUTR AM ERICA.
div.p: TERRIBLE DISASTER IN SOUTR AM ERICA.

From Valparaiso lull information has been received of the bursting of a water pond 809 feet above the level of the city of San Juan di Dios, and the deluging of the streets, causing a frightful loss of life. The despatch is dated Valparaiso, the 1.5t1i August, anti says that fo.:e days previously the pond burst. The water rushed through the city in a wave 12 feet •high, carrying nearly everything before it. At first it was thought that an immense tidal wave had come from the sea. The shops were flooded. and their contenta destroyed. The people who were in the streets at. the time were washed up . and down, some being drowned and others sustaining terrible injuries. Four days after the disaster the streets were still in an impassable state. The col/MIMI of the bodies of the drowned and killed VMS aspj woik. No fewer than _ 57 bodies wen itteogisrAd up to the tirre tbgOelrtitiew was sent off, but. this uweb,r it ws as thought would largely increased when matters were put right again.. The soldiers tuil Loiters were enaaaed at the time of writing In clearing ititay. the ,rel 43. In one case a tailor named Torres lost his wife and fur children, whilst the contents of his shop were entirely destroyed. 'rhe loss of property alone was more than 1,000,000 dollars in value. The mind was an artificial one, and belonged to a brewer named Nicolas Mena.

div.head: CONGHF,GATIONAL UNION.
div.p: THE CONGHF,GATIONAL UNION.

The annual meetings of the Congregational Union of Enodand and Wales commenced at Nottinollain, on Tuesday; Dr. Robt. Bruce (rluddersfield) being chair- man for the year. Upwards of 1,000 delegates were present in the Castlegate Chapel, when the inaugural address was delivered.

The CHAIRMAN dealt with the subject of national education, and strongly condemned the proposals of the Royal Commission, which recently inquired into the working of the Elementary Education Act, as being alarming and reactionary, especially as they affected their denomination and other churches. The Commission, he said, was set tip by the Tory Government at the instigation of their clerical sup- Porters mad other ardent denominationalists. The main grievance felt by Nonconformists was the suggestion to apply rates, raised compulsorily. to denominational schools. National education should be broad and on- sectarian, though not indifferent to the supreme im- portance of religion, but religion would be benefited and promoted by being taken out of the arena of political strife. . _ .

- The Rev. Griffith John. missionary in China to whom the chairmanship of the Union had been offered next year, wrote declining the honour, which was conferred upon the Rev. Dr. Pordby, Principal of the Yorkshire United College. The Rev. Gormsivss-lionvres moved n resolution ex- pressing strong disapprobation of the educational policy embodied in the recommendations of the majority of the Royal Commission, emphatically objecting to the pro- posed appropriation of parochial rates to schools under private management. A remarkable scene was witnessed, as the result of a remark by a Mr. Crossley that the Liberal Unionists were chained to the Tory chariot, and that they hoped to enact legislation on the lines of the Royal Commis— sion's recommendation, with the help of those who bad denied Liberalism. This evoked strong opposition, and cheering and counter-cheering between the Unionists and Gladstonian deleeates filled the chapel for several minutes; Mr. Crossley not being allowed to, proceed until the chairman interposed. Mr. EDWARD Cnossr..xr, M.P., seconded', and the reso- lution was carrried.

On the resumption of the meetings of the Union on Wednesday, a resolution was adopted acknowledging the services rendered to the Union by the late Mr. Henry Richard. Papers were read and discussions took place respecting the work of Congregational churches in villages and in towns. A large meeting was held in the evening in Wesley Chapel, in connection with the Young People's Guild. On Thursday deputations were received representing the British Guiana Congregational Union' the Irish Con- gregational Union, and the Ontario and Quebec Union, expressing gßodwill towards the English brethren. Papers on • Methods of preaching" were afterwards discussed.

SIR WHARCOURT AT OLDRAm.—SirMain Harcourt, addressing a great Liberal meeting at Oldham oq Wed- nesday night, condemned not only the acts of the Irish Adthinistration, but the tone and temper of its policy. Mr. Balfour was making the worst of a bad policy. It was a policy of coercion with insult. He was adminis- tering Ireland upon the Hottentot principle of contempt and hatred of the people with whose fate he was charged. His insults wereso many nails in the coffin of Unionism. Mr. Balfour was a practical, and Mr. Chamber- lain a theoretical coercionist. Mr. Chamberlain was ' also heaping insults upon the Irish. He had declared it disgraceful to associate with them, but he was not himself so squeamish in 1885, when he was concerting measures with Mr. Parnell to effect a revolution in Irish Government, and furthering a plan he afterwards Con- fessed he got from him. His language about paid agitators and a kept party wo a not the language of the democracy, but of a purse-proud plutocrary. Lord Hartington took a despondent view of the future of his party, and his policy was one of desperWon and paralysis. The Liberal policy was one of conciliation, and not of coercion ; justice ard not wrong.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.

MR. JouN MORLEY paid his first visit to Wales as a politician on Monday, but it will not, in all probability, be his last. He was delighted with his reception at the hands of the Newtown Libe- rals, and they were delighted with him. Lord. SueeLey, who is a large laridownerinNewtown, and was supposed to be a sound Liberal, was so illiberal as to try to spoil the demonstration by issuing a letter expressing his disapproval of the policy of Home Rule. Ho chose this particular time for letting it be known that his interests were, With the classes and not with the masses: but the, result was not quite what he expected. It did not damp the ardour of Welsh Liberals; it rather stimulated it; and so it happened that Mr. IioaLEY witnessed a demonstration of the most enthusiastic kind. The time has gone by for Lord This or Earl That to pocket a place like Newtown.

The nation does not now depend upon what Mr. MORLEY aptly called "the gilded forces"; it depends upon the people ; and *Welshmen, to their credit be it said, have with liPecial emphasis taught this lesson again and again. Mr. MORLEY went on to deal with topics of special moment to Welshmen such as intermediate education, the tithe question, and disestablish- ment—enforeing, as he did so, the lesson which cannot be too often repeated, namely, that the quickest way to these reforms is to give Ireland Home Rule. His speech was in every way worthy of him as a Liberal leader: it was worthy of Mr. GLADSTONE himself.

THE Education question was under considera- tion at the meeting of the Congregational Union, at Nottingham, on Tuesday. Those who were beginning to fear that Dissenters were not, as a body, alive to the importance of the movement which the Tories are making to bolster up the Established Church in the matter of education will now see that, when the issue is raised, Non- conformists will be found resolute and united as of old. Even the Wesleyans, leaders amongst whom have occasionally shown Conservative tendencies, have begun to be alarmed at the attack which is being made upon the Education compro, mise of 1870, and are showing that, I/ they are to be represented at all in this matter, it shall be in opposition to the majority report of the Ecrucation Commission. Dr. BRUCE, as President of the Congregational Union, took as the subject of his address—" Education free from the Creeds and control of Priests and Churches." As might be expected from the title of the topic, he took a bold and clear course ; and ruthlessly exposed the weak places in the majority report. But he did more than that ; he assailed its constituticai, and urged that it was never intended to be of a representa- tive character, or it would have had such members upon it as Messrs. Broadhurst and Burt. Giving his impression of the result of the Commission, he said :

' "The report which emanated from the majority was more worthy of the worst days of Queen Anne than of the best days of Queen Victoria. On that denominational majority would rest the onus and , the odium of this new controversy. The burden of the majority report was more and more money from the State, and more and more liberty for the denominationalists, with not the slightest intention on the part of the latter of raising any more money themselves, or of giving up any corresponding share in the control and management of the schools to representatives of the ratepayers." In these few sentences Dr. BRUCE, as it seems to us, goes to tho root of the matter. The Anglican and the Catholic party want to extend their denominational views at the expense of the ratepayers. They do not, of course, put their proposal in this naked form; but that is really what it will come to, if they are permitted to have their way. What they plausibly claim is that, seeing that Board Schools are sup- ported out of the rates, it is no more than reasonable and fair that the rates should be applied in maintaining voluntary schools. But if they would be supported from the rates, they must be prepared to accept the conditions which attach to that kind of suppport. Board Schools are really Ratepayers' Schools; that is to say, the ratepayers appoint men to manage them who are responsible to the ratepayers. Are these distur- bers of the educational peace willing to accept a ratepayers' Committee ef Management in case they obtain aid from the rates? Not a bit of it. Their -theory is that the management of voluntary schools must be left, as at present, in the hands of irresponsible denominational managers. Their , desire is to utterly ignore the great doctrine that, taxation and , representation must go together;' and it is because they ignore it that they will find, , when the question comes before the electors, that they will utterly fail. It is,to be sure, hoped that a victory may be snatched whilst the present Government is in office; and at the Conference Mr. EDWARD CROSSLBY? ALP., expressed the opinion that, during next SOSSiOn, a bill woUld be introduced based upon the majority report. It may be so, but we very much doubt whether the Tories will run the risk of being driven ' to the wall. The Dissentient Liberal, as many of us know, is a stiff-necked individual, and if we are not wholly mistaken, he is just as stiff-necked in his opposition to sectarian education as he is to Home Rule. Be that as it may, the Congrega- tionalists are up in arms and ready for the fray; for,on the motion of the Rev. J. Guinness Rogers, a resolution was unanimously adopted expressing. the opinion "that no systemof education will be satisfactory under which national funds are appro- priated to schools or training colleges which are under the solo control of denominational managers:'

PEALEERANcE Reformers of this part of the country have had a " stimulant " during the week. On Tuesday there was a meeting, in Manchester, of the General Council of the United Kingdom Alliance, and in the evening there was a great gathering in the Free Trade Hall. The presence in the neighbourhood of so many eloquent advo- cates of temperance has resulted in the holding' of a considerable number of purely local meetings ; and amongst those was one at Warrington, on Thursday evening, with the Rector, the Rev. F. W. Wims,in the chair, and Dr. LEES, the Rev. Canon HuLL, and Mr. JOSEPH LEICESTER as speakers. Sir WILFRED LAWSON presided at the Council of the Alliance, and reviewed in a charatteristically humorous fashion the progress which 'had been made during the year, referring with especial satisfaction to the defeat of the Government on the question of compensation to publicans. Mr. W. S. CAINE moved the adoption of the report, and made an allusion to local option which seems curiously at variance with a statement attributed to him the other week. He was re- ported to have said, not long since, that he did not believe that there was a single town in the king- dom that-would put local option in force if it had the power. On Tuesday, he said that, "having converted lord SALISBURY to local option, he did not think there was anybody else to convert." In another part of his speech, he said "satisfactory local option -was the direct veto." It seems pretty evident that there is more than one sense in which the word local option is used by him. Re- ferring to the phrases Permissive Bill, local option, and direct veto, Mr. WRITTAILER, of Scarborough, pointedly objected to a continual change of names. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, in the course of the powerful speech which lie made as chairman .of the evening meeting, defined local option as meaning "that in each locality the local authority shmildtlecide the question of the Iliquor traffic according to the wants, the senti- ments, and the will of the people of that district," Again, referring to the opinion of the Liberal Government of which he was a member in 1883, he said We desired that the local authority should have complete control over the drink traffic, and that the locality should determine what houses should be licensed and whether any or none at all. (Cheers.") There can be no mistake as to language of this kind, and we ven- ture to say that it is the view of local option which is generally adopted, notwithstanding any crotchet which Mr. CAINE may have on the point. Sir WILLIAM reviewed at some length the position

Mr. Parnell has the "Times.' in hand; but it is in addition being tackled by Mr. Henry Campbell, M.P., who was at one time Secretary to the Irish lewier. The "Times" has ceased to cry—" Come " It finds to its sorrow that ff 11.1; Campbe! are coming." There is a. move in the direction of increasing the salaries of the Warrington Workhouse officials. But' it is a fair question to ask whether it is wise to raise wages at a time when the price of bread is rising by leaps and bounds? As things go, before the winter is over the money will be required to provide for people who cannot afford to buy bread.

The " World " pays :—" The last literary work which Mr. Proctor, the astronomer, did was an article for the 'New York Tribune'. It was a paper on the yellow fever. A week before it ap- peared Proctor was in the grave, having died of yellow fever."

It is to be hoped ;the " World " is better inform- ed in foreign than in home affairs. It describes Lord Cross as President of the Local Governbient Board, and speaks of Mr. Ritchie (who is president of that department) as succeeding him. The " World " ought to know that Lord Cross has charge of India, and that he spends his leisure hours in looking for a "scientific frontier."

A cat is said to have nine lives; but Alice Ward, of Dublin, aged 20, and a widow, would appear to be better off than puss by a long chalk. She has made as many as twenty attempts to commit suicide, and still lives to be brought up at the Police Court. She will try ,pgain ; but we cannot hope she will succeed.

Widow Ward's last life-taking experiment was with rat poison; but the prime favourite now is carbolic acid. There is no accounting for taste; and when people contemplate suicide it is a matter of course to say their taste is depraved. It has boon suggested that restriction should be placed upon the sale of carbolic acid. But would it be of much use P Those who are bent on destruc- tion are seldom at a loss for a mode of accomplish- ing their object.

The drowning of the little ' boy Keen in the brook at the bottom of Napier-st., Warrington, has called attention to what the Coronernot too strongly called "a regular death trap." It may be that the Corporation are not directly responsible, but they will be held ,responsible by public opinion, in case of other fatalities, if they do not, after the presentment of the jury, see that the trap is closed.

Smoker- and non-smokers beware :—" A single drop of nicotine applied to the eye of a cat will kill the animal in a few minutes' A small bird will die from the inhalation of a portion of nicotine vapour so small as to be inappreciable by a fine balance. Rabbits, cats, and dogs die in from twenty to thirty seconds with less than a drop oP the tongue; and man suffers severely: only the 25th of a grain."

Miss Twining, who is a member of the Kensing- ton Board of Guardians, states that there are 64 women acting like herself in that capacity in England and Scotland. Curiously, there are two only in the North of England. Lancashire has now a chance of distinguisinnent. It would be an act of politeness to take the hint which Sit U. Kay Shuttleworth and others are giving. Besides, it would give a polish, which is much needed, to ; the average; "board."

There does not seem to be muth enthusiasm about the movement for establishing Recreative Evening Classes— in Warrington; but it is to be hoped the Committee will give the matter a fair 1, trial. They will do well to see to it that the classes are "Recreative," and thatthose for whom they are intended have a finger in the pie. Classes of this kind have been a great success in London. There is an average attendance of 6,030; and the number of volunteer workers has risen from 130 to 570.

"Noblesse Oblige has ceased to be the rule with some of the nobility. Contrary to what has been the custom, Lord Egerton declines to allow the schoolroom at High Legh to he used for the Liberals. He objects "to allow the room to be used to further the work of those who wish to dismember the empire." "Dismemberment," as a parrot cry, still survives, it seems, amongst lords of the Egerton type. He might as well talk of England being dismembered by the establishment of County Councils. However, the Liberals will survive this petty tyranny; it should have the effect of making them more ardent in the cause.

The Beauty Show at Spa, did not please every- body. Some of the disappointed fair ones were furious. One of the prize winners says :—" Some- body spat upon the dress of Mdlle. Soukares—the Gaudeloupe girl—who got the first prize, and Vilain, who obtained the last or fourth prize, whacked me with her fan and cut my arm. She had to be ejected from the place by the police, and Mdlle. Soukares and I had to fly literally for our lives." It is pretty clear from this that some of those who were "scratched " were disposed to scratch in return. They have yet to learn that "Handsome is as handsome does."

Something will have to be done in the way of punishing people who are guilty of Making bogus confessions of crime, for they give the police a great deal of trouble. There is never a murder of moment, but some drunken vagabond or other gives himself up as the criminal. -At Warrington, on Monday, a young fellow was brought up for being a deserter, but it was found that his tale of desertion was an invention. As the law does not, at present, take cognizance of offences of this class, it requires amending. The rogues who seek cheap notoriety will be disposed to "sing small" when they find that their larks may land thorn in gaol.

Sergeant Winskill, who lost:his life through fall- ing down the cellar steps, at the Hop Pole Inn, on Saturday evening, seems to have been curiously treated by his brothersergeants. Although bleed- ing and insensible from effects of the fall, and although the landlord suggested that he should be taken to a doctor, he was convoyed to the bar- racks, put to bed with his clothes on, left there, and next morning he was found dead One witness states that both the sergeants who took the dying soldier to the barracks were "the worse for drink ;" and another witness says they were "a little intoxicated." The sergeants say they were sober; but if they were sober, how account for their stupidity ? And if they were tipsy, ought they not to be punished? In any case, it was the duty of the jury to take their negligence into account, and ask the coroner to censure them.
