RUNCORN STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—III con- nection with the first Society an appropriation was held at the office on Monday. The lucky member is Mrs. W. Hedley of High-st., who is entitled to £2OO free of interest for 12* years. Sr. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC CHURCII.—SpCCiaI services, as announced in our advertising columnt, will be held in this place of worship to-morrow (Sunday). On Tuesday evening a temperance demonstration will be held in the Public Hall. POLICE INSPECTION 4T WlDNES.—Captain Ibbetson, Deputy-Chief Constable of the County, on Monday in- spected the constables in the Widnes Petty Sessional Division. The men were paraded in the Market Hall by Inspector Keighley, and their clothing and accoutrements were examined and found satisfactory. The offices, cells, and books were afterwards inspected, and were in good order. ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH WIDNES.—The anni- versary sermons were preached in this chapel on Sunday last by the Bev. Father Bonifaceof Sutton. In the morn- ing solemn High Mass was celebrated, and in the evening there was rosary and Benediction The attendance at the morning service was very good, andiin the eVening the church was crowded to excess. Collections were made in aid of the funds of the church

HEALTH OF WlDNES.—During the month of September there were registered in Widnas 82 births and 40 deaths being at the rate repectively of 32.8 and 18.0 per 1,000. There were 15 deaths amongst children under one year, and 8 amongst children between one and five years. Zymntic diseases caused ten deaths. There bad bect a few fatal ences from diarrhea and two deaths from •,;zarlq fever. There are still a few cases of fever in the district. •

&Olen OPERA COMPANY AT' naleeente.—Next Thurs- day, and two following days, Messrs. Leahy and O'Beirnes' English Opera Company will occupy the boards at the Runcorn Public Hall. The alterations made to the stage have rendered the building admirably adapted for theatrical companies, and scenery can now 'be fixed to the utmost advantage. In each of the numerous towns visited by the English Opera Company, the press have spoken in high terms of praise of the performances. Fonue Wessirert AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday night a dense fog prevailed on the river, and traffic was con- ducted with great danger. The Dukes steamer's suc- ceeded in reaching Runcorn safely, towing the usual number of fiats, but it was deemed unwise to return to Liverpool on the ebb tide. Traffic was resumed at noon on Wednesday. The schooner Mary and Jane, of Diver- sten, and the steam flat Harvest grounded in a dan- gerous position below Weston Point, but were floated without damage on the flood tide on Wednesday. Trzerr OF BLANKETS AT RIINCORN.—Before Major Hazlehurst at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Ann Hughes. a married woman was charged with havin,g,. on or about the22nd September, stolen a blanket, the property of Martin Gilligan, lodging house keeper, Cooner-st. The woman who had been an inmate of the lodging house on Monday the Ist inst.. informed Gilligan that she had stolen the blanket and pledged it with Mr. Marsh, of Church-st. He excuse was that she was hard up. The prisoner was committed to the Quer Cr Session for trial, as she is an old offender. - BRIDGE HOTEL BOWLING CLUB, RIINCORN.—The mem- bers of this club brought the season to a close on Tues- day. In the afternoon a handicap took place, the first prize being a pair of woods, given by the landlord. Most of the cracks entered, and some good games were witnessed, the last four being Messrs. R. Wright, R. White, S. Y arwood and Captain Abrams. The final was contested by R. Wright and S. Yarwood, the former running an easy winner by 13 points to two. After- wards the members sat down to an excellent tea, and the evening was spent in P convivial manner. Mr. T. Dean, the president, conducted the proceedings. NEW GOSPEL MISSION CHURCH AT RUNCORN.—The ' members of the Gospel Mission Church, Runcorn, which is under the ministrations of Mr. George Marshall, are about to erect a more pretentious edifice in which to worship. At present the congregatisns meet in a wooden building under one ;of the arches in Ashridge-st., but plans have been drawn by Messrs. Linaker and Davies,- architects, of Fmdsham, and approved by the Board of Commissionerefer a new structure capable of accommo- dating about 600 persons. This building is to be of brick, with terracotta dressings, and a frontage to A.shridee-st., and it will form a prominent and hand- some feature of the neighbourhood of Dukes Field. 'rho contract has,not yet been decided. THEFT or COAT, AT Rusiconer.—John Hillier, a boat-, man, who lives in Heath-road, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on• Monday, charged with stealing 2ttcwts. of coal belonging to Matthew Sweetman, coal' dealer, of 14 Union-st. On Saturday morning the prisoner, with several other men, were employed discharging a flat, and wheeling the coal into the yard in Heath-road. Mrs. Elizabeth Oats and Mrs. Mary Ann- Bate saw the prisoner take two lumps of coal into his house during the absence oithe prosecutor. Afterwards P.S. Gosling visited the house, and in the pantry found a large quantity of lumps f coal. Tne prisoner said they had been there for four months,and were given him for discharging.—The prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, was sentenced to a month's hard labour. THE COUNTY CORONER AND THE WIDNES POLICE.— The county coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse, on Tuesday even- ing held an inquest at Widnes Police Court. At the time fixed fcr the inquiry, only eleven jurymen had put in an anpearance and the police officers left the court to fetch the absent juryman. Shortly afterwards Inspector Keighley entered the court and the Coroner said he could not congratulate the police upon the way in which they were managing this inquest. There were only:eleven jurymen, and one officer had dtsappeared io fetch another, and the Sergeant had disappeared 'after the constable. At this point the defaulting juryman (Elijah Withineston) arrived, and explained that he had been mistaken in the time. He thought his clock was ten mirutes fast, and discovered that it was half an , hourslow.—The Coroner said it was a peculiar mistake to ' fall into; he did not understand it. .That day he had td. hold tereinquests in different partsof the county ; and , this was his fifth, and it was impossible for hire to do his work unless time was kept. The defaulting jury- man wastold to sit down, 'and another juryman was empannelled. "NATURAL CAUSES "AT WIDNF.S.—An inquest was held a' Widnes Police Court on Tuesday by Mr. S. Brighouse, touching the death of Thomas 8a11,58 years of age, of 48, Midwood-st. It appeared that the deceased was employ- ed by the Local Board as a street sweeper, and on the 13th September he was crossing Waterloo-road, when he was knocked down and rim over by a light spring cart driven by William Carney, grocer. Mersey-road. The wheel of the vehicle passed over his leg.—Carney deposed that he was only driving at the rate of five miles an hour, and said the accident occurred through the deceased suddenly turning round from the parapet just 'as the cart wee passing.—Dr. Hutchinson said he , attended to the deceased for injury to the knee joint. He ' was convalescent in ten days. He did not see him again until he died on Sunday last. He had made a post marten', ' examination of the body and was of opinion that death was the result of fatty degeneration of the heart. He could not say whether death was accelerated or not through the accident—A verdict of natural causes was returned.—Mr. J. W. Knowles watched the proceedings on behalf of Carney. ALLEGED RCIRBERY FROM A RELATIVE AT NORTON.— John Hoffiand, a young man, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with having on the 2nd rust stolen 14s. 44., belonging to John Hoffiand, of Marsh Gate Lodge, Norton. Prisoner is the nephew of the prosecutor, and had been living with his uncle fora week. On Monday night the prisoeer retired to bed the last, and next morning he went away early, stating that he had got work at the stables on the Ship Canal. Some hours later Hoffland was walking towards Warrington when he found on the road a check from the Co-operative Stores. He took it home to his wife, who at once said it was from her purse, and she then discovered that the money had been taken from the sewing machine drawer. Inquiries revealed that the prisoner had never been to the ship Canal stables, and on the Thursday following he was received into custody from the Wrexham Police by Inspector O'Donnell.—Mrs. Hoffiand said she had two lodgers in the house, who worked on the Ship Canal.—The Bench sail there was very grave suspicion that the peismer bad taken the money, but the evidence was not conclusive, and he was discharged. 'HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY, RUNCORN.—The 15th session was commenced on Monday evening in Trinity school-room. Refteshments were provided from 6 o'clock to 7.30, when the Chairman called upon the Secretary to read the report, which was on the whole a very satisfactory one.—The first item on the programme was an address by the Chairman, Mr. Philip Speakman, who set forth the claims of the institution in a powerful manner and urged all young men (who were at present members) to do all they possibly could to increase their numbers, as much benefit might. be derived by any who would associate themselves with the society. A trio by Messrs. Owen, Leathwood; and Findlow 'having been given, Miss Clara Taylor, who was in good voice, sang " Tell me my heart," and ,receiving every hearty encore, sang "Home sweet home." Mr. Bixter gave two reci- tatioris. "On the Line "and a Lancashire sketch. Then folloseed the song "Good Company," by Mr. Charles Pawned, who merited the hearty plaudits that followed. Miss Isherwood was encored for a pianoforte solo, after which Miss Preston gave "Sometimes " in a very pleas- ing manner. The ever welcome" Kathleen Mavourneen" was sung with much sweetness and expression by Mr. R. Moor, and then came a leery able address by Mr. Preston,the president of the Association. He said that a great amount of good work had been done in the Mill Brow district, mainly by the efforts of the young men who were belonging to the Association. 'Mr. Frank Eberell was next called upon for a song,entitled" Money," which he rendered aceedingly well. Mrs. W. B. Kay, who is very popular in connection with this class of entertainment, received a hearty encore for her solo on, the pianoforte; Miss Taylor next sang in a most capti- vating style Meyerbeer's song "Noble Signora" and received a well deserved recall. Votes of thanks to all in connection with the arranging of the programme, the decorations in the room, and to those who had given fruit and flowers were proposed by Mr. Lunt and secon- ded by Mr. Leslthwood. After the usual voteof thanks to the President of the Society, and to the Chairman, the glee party sang Bishop's "Good Night," yand a very , pleasant evening was brought to a close.

Si. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—OR Monday evening a harvest thanksgiving service was held in the above-named chapel, when the Rev. J. Thomas, of Liverpool, who was appointed by the Presbytery, preached an eloquent sermon. There was a large con- gregatien, and the collection was taken in aid of the Presbytery building fund. HARTLAND CHAPEL MISSIONARY MEETING, WIDNES.— A meeting was held in Oakland-st. chapel on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Wm. Newburn. The report,which was read by the Rev. J. Bryant, was of a very encourag- ing character. The meeting was addressed by the Rev. H. T. Brumwell and the Rev. T. Law. DITTON CHAPEL MISSIONARY MEETING.—ThIS mission- Nry meeting was held on Wednesday evening, and a good numbbor of people attended. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. Duxbury, of Hale Bank, and the usual re- port was read by Mr. Bryant. The Revs. E. Strutt, late missionary in Ceylon, and T. Law addressed the meet- ing, which was a very successful one, the collections amounting to nearly £2 in advance of last year.

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES.—III COG- nection with this church harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday, when the sacred edifice was hmatifully decorated with the products of the earth and suitable mottos. The Rev. R. U. Hughes, the pastor preached in the morning and in the evening the Rev. J. Davies of Warrington, occupied the pulpit. The choir under the leadership of Mr. J. Poole, rendered specially selected anthems. There was a good congregation at each service.

ALL kerb"fiLS CHURCH, RUNCORN.—Harvest thanksgiv- ing Prvices were conducted in the church of St. Michae and All Angels, on Sunday, the decorations being elabor- ate and artistic. In the monaing the Rev. J. H. Hall, curate of Weston, preached, while in the evening the vicar the Rev. A. Maitland Wood delivered an appropri ate discourse. In the afternoon the Rev. G. H. Seeley conducted a special service for children.. There was a capital congregation at each service. Mr. C. Pownall, choir master, had charge of the musical arrangements, which gave great satisfaction. STUBBS' FURNITURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, Id.. 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road. Bus: _

SERIOUS ACCTDENT AT A WIDNES SOAPWORE.S.—Joseph Owen, of Oakland-st., met with a serious accident on Monday night, at theworks of Messrs. Gossage and Sons. Owen was in charge of some silicate chambers, and they being very slippery, he missed his footing and fell about ten feet, on to a platform which broke his fall ; he then fell to the ground, a distance altogether of about thirty- six feet from where he was standing. Three of his ribs • were severely crushed, and he received a scalp wound also. Dr. McDonnell was called in, and Owen is now proaressing favourably. _ .

SAV-AG'i ASSAULT AT WID'NES —At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., John Devlin, 80, Midwood-st., and Catherine Devlin, servant to Mrs. Pilkington, Wellington-st., were brought up on remand charged with unlawfully and maliciously causing grcvious bodily harm to a man' named Archibald Sullivan. of 9, Nelson-st., by striking and beating him, on the 2nd October inst. The com- plainant had received such injuries that he was unable to appear,' and Dr. Hutchinson sent a certificate stating that the complainant was still very ill. Catherine Devlin wa released on hail, herself in the sum of £BO and two sureties of £25, the case being remanded till next Wednesday.

- WIDNES ALKALI (winners of gold medals) v. Comunce- now TEAM (A. Hllftoll'S).—This match was played on the Lowerhous.-lane ground, on Thursday evening, for the bsnefit of John Smith, •he blind newsagent of Widnes. The Combination kicked off against the wind. Just at the last minute, Hufton's men obtainkl a goal. The result, was that the Combination won by one goal five .minors, to Alkali one try and four minors. The teams were :—Widnes : D. Dutton. J. Donoghue, J. E. Farrell, J. Hartle, W. Beasley, T. Wilkinson, T. Hughes T. Gregory, J. Gandy. J. Dolan, Barber, E. Gordon, H. Cosgrove, T. Wheelan, andiJ. Bingham. Combination team: I). Brannan, P. ()Wen; E. Broome, J. Clarke, George Howard, W. Bradshaw. J. Holt, J. Hogan, H, Bingham, G. Hewitt, Beaker, J. Cearns, J. Taokies, A. Robinson, and M. Rooney. , PRESENTATION TO THE VICAR OF WIDNE.S.—A meet- ing to welcome the Vicar (the Rev. G. H: Garrett) and his wife, after their wedding tour, was held in the Waterloo-road Scholls,on Friday evening,by the teachers of St. Mary's and St. Paul's Sunday Schools. There was a tea provided, and during the entertainment which followed two very interesting presentations were made to Mr. and Mrs. Garrett. A Church service and hymnal, fitted in case, beautifully lettered with the followi .g inscription, were presented by Mr. L. Kill- cross to Mrs. Garrett :—" Presented to Mrs. Garrett, with the best wishes of the Widnes Parish Church Sun- day School traebers." A handsome Oxford Teachers' Bible was also presented to the Vicar, with a similar inscription. Mr. Garrett, in reply, said he was much pleased with his reception since his advent to Widnes. He had received kindnesses he should never forget. BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.—On Wed- nesdav &dies' evening was "provided in *connection with the al:nye-filmed society in Brunswick schoolroom, which was tasteffilly laid out as a drawing-room. The programme was one of choice selection, and the glee party sang "The Fisherwife's song," "Wreathe ye the stns," and "Good-night" in excellent style. Miss Cook contributed a recitation, and Miss Jones sang "Ow pro nohis." both ladies doing full justice to their particular items. Mrs. W. B. Kay gave a solo on the pianoforte.) whilst a selection from Shakespeare—" The Taming Of the Shrew "—was rendered with equal success by the lady members. Mrs. T. Leach sang" Should he upbraid." and Miss Simkin "The Soldier's Dream" (encored), whilst Miss C. Ltitler recited "Maud Miller," and the trio party, consisting of Misses Jones, Crosby, and Simkin, gave a capital rendering of " Memory. ' Miss Simister officiated as accompanist. There were about 300 persons present, and the proceedings were of an enjoyable character. FUNERAL OF Mn. • Wivrox, OF RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Parish Church, on Wednesday, there was interred the remains of Mr. John Wil•on of Greenway- road. The deceased gentleman who had attained the age of 79 years, was an old resideht of Runcorn, having about 60 years ago occupied the position of a doctor's assistant. He afterwards carried on the business of chemist and druggist but rmired in favour Of his son Many years ago. He was a man that was much respect- ed in the town for his amiable qualities and honest pur- pose. Previousto conveying the body to the churchyard the Rev. Mr. Benson. superintendent Wesleyan minister, conducted abrief and solemn service at the house. Preced- ing the hearse, and two coaches containing, the relatives of the deceased gentleman, there walked in procession the Rev. Mr. Benson, Messrs. J. Simpson, T. Simister, James Dutton, R. Norman, G. Yarwood, R. Evans, J. Abrams and. Samnel Taylor, senior. The bearers were Messrs. James Higgins, 'James Wright, J. Lunt, and T. Molyneaux. The service in the church and at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. J. Holden, curate. THE RENOWNED RITNCOR-N RELISH is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which render it of most valuable assistance in the digestion of food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Runcorn.— Adrt. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. E. Imison presided and there , were present Messrs. J. Handley J.P. H. Coleburn, R. Morris, W. Mellor, W. H. Rogerson, and W. F. Salkeld (surveyor.)—The report of the Finance Committee,adop- ted en the motion of.mr. Handley, stated that the fees received during the past month amounted to £31183.6c1., and rent amounted to £8 15s. 6d.; total £4O 14s. Wages amounting to £9 Bs. had been paid and the balance £.31 6s. deposited into the bank.—The Chairman reportedl that the interments for the six months ending Sept. 25th numbered 165 ; corresponding period last year, 157: increase R. The fees received during the same period ' amounted to £lBB 75.; last year £173 12s. 2d. ; decrease £.5 ss. 2d.—Mr. G. Hunt was granted permission to letter gravestones in the cemetery—Mr. Coleburn stated that some time ago there was a basket of flowers stolen from a grave in the cemetery. and Mr. Blease, the injured party, thought the Board should prosecute. He had dis- covered a case ',exactly in point. It was McGough v. Lancaster Burial Board.—Mr. Mellor said: That amounts to this: we allow them to place wreaths &c. on the graves but we are not responsible for their safe custody. —The Chairman said he was sure the Board wasmuch obliged to Mr. Coleburn for his information. It con- firmed the view they had held that the Board were not responsible.—The Clerk having reported the result of the ratepayers meeting re Weston burial fees, the proceed- ings terminated. It has been a most successful one notwithstanding very unfav- ourable weather. The realistic picture and brilliant representation of the siege of Malta has been a great attracticn. All those intending to avail them- selves of the opportunity to see the siege will need to do so within the rext two or three weeks. REV. G. S. But, unhappily, not because it has been decided to discuss the question else- where, but because of ill-health Mr. Reaney has been deeply affected by the illness and recent death of his only brother, and he is under medical orders to rest. Much sympathy will be felt with Mr. Roney in this affliction." "THE Jolla BULL" Boor, twelve months' wear 'thwart- -lee4. Usually sold at 13/6, our price 10,65.—Ilaynes', Horse- market-st., Warrington.—Adrt. ANOTHER CASE OF CHILD MUTLPEIL—A Case of child murder similar in its features to the one at Haydock has occurred at Bowdon On Thursday: Elizabeth Booth was remanded at the Altrineham Police Court on a charge of having drowned her daughter Ada, aged 15 months, in the river B .Bin, at Bowdon. on the 9th October. The child was found in the bed of the river by a police officer who went in search of it after receiving a communica- tion from the mother to the effect that she had been attacked by two men, one of whom threw the baby into the water. -

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—At Warrington Police Court,on Tuesday, a Runcorn man named John Jones was charged with having ill-treated a horse, by working it when it was not in a fit state. Constable Meecock saw two horses pulling a boat up the river, and noticed that one of them was very lame. Defendant, on being spoken to, said that he was. aware the animal was lame, and he was glad it had been stopped. Subsequently the horse was examined by Inspector Greatrex, R.S.P.C.A., who said that it was exee-sively lame on, the off fore foot, and it had also a diseased fetlock joint. As deferdant had been locked up all night, he as dismissed, but the Bench expressed the hope that the owner of the horse would be proceeded against. FOR Boors AND &tons of every description go to Haynes', Horsernarket-st., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. _ . .

The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Thursday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, I'. Hall, Stokes, Whitlow, Weir, Parr, Wallington, Heywood, Taylor, Bmndreth, Jackson, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). The CHAPLAINCY.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the appointment of the Rev. Mr. Bennet' to be chaplain of the Worktiouse. The LUNATICS.—A letter was read from the Rev. „T. W. N. Tanner giving notice that he would, at the next meet- ing of the Board, move that a committee be appointed to visit the lunatics from that Union at Chester Asylum. '

THE FUTURE OF THE SANITARY ACTHORITY.-.-MT. Stokes said he should like to ask the clerk if the Rural Sanitary Authori.y would be abolished when the County Council was established.—The CLERK said it would not, but it was expected that Rural Sanitary Au hOrities wouldbe abolished in 1890.—Mr. ISICINTYRE said the Dis- rict Councils would take the place of the existing autho- rities. Mr. WHITLOW: It would be a good thing if they would take the Local Government Board with them. (Laughter).

AN'EXPLANATION BY MILWALLINGTON.—Mr. WALLING- TON said he should like to say a word with respect to the proposed appointment of Dr. Gastaldi as Chaplain of the Catholic inmates of the Workhouse, which was considered at the previous meeting. He had been challenged with shirking the business last Board day, but he wished peoplb-would only just consider and not bo so rash in their judgment. He was sorry that he had not been at the meeting, but the reason of his absence was that he was called to Liverpool, last Board day, on business, and he could not get to the meeting. He thought that the explanation lie had given ought to be satisfactory. There was a ques- tion he should like to ask; was his absence from the meeting commented upon on the last Board day P—The CHAIRMAN did not think that matter was mentioned.—Mr. WALLINGTON said he should like that to go into the papers, as it had beeri stated in one of the papers that his absence had been commented upon. APPOINTMENT OF NIIRSE.—It was stated that there had been six applications for the post of nurse at the Workhouse, and two of the applicants had been asked to appear before the Board that day. These two were Miss Humphreys, Knutsford, and Miss Ainsworth, Wrexham, After the candidates had boon interviewed Miss Humphreys was appointed by twelve votes to three.

RESIGNATION OF THE REV. J. LOCKWOOD.—A letter was read from the Rev. J. Lockwood resigning his position as guardian for Halton. He thanked all con- nected with the Board for past kindnesses.—Mr. SroxEs proposed, and it was agreed, that he Local Government Board should be asked to sanction the election of a successor to Mr. Lockwood.—Mr. TAYLOR moved that a letter be sent to Mr. Lockwood, expressing the regret of the Board at his resignation.—Mr. BaaNnarriz seconded this proposal,remarking that Mr. Lockwood had been a. VE ry useful member of the Board, and one who always tttended committee meetings much better than some ethers that he knew. He was a great loss to the Board. —Mr. PARR: I think we have lost a very good member. This was all the business.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

S. MARY'S CHURCH, WIDNES.—The harvest thanks- giving services in connection with this place of worship were continued on Sunday. The Vicar preached in the morning, and the Rev. William Edmondson, curate-in- charge of Farnworth, preached in the evening. In he afternoon a special service for children was held. Offer- tories were receivdd in aid of the re-slating of the church.

..... Havron PARISH CHURCH--The annual services of thanksgiving for the harvest were commenced in this church on Friday evening, and the decorations were on the usual scale of magnificnce. The pulpit was occupi- ed by the Rev. J. Lockwood, who preached a most appropriate sermon. The services were continued on Sunday, when the sacred edifice was crowded. The collections which were made on behalf of the Rev. J. Lockwood realized nearly £l4. HUTCHINSON-STREET PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. Wiresiss.—This chapel was beautifully decorated on Sunday, on the occasion of the annual Services of thanks- giving for the harvest. There was a good congregation at both morning and evening service and the preacher was Mr. R. Pinches, of Chester. In the afternoon a sevice of song entitled "The basket of flowers" was rendered by the choir and scholars. Mr.Sarnuel Drought read the narrative. On Monday evening there was a fruit banquet. The chair wa.s occupied by Mr. Thomas Rollason and appropriate addresses were delivered by the Rev. R. G. Hughes and other friends. A programme of musical items added to the enjoyment of the large audience. The collections on Sunday realized £6 2s. 9d. AN UNPROMP•ING BOY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police C,ourt,on Monday,John ThomaeGuest (10) of Speke, was charged with stealing is. belonging to his father, Henry Guest. It appeared that on Saturday night Guest left some money in his trousers pocket, next morning he missed a shilling, and the prisoner had left the house. On returning the boy denied having stolen the money, but subsequently admitted his guilt and said he had spent die shilling in purchasing toffy.—About a mond' ago the boy was sentenced to receive six strokes with a birch rod for stealing £8 6s. 6d., and the father said he had no control whatever over his son, who was leading the younger children astray. Beating him was not of the slightest use.—The Bench sent the boy to goal for 14 days. afterwards to be confined five years in a reformatory school. ROBBERIES FROM WinNes MARKET.—EIIen Byers, of 39, Sankey-st., was brought up on remand at Widnes Police Court on Monday, charged with having on the 29th September stolen three shawls and a frock from a stall in the market, the property of Alfred Walker, draper, Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester. The prisoner was also charged with stealing a shawl from a stall occupied by Benjamin Golstent, of Liverpool. The details of the case have been previcAisly published. The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprisonment--a month on each charge.—There was a third case of steal- ing numerous pairs of boots, but the police were not prepared to proceed at present—William Byers, husband of the last prisoner; was also sentenced to a months' imprisonment for haying on the 29th September, stolen a shawl, the property of Alfred Walker. BRUTAL ASSAULT AN A WOMAN AT WIDNES.—OB Mon- day, at Widnes Police Court, Thomas Gibson, of it, Peel-st.. was charged on remand with maliciously caus- ing grievous bodily harm to a woman named Margaret Howard, of 11, Peel-st. The prosecutor stated that on the 29th September she was walking home, when a woman named Roach invited her into the house where the prisoner lives to have a cup of beer. Mrs. Reach dragged her into the house, and _when inside the prisoner struck her twice on the face with his fist and the wounds caused bled very much.—Margaret Ilynan, aged 14 years, of 19. Wellington-st , corroborated this statement, and said Mrs. Howard did not give the prisoner any provocation, nor did she ',reek any of his property. Both were in drink at the time.—Dr. Hutchinson de- posed the, he had attended to the woman's injuries. She had suffered severely from two clear cut wounds near the rights Te. and he was of opinion that she had been stabbed with some moderately, sharp instrument. A blow from the " punch " produced, if stack in a slanting direction, would inflict the injuries.—P.C. Hol- brook deposed to apprehending the prisoner on the night of the offenee. In answer to the charge, he said" I did not stab her, but I struck her with my. The "punch "was found in his possession.—For the defence two witnesses were called, who stated that Mrs. Howard entered the house without permission and called the ' prisoner lad names. She also overturned a table and smashed a quantity of crockerv.—The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool Quarter; Sessions.

A DRUNKEN SPREE AND ITS RESULTS AT WIDNES.— Mr. J. Knowles. solicitor, appeared before the Widnes magistrates on Monday on behalf of George Hunt, of Church-street, who surrendered to his bail to answer a charge of having caused grievous bodily harm to Walter Davies by kicking him in the side and chest.—Mr. Knowles said the men would settle the matter with the consent of the Bench, as the prisoner had offered to pay £3 for a fortnight's wages to the prosecutor for loss of iime, and he (prosecutor) was willing to have the matter hushed up so as not to send the man for trial.—Dr. Hutchinson said he had attended to the man since he had received the injuries. He examined him last Sun- day week. Complainant had then great paint in the left side, and one of his ribs was slightly staved inwards, He considered that considerable violence had been used. There was pleurisy over the left lung, but it had since disappeared, and a week would elapse ' before he SIMS better.—Walter Davies was called, who said he did not want to pressahe ease against the man. He was in his lo Igines when Hunt came in and kicked him. saying his wife's son had sent him to do that.—Mrf Knowles said the two were having a row over some mutton chops, and they were both in drink at the time, and the young man was now sorry for 'what he had done. There was nothing against his character before, and he regretted this ease had occurerd.—Mr. Gossage The question about him being drunk at the time is no excuse; we cannot excuse him if he. was in drink.— Hunt was fined £5, or go to gaol for two months i n default of payment. 'PRESENTATIONS AT THE MRRSEY MISSIONS. RUNCORN. —The workezt of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions were entertained to tea at the expense of the Liverpool Committee on Monday evening. Afterwards meeting was held under the presidency of the vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, who said he felt a great interest in the work carried on at that place, because those who worked on the canal in boats, the most important industry in the town, and their sailors, who were the means of bringing employment to the town, deserved all that could be done for them, not only , morally bit. spiritually. (Applause.) Anyone Who was engaged in the work of helping boatmen, their wives and children, and erideavoured to do what they could for sailors who came to the port, ought to have the ' support of the clergy- He wished Mr. Shaw every success in his endeavours to obtain a more commodious and convenient mission-room, and also a recreation room for sailors. (Applause.) Mr. Allen, on behalf of the Sunday school teachers, and workers in the Runcorn mission, proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the Liverpool Committee for supplying so admirable a tea. —Mr. Reid seconded the !notion which was carried by acclamation. Mr. W. A. Tomlinson (hon. secretary to the Mersey Missions) acknowledged the vote.—A number of presentations were then made.—On behalf of the choir and friends, Mrs. Mame presented Mr. Thomas Tonks with a toilet set. Mr. and Mrs. Richard Shaw, who have been recently married, were the recipients of a china tea service, a flower vase and a bouquet. from the choir and members of the Sunday school. Mrs. Allen made the presentation, and Mr. R. Shaw replied. Mrs. Hulme then handed Mrs. R. Shaw a set of jugs. The most important event was the presentation to Mr. Fred Mack' of a silver m: dal and cer- tificate of merit. awarded by the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Soeiety for his bravery in having jumped into the Mersey and rescued a boy from drowning under circumstances recently narrated. Mr. Shaw, the mis- sionary made this presentation, and addressed a few appropriate remarks to those present. Mr. Mack suitably acknowledged the gift. Mr. Shaw then handed 3s. 6d. to Mr. Wm. Byfield, this sum having been forwarded by the society, in recognition of the timely assistance he had rendered Mr. Mack at the time of the rescue.—Mr. Andrew Christian, a Norwegian sailor, made a speech, and Mrs. Norbury gave two recitations. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.p: RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Thursday. Col. tsliton presided, and there were also present Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Stokes, Parr, Lewis, Wallington, Ileywood, Weir, W. Hewitt, Brandreth, P. Hall, H. Linaker (clerk); W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk); Dr. Adams (medical officer); and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.) FRODSHAM ARREMITS.—It was reported that Frod- sham was in arrears to the extent of £360 in the payments of the special Sanitary rates.—Mr. AARON moved that the overseers of that township be summoned for not paying this call.—Mr. MclNrrna seconded the proposal which was agreed to

OYERCROWDING.—Dr. Adams reported a case of over- crowding at the Main-st., Haßm.., in a cottage on Sir Richard Brooke's estate. The family consisted of two parents and six children, and four lodgers were taken in, these latter causing the overcrowding. The maxi- mum sleeping accommodation was only sufficient for three lodgers and he suggested that one lodger. be should dismissed. He had also to report an over- crowding case at Walton Inferior. on cottage premises near the Stag Inn, belonging to the Wilderspool Brewery Company. The number of occupants was 9, six of whom were children, while the maximum accommodation for sleeping purposes only provided for six adults.—The Inspector also referred to these cases in his report, and it was decided that notices for abatement should be issued. THE SHIP CANAL AND THE AUTHORITY'S Sawints.—Some discussion took place with regard to the manner4n which the outfalls of the Authorities sewers would be effected by the Ship Canal, and it was decided that Mr. Wells, late engineer of the Weaver Trust, should be asked to examine the outfalls and report thereon to the Authority. It was stated that expenses incurred by the Authority in this respect would fall upon the Ship Canal Company. . This was all the business.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. A special meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were presents the Rev. Dr. Gasteldi. Dr. McDougall, Messrs. F. A. Lake, T. Handley, S. C. Beckett, E. Imis‘n, and G. Moss (clerk.)

div.head: FINANCFS.
div.p: THE FINANCFS.

The Clerk read the balance sheet for the past twelve months, which showed that the balance in hand on September 27th, 1887, was £lOB us. 4d. ; the grants from the Committee of Council on Education was £352 13s. ; payments by ratingauthority, £750; school fees, £223 13s. 9d.; books and other articles sold to children, £7 2s. 4d. ; income arising from other sources, £l9 95.; total receipts, £1,459 9s. sd. The expenditure was as follows :-Salaries of officers of the Board, £217 12.5. 6d. ; legal and other expenses of administra- tion £B4 14s. 3d. ; salaries of teachers. £467 12.5. 2d. ; books, apparatus, and stationary. £37 14s. 3d. ; fuel, light, cleaning, and repairs, £lOO les. id.; rent, rate. taxes, and insurance £7 15s. 9d.: other expenses of maintenance, £l5 7s. Bd. ; contributions towards maintenance of boys in industrial schools, £lB 17s. 5d ; repayment of loans, £124 6s. 2d..; interest on loans £lBl 15s. 7d., balance in trea.surer's hands £l9B Os. 9d.: total expenditure £1,45995. sd. The out- standing liabilities of the Board-loans from the Public Works Loan Commissioners-amounted to £4,753 19s. 2d.-The Chairman moved the adoption of the statement and remarked that when the Board established schools of their own the rate rapidly increased to 4Ad. in the £, but he was glad to say there was a reduction in the rate to 3id. the Board having this year received £750. The working of the compulsory clauses of the Education Act, of which all the schools in, the town derived benefit, cost the ratepayers 2d. in the £, and the extra 2id. in the £ was involved in working the Board schools. He noticed that the Board had received , about £BO more than the previous year; also that ' the school fees paid had increased by £4O; and, when they had got the schools into a state of efficiency, he hoped to see the rate as low as 3d. He con- sidered the schools were a very small burdert on the ratepayers, considering their excellent character, and that the suns of £5OO was expended in their erection.- Dr. McDougall seconded the motion, and asked what was the cast of administration.-The Chairman replied £321, and if they were in Board schools that was the only amount for which the Board would be liable. The repayment of principal and interest on loans was £306 is. 9d., but of course that amount will gradually be reduced.-Dr. McDougall said the figures showedthat practically the schools were paying their own way.-The Chairman : The amount of money received out of the rates towards the maintenance of the schools is only £45 18s. 103.-The accomrs were passed.

div.p: IF DOCTORS FAIL, WHAT SHALL AVAIL? [North Wales Observer, August 24th.] EDUCATION, we are told, makes the thief a better thief, just as it makes the divine a better divine. The nineteenth century has, much to its own cost, proved the truth of this adage. Science and art have made great strides during the present century —but little more to the advancement of virtue than to the advantage of vice. To prevent the full growth •of truth and purity, there has always .been the baneful influence of the false and the impure; and to spoil the reputation of the genuine there has been constantly the fraudulent imitation. It is therefore not surprising that in an age in which there is such a mixture of the true and the false, of the genuine and the counterfeit, there should grow an abundant crop of scepticism as well as • incredulity. Nor ie it unnatural that by far. the

largest number of those who are unprincipled enough to face humanity with a sham, should choose the weaker and most credulous portion of mankind—the suffering humanity—as their victims. If anyone is easily beguiled, it is that man who has been driven to despair through illness. But as the number of counterfeit articles increase, so does the scepticism of the public increase. It becomes, therefore, one's duty when he finds I out the genuine article to make it known for the benefit ef others. It is with this object that we give publicity to the history of a somewhat miraculous cure of kidney disease by the use of Warner's SAFE Cure. The patient was Mr. Thomas Hughes, living at 10, Northgate-st., Camarvon, and well known among the husdic fraternity in Wales under the coin de plyme " Isalun." Mr. Hughes called at our office a few weeks ago, and stated how miraculousli he had been cured of a malady that was thy by day rapidly wrecking his constitution. We asked him whether he had any objection to our , sending a representative from this office to obtain some details of his cure, and he replied that, in the interest of others, he would be very glad to do it. This week our representa- tive waited upon him, and being aware of Mr. Hughes's indifferent state of health for the past two years, was agreeably surprised, upon entering the house, to find him so very hale and hearty. Having been acquainted of our representative's business, he willingly consented to give all the details in reference to his case. For 35 years Mr. Hughes had been in the service of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and his engage- ments with them terminated about nine months ago owing to his being incapacitated by ill-health to further discharge his duties. His complain, was kidney disease, symptoms of which appeared considerably over a year ago. His doctor closely examined him, but prescribed nothing beyond an advice to keep still and to seek repose. However, seeing that things did not improve in the least, the doctor asked Mr. Hughes whether he desired to con- sult another medical man. Mr. Hughes said he should like to have another doctor's opinion, and consequently a consultation was had with one of theleading physicians of the town, who, after an examination of the patient, pronounced him to be suffering from two complaints, and gave precisely the same advice as his brother prac- titioner, but prescribed no med "Did this advice prove of any benefit to you ?" our representative asked. "No," said Mr. Hughes, "things got no better." He then proceeded to state how he came across an adyertise- ment of Warner's, describing how a case perfectly identical with his own had - been cured, in one of the Welsh papers published by us—the Genedl. This came about one day when he was in great agony. He confessed that he never, previous to this day, had thought anything of this medicine; but being in acute pain, and finding himself gradually sinking, he decided to invest in a 4s. 6d. bottle. He took in all four bottles of the value 4s. 6d. each, and one bottle value 10s. 6d. These had the effect of causing the pain in his back and hips to gradually subside, and finally, through an eruption in the bladder, he obtained perfect relief. " I suppose von feel yourself a very different man now ?" suggested our reporter. "Oh ! yes, very different, indeed.' "Do you feel that your health gen- erally is improved ?" "Yes, I have changed completiv." "Before you resorted to 'Warner's SAFE CURE, what was your own opinion of your case, Mr. Hughes ? " "Well, to speak candidly, I thought there was no help for me; and, from what I gathered, that was the opin- ion of the doctors too." Some more facts of a less direct character were elicited in the course of the inter- view, which was closed by Mr. Hughes saying that he had recotrtmended the medicine to a well-known gentle- man in the town, who suffered from the same com- plaint; and, speaking from what the gentleman had told him, he could say that the first battle taken by him had been productive of good results. It may be inter- esting to some of our readers to know that Mr. Hughes is in his 72nd year, and is now in the enjoyment of the best possible health.

lionnay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton). Alder- man Harrison, and Councillors Greening And John Pierpoint. SeHoor, ATTRIVDANCE.—George Travis, hamper-maker, Rollins Green, was summoned for having neglected to send his child to school, and was fined ss.oncluding costs. _ _ _

IhraEGISTE.I.ED LODGING-HOUSE. —Catherine, Morton, charged on remand with keeping lodgers without having her house registered, was now dismissed, she in the meantime having got rid of them. DTSORDERLT CONDUCT. John Fallon and Patrick Dooley, youths, were each fined 3s. 6d. for having been guilty of disorderly conduct in Bakehouse-yard, on the 30th September. WaRNING TO PARENTS.—Two boys, named Walter Ball and Wm. Shelmerdine, were each fined 3s. 6d. for having thrown stones, to the danger of passengers, in Museum- at., on the 2nd inst.—Another lad, named James Tickle, was ordered to pay the costs of a sum..nons, he having let off fireworks- in Grappenhall-road, on the 27th :September. DOG WITHOUT LlCENSE.—Elizabeth Green, St. James's- et., was fined ss. and costs for keeping a dog without a license.

--- • A DEsrnorrivz EIGSBAND.—John Fleming, living in Rose-yard, was summoned for wilfully setting the chim- ney of his house on fire. P.C. Mather said that defen- dant had quarrelled with his wife, after which he began to burn the furniture.—The Bench fined him ss. and costs, or seven days. CHARGE AGAINST AN INJURED CABMAN.—Arthur Mill- wood, cab-driver, Dixon-st., was summoned for furious driving in Horsemarket-st. on the 30th ult. Mr. Russell, manager for the Warrington Carriage Company, ap- peared in answer to the charge, and said that Millwood was unable to appear, having met with an accident which it was feared would end fatally. He hoped the Bench would dismiss the case. The Chief Constable explained that the man fell off the Stockton Heath omnibus on Saturday night, and asked for the summons to be adjourned for 14 days.—The application was granted. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Francomb and Mr. E. G. Guest. AN UNTRUE CONVESSION.—Henry Scoging, a young man, was charged with having falsely confessed himself to be • a deserter from 11M.S. Penelope, stationed at Harwich. He made a confession to that effect to three Warrington policemen, but it was found that no one answering his description could be traced in the official register kept by the Admiralty. As he had been in pri- son under remand for a week, he was discharged on pro- mising to leave the town. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman Chandley. _

A DRUNKEN NAVVY.—Thomas- Longdon, a Ship Canal navvy, was fined ss. or seven days, for having been drunk in Winwick-st. on the previous night. He went to gaol. WIFE ASSAITLT.—MichaeI O'Loughlin, 17, Portland-st., was charged with having assaulted his wife on Tuesday morning. Complainant stated that she went out to work on that morning and defendant sent a girl after her, to ask herfor money for drink. She sent 21d., and went on a little way when she was overtaken by the defendant who came to ask for more. She refused to give it to him and he knocked her down, and kicked her. The Bench ordered the defendant to find two sureties of £lO each, to keep tl7l, peace for six months. . .

TUIIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. DRUNICENNESS.—For this offence Elizabeth Almond was sent to prison for fourteen days.—A man named Thomas Mochin was brought up on a charge of drunkenness, and on a further charge of having asked alms. He was sent to prison for a month. . FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall.

A RAILWAY STATION NUISANCII.—John Whittaker, a youth, was charged with having trespassed on the railway station premises at Bank Quay, and with having refused to quit when requested to do so. It was stated that he was in the habit of importuning passengers to be allowed to carry their luggage, and of using abusive language when his request was not complied with. He was fined ss. and costs, or in default of payment, imprisonment for seven days. A QUARIZEL.—John Dooley was summoned for having sesaulted Mary Hughes, on the Bth mat, and _Mary : Hughes was summoned for having assaulted Mary Aft& bearing evidence the magistrates fined

John Dooley ss. and costs, and dismissed the charge against Mrs. Hughes. THass.Ts.—Kate Griffin, summoned for having used threats to Sarah Ann Edgar, was dismissed. MAINTENANCE ORDER—William Flattery consented to pay Is. per week towards the maintenance of his son in an Industrial School.
• WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. Tuunsmky.—Before Mr. John Brock.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Sinclair. no fixed abode, was fined ss. and casts for being drunk and dis- orderly. Similar fines were also imposed upon Flenry Ecob, Church-st. Farnworth ; Ann Edwardson, Derby- road, Farnworth ; John Ford, 2, Witt-road, and Homy Smith. Railway-st.—Robert Birchall, 32, Viaduct-st. and John Fitzgerald, Charlotte-st. were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creating breaches of the peace A STRAY Doo.—Rachael Brown, Appleton View, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing her dog to be at large 6 unmuzzled. _ _ .

WANDERING Cows .—Walter James Houghton' of Lunt's Heath, was fined ss. and costs for allowing four cows to stray. AN AIISENT MILMAUAN.—Henry White, a young man, was remanded on a charge of absenting himself from the 3rd Lancashire Militia. ALLEGED THEFT OF POTATOES.—John Dwerryhouse, an old man, was remanded on a charge Of stealing 361bs of potatoes the property of Margaret Stockton, market gardener, of Speke.

DRUNKENNESS.--Jane Drury was fined 10s. and costs, for being drunk and disorderly in Church-st. He was also charged with damaging the that of P.C. Brew, to the extent of 2s. 6d., and he was ordered to pay 75.6 d., or go to goal a further seven days.—Alice Hampson, an unfortunate, made her 14th appearafice. and was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in St. John-st. RUGBY.

WIDNES HALTON VIEW WANDERERS V. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH (Jununts.)—This match was played on Satur- day at Halton View, and resulted as follows :—Halton View, 2 goals, 2 tries,4 minors ; Parish Church, 2 minors. At half time the Wanderers were 2 goals to nil. WIDNES V. MOSSLEY (" A " TEANis.)—A very interesting match was played between the above teams on Satur- day, on the Lowehouse-lane ground, before a fair number of spectators. Widnes just succeeded in scoring after a hard struggle, but their opponents proved the stronger, the visitors winning by three minor points. When the whistle blew for the last time the game stood—Mossley, one try and three minors, to Widnes one try. RUNCORN " A" TEAM V. PIVERPOOL HORNETS.—PIayed at Sefton Park on Saturday, before a large crowd of spectators. The home team were not fully represented, and played one short. Dabell kicked off for the Hornets, Woods returning into touch at the half-way. Runcorn at once began to 'press, and after a minor had been con- ceded to them, Can-ley secured and, after a grand run, gained a try, Woods landing a goal. On change of ends the Hornets went away with a rush, and had very hard lines in not scoring; Booth kicking the ball dead. After the drop out, through a mistake of the home full back, Andrews scored, Woods again doing the needful. From now till call of time the home team tried hard to score, but without avail, Runcorn winning a very easy and pleasant game by 2 goals, 1 try, and 2 minors, to 3 minors.

WIDNES v. MOSSLEY.—A match between the two teams was played at Mossley, on Saturday. The weather was fine but rather cold, and Widnes presented only a weak appearance, Woods, Plumpton, and Hughes not being present. Mossley made a goodshow, putting their best team in the field. The contest was witnessed by a large number of spectators, who were loud in their enthusiasm, the greatest excitement prevailing all through the game, and more especially towards the close. In the first half Widnes played against a strong wind, but had the slope to their advantage The ball was immediately rushed to the home territory, and in a. few, minutes from the start J Bingham dribbled over the line, and secured the first try near the goal posts. Farrell next made a splendid attempt at goal, but failed in registering the major point. This infused the home team with renewed vigour, and from the result of a bit of good passing Joe Winterbottom obtained a try from an excellent point. The place kick was put in the hands of Lawton, and again the attempt proved a failure. Subsequently the Widnesians invaded the home quarters, and Wright passed to Parkinson, from thence to Clarke, and the latter ran in, in excellent fashion, ground the leather over the line near the touch. , Farrell's kick did not tend to improve matters. Half- time followed with the score :—Widnes, 2 tries, Mossley, I. try and 1 minor. In the second half, with the advan- tage of the wind, the residents had slightly the best of it. Batley managed a try, and three minors were ceded to Mossley. while the Widnesians, who had hard lines on. several occasions, scored two minors. When time was called the result stood: Widnes, 2 tries and 2 minors; Mossley, 2 tries and 4 minors. Teams :—Widnes: Full back, S. Bingham; three-quarters. Hartles, Clarke, and Parkinson; half-backs, Farrell, and Wilkinson; for- wards, Smith, Kiddie, Barber, J. Bingham, Johnson, Wright, Williams, Gordon. and Holt. Mossley: Full back, O'Neill: three-quarters, J. Winterbottom, Lawton, and Pointon ; half-backs, Billing and Neild ; forwards. Ashworth, Cox, Barker, Batley. Meakin, J. Newley, and Walker.

• nu/geom.( V. KeignAL Hoax Runcorn met the Kendal Hornets on the home ground on Saturday in the presence of between 2,000 and 3.000 spectators. The Hornets were not up to their full strength, neverthe- less they showed the usual good form. The Runcorn men, however, were equal to the occa ' sion and they added another success of a brilliant nature to this year's I list. Kendal kicked oft, Walker doing the honours. The sun at the time was full in the face of 'the strangers. The game was of a very fast nature, and a minor was quickly scored from a scrimmage near the line. Faulkner obtained a try for the home team, and„this was con- verted by Crompton into a goal, amidst ringing cheers. The passing on behalf of Runcorn was really splendid, Wainwright, Faulkner. Hughes, and Riley discharging their duties in a commendable manner, and a strong attack was made on the visitors' territory. Crompton essayed to drop another goal, and his success was very nearly complete. Scrimmage after scrimmage after- wards ensued, and both teams worked hard to score, the passing on the part of Runcorn being accomplished i with a neatness which created a furore of excitement. I Neither side, however, scored. Battersby made a dodgy ' run, but was collared before he could carry out his intentions, and shortly afterwards Kendal was corn- pelted to touch-down. At half-time the score stood:— Runcorn 1 goal 5 minors, Kendal 1 minor. On the resumption of play scrimmage seemed to be the order; and for some time very little advantage was conspicuous for either team. Dribbling, passing, and tackling were resorted to on behalf of the visitors, Troup, Arms rong, and Walker giving a good example of what could be done. Gayter shortly afterwards scored, and Brazen- dale essayed to convert the trial into a goal, and his kick was in the right direction; but, owing to the wind being against him, the ball fell near the posts, and no goal was recorded. Shortly afterwards a minor was scored for Kendal, and Wainwright obtained a minor for Runcorn. The result of the game was :—Runcorn, one ' goal, two tries, seven minors, to Kendal Hornets, two minors. WasniNwrox "A" TEAM v. WIGAN ROVERS IsT.—The Warrington " A " team journeyed to Wigan on Satur- day to play their first fixture with the Wigan Rovers, the holders of the Wigan Junior Challenge Cup. Owing to the late arrival of several of the home team a start was not made until 3.50. With a slight wind in their favour J. Bate (who took the captaincy in the absencel of Mr. Adamson) licked off for Warrington, and the forwards dribbled into the home half, Pilkington return- ing into touch. Unsworth broke away from the line-out, and good passing between Lawless. Bibby, and Daniels was witnessed, Anderton returning the ball to Boscow, whose kick was charged down, and the home team had a good chance of scoring, but they failed to take the opportunity, Warringtdi saving near the line. The Rovers pressed for a time, Lawless getting the ball away twice only to see it returned each time from free kicks by Anderton. The Warrington forwards, however, by short dribbles gained considerable ground, then Lawless passed to Bibby, who kicked nicely into touch near centre. Lawless next passed to Daniels, who kicked well, and following up strongly collared the full back near the line, the Rovers averting fur- ther danger by touching down. Anderton dropped out, Holmes saving in mid field. Some splen- did passing now took place among the War- rington forwards, and a try seemed almost cer- tain, but the ball was kicked dead. Hough drciped

out, play again being taken into the home 25, where Lawless transferred to Bate, this player throwing to Bibby, but the pass was intercepted by Anderton, San- son sending the ball into touch. From the line-out the oval was dribbled to Hutchinson, who kicked across the field, and Daniels getting possession, went off at top speed, and after handing off one or two opponents gained a try. Boscow took the place kick, but failed to improve the point, halftime being called with the score standing, Warrington, 1 try and 2 minors, Wigan Rovers nil. On change of ends Ellison restarted for the home side, but through an infringment of the off-side rule a scrimmage was formed in centre. Ellison next broke away from the pack with a splendid dribble, and picking the ball up ran past all but the full back, but Lawless ran after him and succeeded in bringing him down near the line. The Rovers pressed, Warrington saving by touching down. Immediately after the drop out Ellison, Hough and Grundy got off wihasmart dribble, but Bibby neutralized by kicking into touch. Ellison again was conspicuous, and Hogan passed to Pilkington, who took an ineffectual drop at goal, the ball going dead. Bate dropped out, play resting in neutral ground, but a neat pass from Bate to Sanson enabled the latter player to kick into touch near the home line. Warrington now strove hard to augment their score, but were prevented by the safe tackling of the home backs. Their efforts, however, were eventually, rewarded, as from a scrim- mage opposite the goal posts Lawless secured and passed to J. Bate,who dropped a splendid goal. With the excep- tion of a dead ball for the home team, nothing further was scored up to the call of time, when the final score read—Warrington, I goai, 1 try, and 2 minor points; Wigan Rovers, 3 minor points. Teams —Warrington:: Full back, Boscow ; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Bibby, and Sansoh ; half backs, J. Bate (captain) and Lawless ; forwards, Molyneux, Donoghue, Thornley, Reyes; F. Bate, Beard, Holmes, Eyes, and Unsworth. Wigan Rovers: Full back, H. Fair; three-quarter backs, Andertun, Hutchinson, and Pilkington ; half backs, Crompton and Hogan; forwards, T. Hough (captain), Grundy, Sherington, Speakman, Worthington, Horsfield, Connell, Waitson, and Ellison.
WARRINGTON v. ASKAM-IN-FURNESS.
Askam brought a strong team to Warrington on Satur- day, to meet the local premier team, and a toughly-con- tested game was witnessed by a great number of spectators

The visitors started operations against the river goal. Soon after starting Case had a shot at goal, and forced a minor. The drop out found play at the half-way flag, and from a line out here Evans secured possession, and passed splendidly to Massey, who, unfortunately, over- ran the ball, and thus a good opportunity was lost. Gradually the visitors removed the oval out of danger until Case, by judicial kicking, transferred operations to the home quarters. Creaghan and Dillon both came through a pack here, but whatever ground was gained was quickly lost by a brilliant run en thepart of Kendal. Barnes foiled Lewis in hi k endeavour .o part with the oval ; and the next point of interest was a strong run by Sharpe. Antrobus next got away, and ran half the length of the field, but eagerness lost a certain chance of scoring. However, a minor resulted from his good run. Evans met the drop out, and quickly drove his adversaries back to their quarters. A quick passing movement, in which all the home division shone, was loudly spplanded, and after Evans and Kendal had exchanged Icicks, Massey, by a well-judged pun. placed the game at the Askam quarter-flag. The punt, would not be denied, whilst the Askam division was equally as obstinate in not allowing their oppo- nents to cross the line. Littlewood next became promi- nent with smart following up, and from a pack at the Askam quarter-flag Speakman threw Ito Evans, who made off at top speed, and, dodging his opponents with precision, wound up his brilliant run by securing a try. Fair Turner, however, failed to notch the premier point. Nothing daunted by this reverse, the visitors played up manfully. Antrobus tried to effect an opening, but found an obstacle in Troug,hton. Evans again made tracks for the visitors' goal, but this last effort was quickly neutralized by a strong run of Sharpe's. Lewis saved his side from disaster by a useful kick, until Antrobus was seen threading his way through his oppo- nents, and Kendal endeavouring to relieve his side had his kick charged down by Fair Turner, who had the poor satisfaction of seeing the ball gravitate into touch-in-goal. Fair Turner and Kendal both put in goad runs from the drop out, but no addition was made to the score up to the call of half time, Warrington then leading by! try 2 minors,to Askam 1 minor. Turner restarted from centre, and for the first few minutes it required the visitors' best energies to prevent the " vrirepullers" from scoring. , This they did with credit, for after Barnes and Appleton had each been applauded for their brilliant play, Case came away from the thick, until his career was cut short by the smart tackling powers of Massey. From a pack on the home line the home forwards by an extra effort placed the game at midfield, and Evans, passing to Massey at the right moment, again placed the visstors' goal in jeopardy. Case and Pope responded in brilliant style, and a wide pass to Barnes having been intercepted by Trou,ghton, the Warrington quarters were once more the scene of operations. Dillon tackled Sharpe before he could get away, and the Warrington skipper was once:more to the fore with a neat dribble along the pop- ular side. Speakman, Evans, and Antrobus indulged in, some pretty transfers, and certainly ought to have been credited with a better result. The visitors' custodian Lewis, cleared his lines at a critical point of the game, but the relief was only momentary., Barnes next got in a lucky kick, and Kendal, Barnes, Lewis, and Antrobus exchanged kicks, which finally settled play at the visitors' quarter flag. Antrobus, had indeed, hard lines soon after, and although play was in the Askam twenty-five the greater portion of this half, the Furness team kept their opponen s at bay, Warrington winning by the narrow margin of bne try two minors to Askam- in-Furness one minor.

• Broadly speaking the chief features of the game were the dribbling of the visitors and the passing and tackling of the home team. On several occasions Askam carried the ball at their toes from the scrinpnages and some- times it needed a good deal of smartness in the home backs to stop progress On the other hand Warrington showed much superiority in passing while their tackling was of the highest order, and was often called into request owing to the large size and great physical strength of several of the Northerners who made the most of these qualities. It is worthy of note that in the second half not a single point was scored, and this of itself points to the fact that it was a very closely con- tested game, though it is but fairto say that even in the second half Aslcham were generally the defending and Warrington the attacking team. For Warrington Evans played a brilliant game and forward Dillon, Little. wood, Nevins and Cragan showed conspicuously. Of the visitors Case, Pope, Lewis, and Ashburne were most prominent. Teams :—Warrington: Appleton, back; Massey. Evans, and Barnes, three-quarter backs ; Antrobus and Speak- man, half-backs; W. Dillon (captain), Fair. Turner, Ashton, E. Dillon, Povev, Bandies, Littlewood, Nevins, and Creagan, forwards. Askham-in-Furness : Lewis, back; Kendal, Troughton, and R. Sharpe, three-quarter backs; Pope and Case, half backs • J. Sharpe, Anderson, Ashburner, Dixon. Wo xiburn, Whittaker, Tomkinson, Boucher, and OsVdiston, forwards. Referee, Mr. Naylor, Wigan.

• NOTES BY THE WAY. A great deal of interest has been aroused during the past season as to the respective merits of H. Synyer, the mile amateur bicycle champion, and F. J. Osmond, the great southern rider; and a match over a distance of a mile was arranged between the two to take place in con- nection with the National Cyclist's Union Benefit Meet- ing which was held at Kennington Oval, on Saturday After riding for about three laps something went wrong with Synyer's machine, and he had to dismount, a fresh machine being found for him. The race was then recom- menced, and after a magnificent finish resulted in a victory for the champion by about three yards. That Synyer is the better man may now be said to have been settled conclusively. J. IVorrall, of Warrington, who, as a Manchester contemporary observes, "has developed into a sprinter of no mean order," carried off the first prize in the 120 yards handicap at the athletic festival of the Salford Harriers, on Saturday. He had a start of 81 yards. Hollins Allen another Warringtonian who is now well into the first rank as a cyclist, took the premier place in the one mile bicycle handicap at the same gathering. Allen was scratchman, and although between 30 and 40 yards in the rear in the last lap he overhauled all his opponents and won by four yards amidst the applause of the great gathering of spectators. The St. Helens (Rugby) club completely "snuffed out" Audensha.w ley no less than three goals, five tries, and seven minors to nil. ' The match was played at St. Helens, and, as the score indicates, the visitors were overpowered from the commenCement, The home team I have shown remarkably good form during the season ' and obtained a good advantage in arranging for abou, Urn of their first fixtures to be played at home. Theirt team is about becoming nicely settled; and if they keep up to their present standard of play they should render a good account of themselves in the West Lancashire Cup ties. The St. Helens Recs. journeyed to Tylde.slev, when they met the West Lancashire Cup-holders. The Recre- ation team can boast a more powerful "15 "than ever represented the Club previou.slv, and they were ex- ' tremely unlucky in sustaining their first defeat of the season at Tyldesley. A special train was run io that town, and about 600 supporters accompanied the team.' ISome of the flees players seemed dead out of form, and the team as a whole lacked the combination they had shown lathe earlier matches. Notwithstanding this, however, the visitors had rather the best of the play, and if they had been favoured with a corresponding amount of luck their defeat by one try and three minors would have been turned into a victory. The St. Helens Association team met l3romborough Pool in the first round of the competition for the Liver- pool and District Senior Challenge Cup, and obtained a creditable victory of three goals to one. The tie was decided at New Ferry, and the St. Helens men acquitted themselves splendidly,showing a better passing and com- bined play than in any other match this season. Earlestown had as their opponents a strong team from Leigh, who were welcomed on the Mesnes ground by a large number of spectators. The home team tried a new

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.

man in Isherwood. who was said to be of the Bell's Tern-- perance Club, but his "trial" was not a satisfactory one to the spectators generally. The game was a very good and evenly-contested one, Earlestown securing the verdict by two goals to one. The Haydock team journeyed to Bolton with a weak eleven, but they were strong enough to beat the Bolton Rovers by two goals to one. The team of Irish cricketers arrived at Queenstown on Thursday in the Anchor line steamer City of Rome, rafter a verf successful tour in Canada and the United States.

The thousands who gathered at the Irwell Lane ground on Saturday to witness the match, Runcorn v. Hornets, had a magnificent treat. The game was universally voted one of the best seen at Runcorn. Both teams know how football should be played, and had evidently made up their minds to act up to their knowledge, for the game was open, fast and exciting from start to finish. There were several superb displays of passing on both sides, and the backs and forwards played together so harmoniously and well that to particu- lance would be invidious. Towards the finish Runcorn succeeded in .getting the upper hand, and within the last ten minutes scored two tries through really sterling play,and this earned a substantial and well earned victory. After the match the teams sat down to an excellent repast prepared by Mr. and Mrs. Riley at Bridge Street Coffee House and the healths of the respective captains were proposed and duly honoured. In responding, Mr. Walker paid Runcorn a very high compliment. There were, he said, few teams that could teach the Hornets any points in football, but they could always learn a wrinkle or two when they met Runcorn. Crompton made two excellent drops at goal, one of the shots striking the cross bar. Widnes could only succeed in making a draw with Mossley in their match on Saturday. Fred Plumpton, the captain, was unable to take his position through illness, and this circumstance doubtless had its effect upon the game.

div.head: WARRINGTON RECREATIVE EVENING SCHOOLS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON RECREATIVE EVENING SCHOOLS ASSOCIATION.

On Monday evening a meeting of this association was held at the museum for the election of officers, and the promotion of the objects of the Association The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided, and there was ROL a large attendance. • The MAYOR said he was sorry that he was not very well acquainted with what had taken place heretofore with regard to that association, but he had had the pleasure of reading the lecture which was given by the Rev. Mr.. Stevenson, and he quite tbonght that it was an important matter indeed for the youths of the town that evening classes should be formed of a kind such as had been sug- gested. He thought it was an important matter that boys, when they left school, should have somewhere to go to in the evenings, to help them to retain that which they had obtained at school. It was, unfortunately, often the case that a boy who had left school had no place to go to ; at all events he was not attracted to any'place, and the conse- quence was that what he had learnt at school was entirely lest. Evening classes such as had been suggested would, he thought, attract boys and not only enable them to retain what they had already learned, but add to it and aid them very materially to become good members of society. At present they seemed to be knocking about the streets, hard- ly knowing what to do with themselves in an even- ing, and very often, unfortunately, they went into ' places which it would be much better to keep out of. He remembered that when he was secretary of the Warrington Mechanics' Institution they used to have evening classes, and he was quite certain those classes did a great amount of good for the youths of the town. In fact he knew many men of eminence now who had been raised to their pre- sent position through those evening classes (Hear, hear.) He should be very glad so far as he was concerned to assist all he possibly could in supporting such classes, because he felt they would be of great advantage to everybody in the town (Hear, hear.) The Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON (lion. sec.) saia he had written to the Hon. Miss Wilson-Patten asking her to become president of the Association, but he had received a reply saying that she was afraid she must decline, as she should not like to become president without showing more interest in the association than she would be able to do living at such a distance. He had also written to Mr. and Mrs. T. C. Parr asking them to be vice-presidents of the Association, and they had replied that they would have much pleasure in accepting the position. Mr. Parr also sent a cheque for £lO. Mr. F. Monks had replied to a similar request in a long and interesting letter expressing his willingness to be a vice- president. Mr. McMinnies asked to be excused, but remarked *at the objects of the association appeared to him to be excellent. Mr. and Mrs. Beamont also declined the honour of vice-presidency. He (Mr. Stephenson) had seen the Rector, and he and Mrs. Willis would be glad to become vice-presidents of the association. He had received notes of apoh6gy for absence froin the Meeting from the Rev. S. Wilkinson and Mr. 51. N. Houghton. . - —--

It was then decided, on the motion of Mr. T. MORRIS, seconded' by MY. HODOSONS, that Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Parr, the hector and Mrs. Willis, the Mayor of Warrington and Mr. F. Monks, should be elected vice-presidents of the association. It was also decided that the following 1 gentlemen should form the committee :—Rev. Morley Stevenson ; Messrs. Buckton, jun., Elodgsons, Jordan, Madeley, T. Morris, R. Pierpoint, C. Twiss, D. W. Finney, and Stansfield. In the course of sonae discussion Mr. JORDAN suggested that employers of labour should be asked to use their influence to get the lads employed by them to attend the classes ; and Mr. T. Morris said that circulars might be sent round to manufacturers and other employers. He also wished his own name to be put down for £5. (Applause.) The Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON said there Were two or three things in his mind that he should like to mention. The first was the question of teachers which would have to be considered. They should not only require teachers in the elementary but also in the recreative subjects, and gentlemen mould assist them by naming anyone who would be willing and able to give instructions in any of , the subjects he had mentionedin his address a few nights ago. Then there was also the question of subjects. In his address he bad mentioned a good many subjects, not with the idea that they were going to teach them all, but with the idea that they might make a good selection. And then if the thing was to be a success they would have to take a liittle trouble in making it thoroughly well known to the children and their parents. The question of schools Would also have to be considered. They could not start recreative classes in all the schools of the town, and a good deal would probably depend upon the wise choice of schools. He had had a conversation with the Rector, and it appeared that he had already had it in his mind to start evening classes, and he was only too willing to fall in with the ideas of the association, and would be vein?. gra eful for any recreative instruction which they might supply in his school. They should also bear in mind that Mr. Jordan was conducting a night school this winter again, and that there was a night school at'lleath-side. It was decided that further arrangements should be left to the Committee, and the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding.

OBJECTS OF THE ASSOCIATION. Mr. C. MADELET," has issued the prospectus of the Recreative Evening Schools Association, in which he says it has been suggested that, as a commencement, the managers of some of the elementary schools should be invited to establish evening classes, under Govern- ment inspection, and' to accept the offer of recreative instruction made by the Association. The objects of the Association are as follows :—" 1. To promote the establishment of evening schools for the igstrudtion of boys and girls, above the age of 13, who' are not in attendance at any day school. 2. To endeavour to increase the usefulness of such schools and render them attractive to the pupils, by the addition of recreative and practical instruction to the teaching usually given In reading, writing, and arithmetic. The subjects to be taught in the additional classes will generally be selected fvoin the following list :—Book-keeping, cookery for girls, elementary science, modelling in clay, musical drill, needlework (hat-trimming, fang needlework, cutting. out, &c.), shorthand, singing, slbjd-work for boys, wood carving for boys. The delivery of popular lectures, illustrated with the lantern, is also part of the plan."

WAGES IN THE COAL TRADE.—The South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire coal masters on Thursday advanced the wages of colliers five per cent., making thick coal colliers 3s. 6d. per stint, and thin coal 2s. 7d. The advance takes effect on Monday next. This action has averted a strike, as the men's notices expire on Saturday. Notices have been given by 17,000 colliers in Derbyshire for an advance of ten per cent. Up to noon, on Thiirsday, 30,000 notices for a 10 per cent. advance had been given by miners in West Yorkshire.
