div.head: ALLIANCE MEETING IN 3UNCHESTEIt
div.p: ALLIANCE MEETING IN 3UNCHESTEIt

Sir William Harcourt presided on Tuesday night at a great meeting in the Free Trade Hall in connection with the United Kingdom Alliance. After referring to the evils of intemperance—evils whioh, he said, had come prominently before him as Home Secretary—he avowed himself a supporter of the principle of Local Option. The strength of the temperance cause, he said, had increased with successive extensions of political power. The strengo of the movement came from below. On this question it was the masses who had converted the classes. There were temperance reformers who would prefer universal compulsory prohibition, but in mat- , tors of that kind he thought it wise to proceed slowly and safely. If they attempted too much they would risk all. If they were to impose prohibition upon localities to which it was repugnant, they might produce a dangerous and mischievous reaction. Alluding to the question of compensation, Sir William said that a more extraordinary, a more unjustifiable, and amore mischievous blunder never was made than that which was made by the Government. The compensation clauses inspired hopes, expectations, and claims which were never thought of before, and difficulties were created in the settlement of the question which never ought to to have been . raised. He gathered from recent local decisions, accepted apparently even by the trade itself, that the idea of a I Wed right had been given up. The country had escaped a great risk. If the claim had been maintained, it would have involved the expenditure of at the very least £200.000,000. He believed no more would be heard of the vested interest doctrine. It was perfectly plail and beyond dispute that the magistrates could refuse to renew licenses on any grounds they thought sufficient, as they did in the Over Darwen case. From that he argued that it was intolerable the community should not be placed in a position to do the same thing. He emphasised the fact that the right of the people to control the liquor traffic was established by the concession of both the great parties now-. That, he said, could never be revoked. All they. had to do was to insist that that principle should be carried into effect. Mr. T. Fry, M.P.. Mr. Samuel Pope, Q.C., Mr. Allison, M.P., and other speakers addressed the meeting, and resolutions were passed calling upon the Legislature to combine with the people in rid- ding the nation of the curse of the drink traffic.

, • NEW BOOKS, &c. " Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry' is 4he title of the issue for October of Mr. Walter Scott's admirable Camelot series. The selections are made and the work edited by Mr. W. B. Yeats, who supplies an introduction which is as racy as it is instructive. The contents are classified under the following heads :—Trooping fairies, solitary fairies, ghosts, witches and fairy doctors, saints, priests, giants, &c. Some of the tales are in the ballad form; but they are for the most part prose narratives which smack of the soil. They are altogether quaint, and make an interesting volume. In the Great Writers we have the Life of George Crabbe; by Mr. T. E. Kebbel, M.A. It is not to be , denied that Crabbe as a poet has been echpsed" by ; men of a later generation, but he has written much th as is picturesque, vigorous and truthful. It is worthy of note that men like Sir Walter Seott and ,Cardinal Newman could read and re-read his faith- ful verse. It is not always elegant but it is always instinct with life. Mr. Kebbel tells the story of the poet's career, (which was a very remarkable one) in a very pleasant fashion. "Chaucer, selected and edited by Frederick Noel Paton," reaches us amongst the Canterbury Poets. The introduction is a careful piece of writing, and tells us pretty, much all that is known of the . father of English poetry. I He was a man of mark in his time and played many parts. He was at one period in Parliament as Knight of the Shire of Kent, and was buried in Westminster Abbey, on his death in the year 1400. The selection covers most of the poems and tales as to which there is no dispute, and forms an attractive book. Thera is a catefully prepared glossary fo the use of those who stumble over "early English." "The World of Adventure" is the title of a new publication, by Messrs. Cassell, which promises to be a great success. It will be a practical illustra- tion of the adage that "truth is stranger than fiction." Part I. to hand, is stirring and crowded with excellent illustrations. It is accompanied with a large presentation plate, handsomely printed in tint, and entitled " On the Brink of the Preci- pice." The Magazine of Art for October has for fron- tispiece a remarkably fine etching -by Smillie of F. A. Bridgman's liorsemarket in Cairo: Mr. F. Wedmore has an appreciative paper on John Sell Cotman, which is adorned with some capital Bins- trations of his works. "Art in the Theatre," by Mr. Lewis Wingfield, is also illustrated. There is a splendid engraving of the late Frank Hall's portrait by himself; Mr. Walter Crane continues the "Lan- guage ot Line"; Mr. W. J. Loftie contributes "Kensington Fifty Years Ago "(illustrated) ; and there is an illustrated paper on the Kepplestong, collection by Mr. James Dow.

• The current issue of the Woman's World is an unusually strong one. Lucy M. J. Garnett leads off with a thoughtful paper OR "The Fallacy of the Equality of Woman." " A Pompeian Lady" (amply illustrated) is followed by "Elementary School Teaching as a Profession"; and "The Lace-makers of Le Puy" (illustrated). We have, too, "A Woman's Friendship—Mary Stuart and Mary &ton "; and several other interesting papers, with the usual record and illustration of the latest fashions. The Official Guide to the Great Western Railway Company, published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., is a most interesting volume. It takes the reader from the starting point at -Paddington station through some of the most lovely scenery and ancient towns in the Kingdom, going west as far as Penzance, across Wales, and as far North as Manchester and Liverpool. The numerous maps are in themselves worth the shilling that is charged for the volume; and there are, besides, innumerable views of noted objects of interest. The text has been carefully ' prepared /with a view to giving the largest amount of information in the space allotted to each town. Cassell's Magazine has an abundance of good things, amongst which may be mentioned :—Love Affairs of some Famous Men; a Preacherfta Jest- book; the Art of type-writing; Some things we say and do in America; On being out of order; What to wear in October, &c. "The Quiver " is in no wise lacking with its numerous religious papers and stories, all well illus- trated. The Rev. George Brooks contributes a paper on "Christ—the Gentle Worker." "Recent Missionary Adventures in Africa" is dealt with by Professor W. G. Blakie ; and "Our Special Corres- pondent" has a paper on "East end poverty." The continued stories are "In her own Right," and "The Beauforts of Beatrice Gardens."

"Little Folks," for 6-ci-Olier, has a brilliant coloured frontispiece, with the title of " Waiting for his share." The serial stories are "King Pen- guin Land," and "Little Odelity." There are be- sides numerous short tales, sketches, and bits of verse, with a profusion of well-executed illustra- tions.

We have also to hand, from Messrs. Cassell & Co, the current parts of the following important works: —Encycloptedia Dictionary; Dare's ; Illus- trated Shakespeare; Dictionary of English History; Familiar Wild• Flowers ; and "The Sea—it's stirring story of adventure;peril, and heroism." Part 24 of the History of Lancashire. published by Mr. John Heywood, brings the record of Man- chester Parish down to last year. An account is given of the Whitworth Pail( and Institute pro- posals, the Ship Canal, and of the Jubilee Exhibi- tion. There is a plan of Manchester and Salford as they existed in 1750. and a view of "Ole Manches- ter" as seen at the Exhibition. The numller proceeds to give the history of Ashton-under-Lyne parish aspart of the Hundred of Salford. The work sustains the reputation it has attained for thorough- ness.

"Illustrations," edited by Mr. Francis George Heath, begins a new volume with the issue for October. It is what it professes to be—" a pictorial review of knowledge ;" and it is due to say that both as to text and illustration it is sqlid and good. Considering the price— three pence—it is a most remarliable production, and should command a large sale.

WAItRINGTON TEMPERIaCE FEDERA-

- The annual meeting of this Federation was held on Thursday evening in the Co-operative Hall. The Rector of Warrington- (the Rev. F. W. Willis) pre- sided, and there were also present on the platform the Rev. Canon Hull, Northampton; Dr. Lees,Leeds; Mr. George Leicester, late M.P. for West Ham; Revs. S. Willsinsen, J. J. Longhorn (hon. sec.), G. D. Wray, Philips (Orford), G. Anton. G. a Young, Es 11. Jackson, J. Warnock, W. Graham, T. Easter- ling, Jackson (Parish Church) ; Councillor H. Roberts ; Messrs.. R Garnett, N. B. Percival. E. 'Miss, J. Gandy, W. Coates, W. Roberts, W. Smith, T. Hardy (Liverpool), and J. W. Hall. There was a large audience present, the hall being thoroughly filled, and the meeting was of a most unanimous and successful character. The meeting having been opened by prayer, The CHAIM/AN said he saw that he had been put down for an address but he hoped they would take his presence rather than his words as a guarantee of his deep interest in their object of meet- ing that evening. He felt the very deepest interest in the temperance movement, and it was a very great pleasure to him to see such a large meeting gathered together there that even- ing. He felt it a great honour to have been asked to take the chair, a great privilege to be allowed to take any part in the work of temperance. (Applause.) He felt it was his bounden duty to' try to do all he could for the furtherance of that move- ment, and he had wished very much that their meeting should be opened with prayer because he felt so deeply that it could only be by dependence upon God that they could look for any great and lasting results. He thought there were three great reasons why they should all do their utmost to promote temperance. First of all, for their own sake—for their highest spiritual interests, because he felt sure that they were endangering and imperilling their highest and eternal interests by the abuse of intoxicating drinks. Secondly, for their neighbour's sakes. Nobody could help seeing and deploring the awful effects of drunkenness, and it was theidbounden duty to do everything in their power to prevent that abuse. He grieved to think that it was not only grown up men but young men, and he was afraid it was sometimes not only men but women and young women, who were liable to that temptation, and anybody could see for themselves the awful results, the misery and the suffering that followed from it; and therefore it was their bounden duty to do all in their power to promote the cause of temperance And, thirdly, for God's sake. They might sometimes say that it did not matter what they did themselves if their neighbours did not suffer, but they must remember that they were not their own—that they belonged to God, and that they had to give their body, their mind, and their soul to the service of God. The time was very short even for the longest liver, and they must do all they could not only for their own sakes—to save their own souls—and not only for their neighbours' sake —to help them temporally and spiritually—but for God's sake during the short life He had given them —to use their talents, their money, and their time and everything they had in the service of God. And so, wfor these three great reasons, he would press upon them all, and,he would wish himself to do, their very Utmost in the cause of true temper- ance. (Applause.) He then called upon Mr. Langham to read the report. Rev. J. J. LANGHAId said he should like to state he had received apologies from the Rev. Father Thompson, St. Mary's, Latchford,. the Rev. W. Brooks, and the Rev. J. Yonge who,no doubt, would have been with them had it not been for illness. Ho shOuld also like to make one remark in reference to the report he was about to read. It was the first annual report of the Warrington Temperance Feder- ation,but that Federation was started in May, 1887, and therefore the report treated of &rather longer period than a year, the reason being that they had found that the autumn was the best time in the year to hold their annual meeting. He should also say that the report was cnie which was shortly to be presented to a meeting of subscribers and his object in reading it that night was because is had been thought by the Committee desirable to bring the work of the Federation more directly before the notice of the town, as they wished to enlist the sympathy not only of the few subscribers that there were in Warrington but of everyone who had the cause of tempera nce at heart, and in fact, of every Englishman and English woman who would do what they could to remove the terrible curse that was afflicting their country. (Applause.) Mr. Langli am then read the report as follows ' "It is with feelings of deep thankfulness that the Csantnittee present the first annual report of the War- rington Temperance Federation. This organisation was, it may be remembered, the outcome of a circular issued in February, 1887, by the clergyof all denominations in the Borough inviting all who were known to be interested in the temperance cause to a Conference. At this Con- ference it was decided to form a central temperance association, to which the various local societies in the Borough should be invited to become affiliated. The objects of this association were declared to be as follows —(1.) The 'promotion of total'abstinence principles amongst all classes of the town and neighbour- hood. (2.) The promotion of temperance legis- lation. (3.) The uniting of the various Temperance Societies in Warrington by central meetings, monthly as far as practicable. (4,), The arrange- ment of local meetings so as to harmonise the dates. (5) The extension, as far as possible, of Temperance Societies within the area. (8) The encouragement of united missions in various parts of the town and neigh- bourhood. (7) The formation of a strong and amalgamat- ed temperance choir. (8) The provision of counter attractions to the public house. The inaugural meeting of the Federation thus formed was geld in the Public Hall on May 9th, 1887. when addresses were delivered by the Rev. the Hon. Canon Leigh. Rector of St. Mary's, Brya.nston Square, and Major Waterton, a Edinburgh. This meeting was a tlaorosigh success. Nearly every denomination in the borough was represented on the platform, and a convincing proof was thereby given of the act that the moral forces of the town are entirely on the side of temperance. During the summer months that followed the inaugural meeting little indoor- work could be done. The work was, however, main- tained by a series of open air meetings that were well aell attended. On June 13th, 1887, and following ay five days' open air mission was conducted by Messrs. Hardy and Smithe, of the United Kingdom Alliance. In addition to work such as this for the dissemination of temperance principles, the Federation has striven, as far as possible, to prevent any incre.ase of temptation. At the Brewster Sessions, both in 1887 and in 1888, deter- mined efforts were made to obtain new licenses in dis- tricts already over-exposed to temptation, and in which a canvass undertaken by the Federation last year showed that the people concerned were strongly opposed to the applications. The Federation on both occa- sions opposed the applications in court, •in 1887 by solicitor' in 1888 by counsel, and on both occa- sions opposed them successfully. (Applause.) It is true that at the las, sessions two new applications were granted by the Licensing Committee, but on the appli- cation of Mr. Ridgway, acting in behalf of the Federa- tion, this decision was subsequently reversed by the full bench of magistrates. (Applause.) On Jan. 27th, a meet- ing of ladies was called together by the Federation, and a ladies branch was formed. Its main object is to under- take rescue Work, besides generally acting as the hand- maid of the Federation. A committee of ladies has been formed, one of whom, (through the courtesy of the Chief Constable) attends the Police Court every week and enBeavours to influence those who, have been con-. victed of drunkenness. Of other important meetings held, should be noticed one on February 7th in behalf of the United Kingdom alliance, which was addressed by the Rev. Canon Barker, rector of Maryiebone and J. H. Raper, Esq., and another held in the ;Co-opera- tive Hall, on May 29th, to protest against the 1 Licensing Clauses of the Local Government Bill. The 'account thus given of the work of the Federation gives a very inadequate idea of the work done. The new organisation is becoming more than ever a centre of temperance thought and work. It is ever ready tosend a helping hand to fellow workers in the good cause, and many a local meeting has been helped during the year by speakers sent from the Central Association. InAssu- ing this report the Committee desire to express their deep sense of gratitude to Almighty God for the measure of success that He has given them, and their deep conviction that, under His continued guidance, the great cause of emancipation from the drink curse, must go on and prosper." (Applause.) Mr. W. ROBERTS read the balance sheet of the Feder- atidn w,hich showed that the expenditure had been £56 75., leaving- aThalance in hand of £2 ss. 11d.

div.head: letter to the Obitor.
div.p: letter to the Obitor.
ST. PETER'S PARISH..

Sir,—l have much pleasure in stating that a most generous response has been made to my appeal, which you so kindly inserted in your last issue. The Rector of Warrington writes—" I wish much to do all I cart my- self, and to encourage others. But there are difficul- ties. The income of this benefice has fallen consider- ably, and the expenses on entrance have been very great. I will, however, give £5O unconditionally to- wards the building of the church, and £5O more pro- vided the remainder of the required amount is raised at once." I sincerely hope that all Churchmen will show their appreciation of the Rector's liberality, by meeting his generous offer with a like liberal spirit. For 14 years this churchless parish, densely populated and wretchedly endowed, has been a blot on church work in Warring- ton. Now is the time for Churchmen to come forward, and take away this reproach.—l remain, GEORGE DANIEL WRAY. 16, Salisbury-st.

div.head: SELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: THE SELECTION OF MAYOR.

Sir,—l cannot help thinking that members of the Warrington Town Council have queer ways of doing business in more respects than one. What seems one of the queerest of queer things to a simple " outside " intelligence like mine is that of the old Council selecting the new Mayor. This is what appears to have been done last Friday night when about half—and I should say, speaking broadly, the influential half—met in ", Caucus " to settle business with which they properly had nothing whatever to do. The selection, in fact, and in law, rests entirely with the new Council as it may be constituted by the rabipayers at the elections on the first November, and the meeting of Friday night was guilty of an imperti- nent and persumptions usurpation. It is an insult to the new members to have one of their rights taken from them in this unjustifiable fashion, and they will certainly be amply supported by public opinion if, when the legally-appointed time comes for the election of Mayor, they entirely igncre the decision of last Friday's hole- and-corner conclave.—Yours, &c., Warrington, Oct. 10th, 1888.
CITIZEN.
LODGERS AND THEIR VOTES AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—At the Revision Court held a fortnight ago the Bar- rister, I noticed, made some rather strong remarks with regard to lodger claims that had been put in, and it would appear that the words were addressed to Liberal claimants only. The cases enumerated below will dissi- pate this illusion, and show that the Tory claimants were deep in the mire. In the only case which is particu- larized in the report alluded to, it can be proved that the evidence upon which the claim, was rejected was inaccurate, and that the claimant had good graunds for his declaration. Several lodger claims had been made by the Conservative agent, in which the claimants stated, and the statements were attested by declara- tions, that they were paying their rent to persons who, i as a matter of iact,had been n their graves for months, and the names were erased from the list. The Barrister said he supposed the claims had been made out by the agent from the old register, but there ought to be more care taken in those cases. ,A lodger claim was also made by the Conservatives on behalf of George Wain- wright, who stated that he had the sole use of a bed- room. It was shown that the family consisted of father and mother, two brothers, and two sisters, and there were only two bedrooms in the house. The claim was disallowed.—Yours, &c.,
ONE WHO KNOWS.
THE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

Sir,—The unsatisfactory condition of the Society has called for some remarks from those interested in its wel- fare, and I think that the questions of "A member" are worthy of some consideration. The Ist, respecting the president and vice-presidents, is one for the secretary and treasurer to dispose of. At the same time I think Dr. White is deserving of the- thanks of the Society for his guarantee to . .

wipe off the debt. I cannot see that the gentlemen —excepting Messrs. John White and Reynolds—take such a lively interest in musical matters beyond sitting on the presidential bench and in the dress seats at the concerts. The 2nd question,—The Conlinittee—" Are they truly representatives of a Musical Society ? " I should say not: They may represent a "Choral Society ; " that is al?. Withent alluding in any way to the musical qualifica- tions of these gentlemen I think we may safely say that their efforts to make the Society a success have been a failure ; and as the Committee has been composed of the same gentlemen—wi h few exceptions for many years, those interested in the welfare of the Society are perfectly justified in asking for a change, or the addition to their number, of the names of local gentlemanwho are taking a lively interest in music, of whom we may find several close at hand, who, I am sure, would prove very useful members. But then the strong objection which Dr. Hiles has against the instrumentalists of Warrington having anything to do with the Society would prevent some useful members being placed on the Committee. No wonder that the subscriptions are falling off. and I can say that subscribers, instead of responding to Dr. White's appeal for increased subscriptions, are intimating their intention of reducing their subscriptions, or dropping them off altogether, until something is done in the right direction to improve the musical condition of the Society. So long as the Committee can see that the musical public of Warrington are not satisfied with their determination to retain the services of the present conductor, they must not expect to receive much support, although they may act upon his suggestion, to go canvassing. Rather a sorrowful state of affairs that a Society cannot stand on its merits. The 3rd question, relating to the members, is one which has called for a great deal of comment amongst the musical community. Without going into detail concerning the abilities of many. mem- " bees of the choir, I may say that in my opinion the test is a mere farce, for a choral class attempting the per- formance of such works as are chosen by the Committee. The society can never receive the support it ought to have, until it shows more respect for itself by, making the admission into the choir a musical honour, instead of a fashionable craze. I think the Committee are very much to blame for empowering Dr. Hiles to encourage people to join the choir by lowering the standard of the "qualification test." But even this has not had the desired effect of swelling out the funds of the society,. It would appear that the Committee are staggering at making some improvement in the financial condition of the society, without attempting to remove the cause; hence the failure. The next question, that of rehearsals—should they not take place regularly each week during the semen? My opinion is that they should, if only to give tiff choir a better knowledge of the works they have to perform, especially those whose books are not opened except at rehearsals. This of course would incur extra expense if the services of Dr. Hiles were to be retained. But this question gives rise to another suggestion—why not have a chorus master and do away with the weekly services of Dr. Hiles, engaging him as conductof only? This would in some measure reduce the expenditure, as the Committee need not go a hundred miles out of town to meet with one who has had considerable experience in the training of choirs with creditable .results. What is wanted to make the society successful is in one respect, not merely an able conductor, but a good choir trainer; one who has a keen sense of the duties he has to per- form, and a reputation to make. But then the "personal peculiarity" of this idolized conductor, would very likely prevent the amicable working of such an arrange- ment, as in the case of the "Orchestral Society" and Mr. Veerman. 'Tis a pity that this "personal pecu- liarity" should stand so mucli in the way of encourage- ment to local talents, and,in a great measure, in the way of what might make the society a success. It has been suggested that the most effectual way of removing it would be to withhold subscriptions, and allow the society to collapse. I see the members of the choir have notice to commence rehearsals: accompanied with the beggarly request to do what they can to get fresh sub- scribers. Now to do this, what are they to say in recommendation of the society? They cannot boast of any honour or advantage in belonging to the choir, snd I think they cannot say much forthe performances given in exchange for the subscriptions. It is quite plain that something besides a mere appeal must be done to save the society.
AN OLD SUBSCRIBER.

C.E.T.S.—The Huyton branch had a crowded first gathering on Monday evening. The Rev. J. W. Tyrer was in the chair, and gave an interesting address. There was no arranged proFramme, but a number of ladies and gentlemen contributed to a musical enter- tainment.

div.head: TWO WARRINGTON MEN DROWNED AT
div.p: TWO WARRINGTON MEN DROWNED AT
WIDNES.

A shocking drowning fatality occurred at Widnes on Saturday night. It appears that James Wilson, aged 24, a single man, of Doe-lane, Sankey Bridges, had brought a flat down the canal to Widnes, and about 8 o'clock was returning home, riding on the horse's back. Near Carterhouse Crossing signal box, he overtook John Casey, 38 years of age, a /dr.. worker of Sankey Bridges' and invited him to ride alongside him on the horse's back. Casey mounted and the journey was proceeded with. In a few minutes Richard Hartshorn, the signalman, heard a splash and cries of distress, and taking his lamp he , walked on the canal bank. About five hundred ' yards from his cabin he found the horse struggling in the water, but there were no signs of the men whohad been upon its back. Hartshorn succeeded in getting the animal out, and afterwards the dead bodies of the men were brought to the surface. The night was very dark. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the bodies of the deceased on Tuesday after- noon, at the house of Mr. Plumpton, Moss Bank. Mr. Brown appeared on behalf of Messrs. dare and Ridgway, slate merchant, Sankey Bridges, for whom the man WiLson worked. Mrs. Casey identified the body of John Casey as that of her husband. He Was 41 years of age, and hved at Sankey Bridges.—Mr. Wilson, father of the deceased Joseph Wilson, said his son was 24 years of age. He was a single man, and was eniployed as a carter for Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, Sankey Bridges. He was a steady man.—Richard Hartshorn said he lived at Bold, and worked for the London and North-Western Railway Co., as a shunter. On Saturday night he was working at Carterhouse signal-box. He saw the deceased men about a quarter to eight on Saturday night oassing his cabin, about 500 yards from where the accid- ent occurred, but could not tell then whether they were riding on the horse. Shortly afterwards he heard one man inviting the other to get on the horse's back to ride. The next thing he heard was a shout of "Oh," and he immediately took the signalman's hand lamp, and ran along the, canal bank. This was nearly ten minutes after he saw them with the horse. The shouting ceased- before •he got to the men and two or three workmen from Messrs. Sullivan's works, came and assisted him in trying to find the men. tie turned his lamp towards the water and found the horse in the water. A flatman, who was coming down with his boat, also tried to recover the bodies. Witness could not see the men and called out, but received no reply. Eventually Casey was found first.—Cross 37C- amined : He could see where the horse had stumbled, and he found one of the men's hats on the bank.—Thos. Simcock said he was one of the men who helped to grapple for and recover the todies. Casey was taken out at twelve o'clock on Saturday night. Wilson VMS recovered at half-past nine on Sunday morning.—The jury were of opinion that the men were accidentally drowned, and returned a verdict to that effect.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A SERVANT AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A SERVANT AT WIDNES.
TOUCHING LETTERS.

About half-past eight on Thursday morning, Mrs. Lea, wife of Mr. J. B. Lea, cab proprietor, Victoria- road, went upstairs to awake her housekeeper, Elizabeth Cartmel, and to give her a cup of tea as usual. She was alarmed to find that she did not( answer •to her name and that she could not be aroused. Dr. McLennan was sent for, and on his arrival he concluded that the woman was suffering from opium poisoning. He applied the usual re- medies, but death occurred about half-past one. Yesterday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, held an inquest upon the body in the Parade room at the Police Station. Mr. Gervas was the foreman of the jury.— Mrs. Lea said the deceased was a single woman, 33years of age, and had acted as her house- keeper for about four years. Deceased slept with another servant named Bella Jackson. On Wednes- day she called Jackson at seven o'clock, and at that time the deceased was lying on her back with her hand on her breast over her heart. Thedeceased was not strong, and it was usual for her (witness) to take her a cup of tea upstairs. She did so at half- past eight on Wednesday morning, and deceased , was lying in exactly the same posture as at seven o'clock. She could not arouse her and thought there was something wrong and ran downstairs, and fetched Mr. Lea, who at once sent for Dr. McLennan. The doctor attended to her but she died at half past one. She found the cup produced on the dressing table.—[The Coroner remarked that it smelt like coffee]. There were drugs kept for horses in the kitchen, and the decased bad the run of the house. The bottle labelled "Tikheel " belonged to the deceased, who suffered much from neuralgia. They could only imagine that she had taken some drugs from the kitchen. The following letter was found in the dress the dece'ased had worn on the previous day.— "Oct. 10th 1888. Dear Bella,—l have long beena source of grievance and annoyance to you, but now 'tis all over. When you are reading this my body at least will be free from pain. I have tried hard to fight against this, but I cannot any longer. It would be cruel on my part to make you unhappy any lungei , therefore I now ask your • forgiveness for anythingl may have done or said toyou at. any time. All the world seems against me. I seem to cast a shadow, or rather my presence does,wherever I go. Tell the missus lam sorry but I cannot help it. You will get on better without me and I shall soon be for- gotten. Kiss the child for me. I cannot bear to think of leaving the dear little thing. God bless her! I have fought hard against it for her sake, but it is no use, I am heartily tired, and sick of everything. • Goodbye. E. Cartmell."

Mrs. Lee (continuing) said she had no suspicion that the deceased contemplated taking her own life. Some years ago the deceased attempted to throw herself through a window. The child referred elf was hers. (Mrs. Lea's.) The Coroner said the deceased had sent a letter to her father, John Cartmel of 22a Prince Edward-street, Liverpool. This letter concluded as follows : .. . . _ . _ _

"As for myself I am not half well. I feel tired of every thing, and everybody. If anybody looks at me it is enough; there seems to be a terrible weight crushing me down. I can neither eat nor sleep, and I don't want to talk to anyone; but I must now conclude, with kind love to all, father, mother, George, Tom and John, hoping you are all well, and I shall soon be better. I remain your affectionate daughter, Elizabeth Cartmel. God bless you and keep you." -

Bella Ja'ckson, a yoluig, woman, said she was servant to Mrs. Lea. The deceased had been very low spirited lately ; and had been awfully miserable since Sunday. She had complained of a pain in her side for along time, and she (witness) told her on Sunday that something else was troubling her, but she could get nothing from her. After tea, or,. Sunday , she saw deceased upstairs, and said "Now Milly, I know you have been crying; tell me what it is 2" The deceased said "No, I won't, I will leave it behind me on paper." On Wednesday night they went to bed together, and slept in the same bed. At seven o'clock, when Mrs. Lea called her, she thought the deceased was lying very comfortably asleep; and she and the children were very quite, because they knew that she did not have much sleep at nights. She did not hear the deceased get up at any part of the night. The deceased had made slight hints at times about tak- ing her life, but she had been so merry over it, that witness had treated her words as jokes. Tilley had had bits of quarrels, but not lately. Thilt deceased was par- ticularly happy with the family, but she was so short- tempered and low-spirited.—A juryman: Had she any love affair on P—Witness : No, I don't think she had : I think I should have known about it •

Dr. McLennan described the steps he took to revive the deceased. From the tests he had applied, he had no doubt that she died through an overdose of laudanum. The jury returned a verdict that deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily insane by taking an overdose of laudanum.

div.head: ANOTHER PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE IN RUNCORN.
div.p: ANOTHER PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE IN RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, Charles Erinshaw, landlord of the Albion ,inn, Nelson- street, was charged with permitting drunk- enness to take place on his premises.—P.S. Woolley stated that about half-past eight On Saturday night, the 22nd September, he visited the house in company with P.C. Hulse. In the kitchen was a man named John Jones, who was very drunk, and he had a pint cup filled with ale before him. The landlord was not in and the condition of the man was pointed out to the waitei in charge and the matter was reported at the police station. At half-past nine P.S. Woolley, P.S. Gosling, and P.C's. Hulse and Herron returned to the house. Jones was there in the taproom; with a pint cup containing some ale before him. A boatwoman named Harriet Kay was also drunk in the room, and she drank a glass of porter in the presence of the officers. The floor and counters were very wet with liquor, as if a great deal of drinking had taken place. The landlord's attention was called to the state of the persons.—The other constables confirmed this statement.—The defendant said he was not aware that Jones was in the house atrall, and he (defendant) did not serve him and he was not served. The woman I had only had a gill of porter, and was as sober as he was now.—Ellen Longford, boatwornan, Nelson-street, was I called, and said she did not know whether Jones was sober' or not. Kay was sober.—ln reply to the Bench, defendant said he had been in the house 8 years.—Mr. Brundrit : No oemplaints.—Superintendent Holing- worth said there had been complaints,but not sufficient to take action.—Mr. Bxundrit said it was a pity the defen- dant should spoil his record. There was no doubt about this ca-se, and a fine of 20s. and costs 13s. 6d., or a month, would be imposed.—John Jones, of Nelson-st., was fined 55., and costs 7s. 6d:, for being drunk on the remises.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1888.
FRODSHAM.

SCRIPTURE UNION BRANCH.—A public meeting was held in the National Schoolroom, Church-street, on Mon- day evening, when the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of 1 Kingsley, delivered an address bearing on the work and usefulness of the union. There was a good number of members and friends. FIVE CROSSES WESLEYAN CHlPEL.—Harvest thanks- giying serm6ns were preached in the above chapel on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Rev. John Skipham, of Frodsham. The interior of the chapel was tastefully decorated with flowers, fruits, Ezc. The choir. as usual, rendered the harvest anthems and hymns very creditably. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL—On Sunday harvest thanksgivng services were held in the above chapel, when the Rev. C. Finch, of Runcorn, preached. The chapel had been neatly decorated. The choir gave the several hymns and anthems with their accustomed ability. On Monday evening a public meeting was held, when addresses were delivered by the Revs. C. Finch and G. Rennison, and Miss Rosser (Blue Ribbon Army "Captain"), and recitations by the scholars of the Sunday school, interspersed with suitable hymns by the choir. Mr. Peter Booth presided. The usual votes of thanks having been given the meeting terminated.

div.head: ADVENTURE OF A WIDNES MAN
div.p: THE ADVENTURE OF A WIDNES MAN
AT TIMPERIEY.

At the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday, a labourer named Hugh Mitchell, hailing from Widnes, was brought up in custody, charged with being on certain enclosed premises at Timperley, at 11.30 on Saturday night, loran unlawful purpose. —Albert Smith, coachman in the employ of Mr. Lowcock, Timperley, said that at 11.30 on Saturday night, when he reached home, he foundlthe prisoner in the back yard of the house. One of the servants shouted to him that he had been trying to get into the house, but from what he discovered he did not think he had made such attempt. The prisoner could give no proper explanation, and he accordingly took him to the police station. The prisoner seemed sober enough, and had a return ticket to Widnes. The prisoner said he had got out of the train upon the line, and he was glad that someone had found him, as he was completely lost.— Percy Childs, a boy employed by Mr. Lowcock, stated that at a quarter, past eleven someone knocked at the kitchen doot He shouted "who's there? "and a voice replied "A stranger." He refused to let him in, and informed the coachman when he returned. Superintendent Leighton said that on Sunday he asked the prisoner to give some account of himself. He said he lived at Widnes. On Satusday he went to Belle Vue with two friends. He remembered entering the train at Belle Vue, but had no recollection of getting out; he did not, however, think he left the train at a railway station. He gave his address at Widnes, and on the previous night he wrote to the Superintendent of Police, asking fora reply by telegraph. The Superintend- ent of Police replied to the effect that the prisoner bore a good character. His own idea of the affair was that the prisoner had had some drink and fell asleep. While the train was being shunted, probably at Skelton Junction, he got out of the train, and had made for Mr. Lowcock's house. He did not think that Mitchell was on the premises for any felonious intent. The prisoner bore out this staterpent. He said he had not had much drink, and when he got out on the line he saw lights at some distance, and made towards the house for the purpose of enquiring where he was. He was then found by the coachman. The Chairman said it was very lucky for him he had been found, and that he had been kept out of danger. The prisoner was then discharged.

div.head: HARRY 'SPEAKMAN IN AUSTRALIA. INTERESTING LETTER.
div.p: HARRY 'SPEAKMAN IN AUSTRALIA. INTERESTING LETTER.

During the present week the following letter has been received from Harry Speakman of Runcorn, who is one of the members of the English team in Australia:— This letter is from the 3rd of Augult. On our way to Sidney, we stopped at Gourbourn for breakfast, we paid 2s. Bd. for chops and steaks. After this we proceeded on our journey. It is very fine. The sun is at full, and very hot and all the windows of the saloon are open as we speed along. We arrived at Sidney at 12.20, and were at once taken to the Oxford Hotel, but as there was not sufficient accommodation most of us went to Her Majesty's Hotel—a very fine building. My bed mate is Bob Burnett, the Canny Scot. He is a nice fellow. After lunch we went down to the ground for a bit of kicking; then after dinner we went to see "Drink " played by C. Warner's company it is a fine piece, and a good one—plenty in it to make a man consider. Then supper and to bed.' On Saturday, the 4th, we were up early for a walk. Breakfast at nine o'clock, and afterwards I went to see the wedding of a Liverpool man at a printing office. In the af-ernoon we played New South Wales team. I was given a rest, as I had only missed one Victorian game. We won by 16 points to 2. The Australian way of scoring is .5 for a goal from a try, 4 for a drop goal, 2 a try. This is the best way of scoring, I think. In the evening we all went to see the "Lights of Londori," then to bed. lam strictly T. T. On Sunday up early-, and went to St. James Church at 11 a.m. The text for the sermon was the 48th psalm 9th verse We came out at a quarter to one, and went " home "to dinner. We don't have dinner at night on Sundays, and tea is the best treat we enjoy. In the afternoon I walked round he gardens for which Sydney is noted. The grounds are just at the edge of the Har- bour. and this Harbour is the finestin the world. In the Domain Park there were hundreds of folks talking on Free Trade, and all kinds of subjects. There were Blue Ribbon Armies, Salvation Armies, Ranters and Buskers of all sorts speaking to get money. Af er tea, Tom Haslam and I went to the church It is a fine place, and was crowded to excess. We had to stand. A walk round the public park, and home to bed at ten p.m. concluded the day. • Monday.--Bank Holiday at home, but not here. .We were up at 7 o'clock, getting ready for a trip to Bath- hurst. We started at 9 a.m. and were soon in the midst of the finest hilly country I ever saw. We reached I Mount Victoria at 12 o'clock and had lunch. This is on the top of a mountain, and you would wonder how a train could get up. We departed from here at 2 o'clock, and then we were on the zig-zag. We did lot miles to get 2i miles. On the top of the hills, we could see die bottom of the valley below, and are had to get down by the train going back- wards until we came to the Zig-zag station. We arrived at Bathurst at 5.30, and were met by the Mayor of that town at the Shannon's Hotel. Bob Seddon was staying at the Royal Hotel, but we did not know this, so sorheone had to respond te the toast of our team, and this I did for the credit of the country. My Maiden Speech. After dinner we all went up to the Royal Hotel, kept by Mr. Turner, who has a son playing cricket at home with the Australians. I can tell you he is the best bowler in the world—with his father. - - - -

Up early on the 7th and had a good look round the town and visited the foundries. We had a "Kick" he the afternoon and at night we went to the Skating Rink by invitation On Wednesday the Eith we were taken to see the Down Force Drive, and afterwards the Committee picked a team. Bumby and Nolan being hurt I was put half back I had occupied this position in the 2nd at home, so it was nothing new to me. I just showed them the way to pass to the three-quarters. We got 2 goals and 5 tries; most of the tries were got .off me. Stoddart told me I should make a better half than three-quarter, because there was not enough work for me at three- quarter, and the more I did and the better I went. After the game, we were on for a jolly good walk round the town;but there is little to be seen, so we all went to bed early. Next morning (Thursday) we were up at 5.30 and there were drags at the door waiting to convey us out shooting. It was very frosty and bold. We drove nine miles to the camp, and as our buggy was the first there we at once set to work to make a fire, chopping down trees on the estate of Mr. Grist—a nice old gent. By the time the fire was well in we were ready. We cooked 50Ibs. of steak, and 101bs. of sausages, and when it was done, and the tea ready, we just showed them what we really could do, when hungry inthebush on a frostymorning. Harry Eagles told them it was a champion do "—Lancashire style. We all had a try to crack a stock whip with P. Sul- livan. I think I won the prize, so Paddy Sullivan said. You should have seen A. G. Laing throw the lash all round his face. While this was going on, Stoddard was killing little birds with his catapult. We then got our guns and catridges, and had a really good day's sport—shooting kangaroos. I never laughed iso much n my life. Sam Williams, A. J. Laing, and the rest of them were driving the Kangaroos, and we were under a hill popping at them as they came down. I made some good shots During the day we killed about 140 Kangaroos and 46 hares. After this, we went to the camp to have a cup Of tea, and some cake. We gave Mr. Grist, and his wife and daughter three hearty. English cheers, and Bob Seddon thanked them for the support they had given us! 'We arrived back at tawn at 7 o'clock well pleased with our day's out. After dinner we were given some Pawson skins, and Emu eggs and had a Jolly night. Some of our men went home, but I did not as it is very , cold going over the Blue mountains at night. They would not get to Sydney, till 6 a.m. We started next morning at 10.15 and crowds of Bathurst people came to see us off. Sydney was reached at 6.30 in the even- ing. [We shall give the remainder of the letter in our next issue.]

CADBURY'S COCOA Is absolutely pure and untampered with. It has stood the keenest analytical tests, and consists solely of the concentrated extract of the Cocoa bead, the flavour be- ing developed and the aroma improved by a special process of roasting.—Advt. The older portion of Messrs. Bairstowe's corn factory, at Keighley, was burnt out on Thursday morning. The loss is estimated at £lO,OOO, but is covered by insurance.

div.head: MANCHESTEIt SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTEIt SHIP CANAL.
WESTON.

There is little to report or;this -section. The German 'navvy and the other machines on Frodsham Marsh are working well and daily removing a vast amount of material. Upwards of 600 men are now employed. The work of getting out the foundations for the great lock at the entrance to the Weaver is proceeding apace. During the week, a portable engine, and centrifugal pump, ten inch bore, has been fited and the large quantity of water that drains into the workings is now kept well under control to the great advantage of the men. There are no signs of operations being commenced in the Mersey as yet.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

After having been very quiet on this section for a few weeks, it is expected that great activity will again pre- vail in the course of a day or we. Arrangements are now complete for drawint, off the Runcorn and Latch- ford canal which is crossed threetimes by the Ship Canal in the neigh:ourhood of Runcorn. Every precaution will be taken to prevent inch an unfortunate occurrence as that which recently caused the stoppage of the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele. An ample supply of water will be provided for these works; probably from the Bridgewater Canal by means of a- culvert. Near these works trial holes have been made in order to ascertain at what depth rock ,might be met with. The holes have been sunk to a distance of 40 feet and there was no appearance of rock. This weekend it is intended to commence the erection of the permanent river wall from No Man's Land up to the Old Quay docks under- neath the first girder of Runcorn Bridge. At the Old Quay dock there are several cargos of dressed granite copings ready for this work. MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.

No great changes have taken place lately in the appear- ance of the work on these sections. The second lift of the cutting has been reached, And, as it is for the most part,composed of hard rock, progress is necessarily slow. The German navvy keeps ahead in removing the sandy soil of the first lift at the beginning of the Moore section. In a very*short time it will have taken away all the loose soil, and as it would be of no use when employeciagainst the underlying reek, it will then have to be removed elsewhere. Besides this, there are only two navvies of the "American" type employed between the level crossing at Moore, and Norley Common. The " con- vertible " cranes, are however, in great use, hauling up and down the large buckets filled with rock deln-is. At Acton Grange the new Mission Hall is nearly completed and will be opened on Sunday. It consists of a well lighted and lofty room, about thirty feet by sixty feet, and two smaller rooms which can be used as classrooms, etc. The large room is fitted with a platform, a little over two feet in height, and a large number of fine seats with comfortable pat3nt backs. The residence of the minister is also completed, and is now occupied. When the Mission Hall is finished the men are to get to work upon a house for the walking ganger, near that of the minister, the building of which is just being com- menced.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

Operations here are confined to the making of the new road, the final removal of George's Bank, a'hd the demolishment of the houses along the canal route. The house lately occupied by Mr. Cunliffe is pulled down and the debris.. is being carried away. Two American excavators working between it's site and Morley Com- mon, are making good headway. INQUEST AT LATCHFORD. _ _

On Monday Mr. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Canal Hospital at Latchford, relative to the death of a youth named Thomas Deganes, who lived at Hollins- green, and was employed on the Warburton section of the canal. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased was working near to the Warrington road at Rixton, when he was knocked down by an engine. He sustainectserious injuries, and was removed to the Latchford hospital, where he died. The jury found that death was accidental. THELWALL. _ _

Progress is still the password on the Thelwall section, the steam navvies having now pushed the excavation up to Cedar Lawn, the late residence of Alderman Pick- mere. This residence and its outlittildings and adjacent cottages a e in course of demolition, and the shrubs and trees in the once-pleasant grounds have been, for the most part, either cut down or rooted up. Thelwall-lane has now been broken in upon and is closed between Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant's tannery and Morris- brook farmhouse, so that persons on the. way from Warrington to Thelwall have to turn up Cross-lane and proceed along the newly-made road. This road, although it at present terminates in Cross-lane, will ulti- mately be continued to, Grappenhall-lane hear Latch- ford Station. The part of the road already made is solidly laid, though the amount of loose macadam that is upon it makes it a heavy/pull for vehicles. FATAL ACCIDENT AT WAIIIiIIRTON.

An accident which has unfortunately been attended with fatal consequences, happened to a boy named Thomas Deganes, who lives at Hollins Green, and was employed on the Warburton section. He was " sprag- ging "-wagons—that is to say stopping them with pieces of wood—on a high bank, next to the Warrington road at Rixton, When he was knocked down by the tipping engine and severely crushed. He was removed to the hospital at Latchford, and his injuries were attended to by Dr. flume, but he soon afterwards succumbed. THE BRICK-WORKS AT STATHAM.

In Statham, as we have before mentioned, some very line strong clay has been cut into, and this is being utilised by the contractor for brick-making purposes. A very complete and elaborate plant has been laid down, with a pug mill in full work and another being erected, and these two, when in full operation, will turn out about 200,000 bricks weekly. This quantity can be continued all the winter through, as large sheds capable of drying by means of flues 160,000 bricks each five days are now in full working order. Five large Scotch kilns (another is being erected), capable of burning 100,000 bricks in four days, are also in operation. This locality, where twelve months ago was unbroken meadow land, is now teeming with busy life. A number of wooden cottages have been built and tenanted, valuable engines and machinery are in motion, lines of railway and locomotives in all directions cover the ground where a few years ago a freshet from the river inundated the land to a depth of four or six feet.

div.head: FLiXTON.
div.p: FLiXTON.

_ During the past week considerable progress has been made with the track railway which is being constructed along the southern, bank of the Irwell at Barton, and immediately opposite the lock-house. The ballact rail- way, which has been constructed from the Cheshire Lines railway at Irlam has been extended to Hulme's Bridge, Flixton. At Carrington, a few hundred yards east of the Manchester Corporation's refuse works, the Mersey is being diverted into the Irwell, and at Partington, where it is proposed to form a number of coal tips, a large cutting from the canal has been made on the east side of the Stockport and Glazebrook Railway. • IRLAM AND ECCLES.

Although during last week the navvies on the Barton and Eccles and Irlam and Flixton sections of the Ship Canal works were compelled to cease work at intervals in consequence of the boisterous and inclement weather, a visit to the works on Saturday revealed considerable progress in their construction. At Sticken's Island not only has the required depth of the canal been reached, but the foundation of one of the large locks has nearly been completed. The formation of the track railway underneath the southern arches of the aqueduct and Barton bridge is in a forward condition, and ledges have been cut in the sblid rock on the southern bank of the river. A portion of the hedge separating the river from a field adjoining the highway opposite St. Catherine's schools has been taken down, and the necessary pre- liminaries are being pushed forward for the construction of the railway- through the field until it reaches the river about 100 yards lower down, and piles are there driven into the bed of the Irwell for the continuation of the rail- way across on to the Salt Eye meadows. At Boat Lane, Flizton, quite a young colony is being established, there being already erected over 20w0rkmen's hutS, in addition to a hospital, the contractor's offices, stores, and engine sheds. Excavations have been commenced in the mead- ows at Lower Irlam, and the ballast railway from a point south Of Irlam station, on the Cheshire Lines, has been extended to beyond the Catemanka locks in the direction of Hulme's bridge, and after two or three wooden bridges have been erected across the river, the Irwell at this point taking a very zigzag course, there will be one con- tinuous length of lines from Salford to Irlam. Three additional locomotives were employed last week on the Irlam and Cadishead section, which now ranks amongst the most active on the whole undertaking. Between the New Barns, Salford, and the Boathouse, Hollins Green, twelve track bridges have been made across the river for ballast lines, and ere the works form one con- tinuous length an additional seven or eight will kave to be constructed.

div.head: ANOTHER DISPUTE.
div.p: ANOTHER DISPUTE.

Mr. W. J. Beadel, M.P. for Chelmsford. sat at the Queen's Hotel, Chester on Tuesday, as umpire in a dispute as to the value of land acquired by the Manche4er Ship Canal Company at Ellesmere Port. The proceedings were private, but it is stated that the land in question, which consists of a narrow strip of 45 acres running from Ellesmere Port to Pool Hall Rock, was purchased by the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company in 1870 for about £12,000, and that they placed great value on the land in con- sequence ef its river frontage, and that the Ship Canal Company offered £6OOO. Evidence was taken on behalf of the owners, and the arbitration was adjourned.

HORRIBLE MURDER BY A SON. The village of Sherburn-in-Elmet, Notts, was on Thursday morning thrown into a state of consterna- tion by a report that during the night Mrs. Catherine, Mountain, landlady of the Traveller's Rest at that place,had been brutally murdered by her son George Mountain. Mrs. Mountain who is said to be between seventy and eighty years of age, kept a small public-house adjoining the Grammar School at Sherbum,and her son, had for some time, acted as her manager. On the previous night, the house had been closed for the night, and the accused, who is now in custody, went into the room in which his mother and the maid were sitting, and locked the door. This was at about eleven o'clock, and shortly afterwards Mrs. Mountain suggested that they should go to bed. He persisted in saying that they were mkt going to bed, and about half an hour later he commenced to knock his mother about, and get- ting her on the floor commenced to kick her to death. With so much violence did Lo carry out his threats that the poor woman expired between one and two o'clock in the presence of the maid, who was per- fectly helpless, and who was threatened by the accused that he would do. her the • same. His brutality did not step with the death of his mother. He stripped her of all her clothing just before she died, and continued kicking her up to four o'clock in the morning. As may be imagined. the features of the poor woman as she laid down in the room were this horrible tragedy occurred were beyond recognition. Such a frightful 'scene as lithe room presented can scarcely be imagined. A policeman who passed the house at about twelve o'clock heard nothing to arouse his suspicions. The prisoner, who is a short thick-set man, of about thirty years of age was found and brought up in custody before the Hon. H. C. Maxwell Stuart and other justices, and, formal evidence having been given by the girl Annie Hutchinson, he was remanded for a week. The prisoner presented a rather wild appearance. and said he did not know what he was doing. He thought it was someone who had come to rob the house.

div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY COLLISION IN AMFRICA.. LOSS OF OVER SIXTY LIVES.
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY COLLISION IN AMFRICA.. LOSS OF OVER SIXTY LIVES.

An accident occurred on Wednesday on the Lehigh Valley Ail way, near Betthaven, in Pennsyl- vania, by which several cars of a Catholic excursion train were wrecked, over sixty persons being repor- ted killed and many injured. The train was pro- ceeding in two sections, and the accident was caused by the second section telescoping the pre- ceding one: _ _

Telegraphing on Thursday morning, a New York correspondent says :—As the fifth section of an excursion train was returning yesterday evening to Wilkesbarre, Pennsylvania, from a Roman Catholic parade, under the direction of the Rev. Father Mathew' at Hableton, it can -1 into collision with the fourth section of the returning excursion- ists, while rounding a cue near Penhaven. • The crash was heard a long way off, and the carriages were thrown into terrible confusion, a large number being precipitated into the river, above which the collision took place. In all about sixty persons were killed, either in the immediate collision, or drowned by falling into the river. Many must have huffered great agony from their injuries, as the carriages were in some cases telescoped, and others smashed into splinters. Over one hundred persons received serious injuries, from which it is feared some cannot recover.

(From the "Daily News.") NEW Volts, Thursday.—Ao appalling disaster took place on the Lehigh Valley Railway, Pennsylvania, last evening. Eight thousand excursionists were being con- veyed in three trains. The first contained nine carri- ages, the second ten the third twelve. The first went through all right. The second was waiting for the line ahead to be clear, when the third dashed into it at full speed Both trains were densely crowded, and the loss of life was terrible. The shock drove the rear carriage of the stationary train through the one ahead two thirds of its length, forcing it into the thirci. Not a single person escaped alive from the rear carriage. The second also Vas left with a mass of maimed and bleeding bodies, and from the third only a few escaped. • The terrified passengers who were uninjured hurried from the carriages to the spa where the locomotive and thelcarriages were lying crushed together. A terrible scene met their eyes. The shattered locomotive was pouring forth streams of steam and water, which hid the full horrors of the disaster, while the hissing sound deadened the shrieks and groans of those imprisoned. Some of the dead sat pinioned erect in their seats. The timbers of the rear carriage were crushed and wrenchM., while on all sides hung mangled bodies and limbs. The few bodies whickwere not mangled were burned and scalded by the steam. The uninjured began at once to de what could be done for their unfortunate companions. The few light tools on thP train nrnvod vary inolßoiont, A Toutig lday %at, foils(' caught by the legs. One was quickly released, but the other could not be freed, and a misdirected blow of ad axe severed it from the body. She heroically bore her torture, and taking out a gold watch handed it to an acquaintance as a gift to a friend at home. She was put on one of the trains and had all possible care, but died in the arms of her friends. To free the bodies in the rear carriage the men attached the locomotive to the wrecked one, and started to pull it out. At first the movement brought from the wounded such cries of dis- tress that the surrounding friends ordered the engineer to desist on pain of his life. They did not wish to see the mangled forms still further mutilated. The few houses on the spot were thrown open to the sufferers. and bonfires were lighted to aid the work of relief. More than fifty persons were found to have been killed, and seventy wounded. , The passengers on the running train say they saw the , train standing ahead of them when a long distance away, and sprang from their seats, wondering why the speecbef their train was not slackened. Suddenly they, saw their driver and stoker leap from the locomo ive. When the shock came, both escaped slightly injured. The stoker says he saw the red light of the lantern which the stationary train had displayed as a signal. He shouted to the driver, and both Jumped off. The accident is charged to the carelessness of the driver, who had half a mile clear ahead, in which the red light was plainly visible He said he had been on duty 48 hours without rest, and had fallen asleep from exhaustitm. NEW Vona, Ocr, 11, 5 rat.—lt is feared that the first report of the number of persons killed in the accident at Mudrun will after all, prove not to have been exagge- rated. Nine more bodies have been recognised, bringing the total up to fifty-eight, and a number still await identification. Two of the persons injured died this morning in the hospital at Wilkesbarre, and six more are beyond all hope of recovery. a

FATAL ACCIDENT AT BOLD.—On Saturday after- noon Mr. Brighouse;coroner, held an inquiry, at the White Hart Hotel, Warrington as to the death of Patrick Kirby, a youth of 19 years of age. The deceased was employed as a labourer by Mr. James Warburton, South-lane farm, P,old, and while removing the thrippers off a cart at Bold, on Wednesday, One of them fell on the horse, and caused it to run away. Deceased wa,; knercked down, and, a wheel passing over one of his leas, broke it. He was at once removed to the Infirmary at Warrington, where he died on Thursday morn- ing. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

THE " WELLs Liorr."—One of the most remarkable answers to the modern demand for better illuminantt has been the invention of the "Wells Light" (Messrs. A. e. Wells & Co., London and Manchester). This light in its present simple and perfect state in the outcome of several years experimenting by the Patentees, Messrs. Wallwork &Wells. It is hard to believe that any further improvement can be made on a lamp which can be carried about by two men, managed by Any labourer, and which gives out a light of t,OOO to 4,000 candle power continously at an almost nominal cost. The light is obtained by burning the vapour of a specially refined tar oil; it will also burn petroleum. The apparatus consists of a strong steel , cylindrical tank, a small hand pump, and a generating burner above the tank, and is designed throughout for rough work and hard usage. The burner may be taken off the tank and connected to it by flexible hose, if required, and by means of masts and hoisting tackle. the light can be raised high above the ground; and whether used as a portable light by Contractors, or as a permanently elevated light for Docks, Goods Yards, &c., the invention seems well-nigh perfect. The flame is white, casts no deep shadows, is unaffected by wind or rain, and will burn continuously for five or six hours if the tank is replenished. It is the only large light in use through the extensive workings of the Manchester Ship Canal, and has been adopted by Her Majesty's Govern- ment.

Dutton, Astley, Ellison, Simpson, Buckley, and Davy ; also Mrs. Astley, the Misses Stone, Brearley, and Bowen, with the secretary, Mr. James Clare. Tan RAILWAY HOTEL, FIEATLEY.—At Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, James John Harrop applied for a temporary licence to sell at the Railway Hotel, HeatleY, in lieu of Miss Steele. Superintendent Leighton said jut had received a letter from the police at Chesterfield grr- ing the applicant a good character, and he had no objec- tion tooffer.—The application was granted. GOOD TEMPLARY.—On Tuesday evening the usual meeting of the Tower of Refuge Lodge of Good Template took place in the Congregational Schools, Bro. Hem+ Thomas in the chair. Two visitors from Birkenhead were present, and entertained the brethren with songs and recitations, after which the meeting took the form of asking and answering questions relating to the work and advancement of the cause of temperance. . MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.--A meeting Of UAW society was held in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening. The evening was devoted to impromptu speaking, the subject being "Cleanliness with relation to mind ann body." Mr. John Harrison opened the subject, and the following members took part in the discussion :—Messrit F. 0 Mpston, Edward Dennett, James Mort, Edward Brown, Edward Moston' J. A. Colyer, W. Skilling, and the secretary (Mr. John Brearley). Several new mem- bers were proposed, and the meetings promise to be verY successful.

• BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—Th° opening meeting of this society was held on Wednesday. The president, Mr. W. Brundritt ; sense. tary, Mr. W. Gould • treasurer, Mr. T. Griffiths, ,Readings from Longfellow vOere given 137 the fel' lowing members :—Mr. S. Gould, "Resignation ;" Mr. A. Perkin, " Two locks of hair ; " Mr. G. Diamond, "Killed at the ford ;" Mr. Eaton, " The driftwood fire. A very amusing recitation was given by Mr. Hurs.field, entitled "Nothing to wear." An able and instructive paper was read by the president, Mr. W. Brundritt, entitled, "The influence of society on the formation of character," and speeches were delivered on the sanle subject by Messrs. Hurstfield, G. Clarke, and Diamond. —This brought the proceedings to a close. Rev:mum—The revision of the lists of Lymm and adjoining townships took place at Lymm Police Court, before Mr. W. T. Parkins, the revising barrister. The Liberals were represented by Messrs. A. E. Paterson (solicitor, Altrincham), E. L. Kenyon A. W. Barrett, and William Skillingt, and the Conservatives by Messrs. F. R. B. Lindsell (solicitor, Altrineham), J. Plant, J. Goodwin. A. Callinder, and C. E. Ardern. The business was mostly of a routine character and was expeditiously transacted. Sergeant Harrington, who is entitled to be on the Parliamentary list, claimed to be on "list 2," for the County Council franchise, but, though neither side objected, the Barrister held that the law gave him no power to put him on. Sergeant McHale, of Brooln Edge, got on, however, as the word "police" nowhere appeared on his claim. DEATH or MRS. J. DIICKWORTH.—In the announcement of the sudden and unexpected death of Mrs. J. Duck- worth, the eldest daughter of Mrs. Ba-tersby, of Lymni Hall, which took place at her residence in Savannah, Georgia, U.S., last Friday, has been received in Lymin with general regret. Mrs. Duckworth, with her husband and family, had been staying at the hall on 3 short visit during the summer, and sailed for their home on Saturday, September Bth. During the time of her visit here her health had not been so good as usual, but nothing of a serious nature was anticipated ; the cable- gram received at the hall on Friday evening announcing a fatal termination to an inflammation of the stomach was therefore a very severe shock to the family. The deceased lady was in her 36th year, having been married at St. Mary's Church, Lymm, in the spring of 1872, and she leaves a family of five children. HARVEST FESTIVALS.—On Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held in connection withLymm Congrega- tional Church. The preacher was the Rev. W. /1,.. Cheesson, of Eccles. A large audience was present each service. A collection was made at the evening service in aid of the fund for the purchase of a nevi organ, the amount realized being £3 4s. On SundaY the harvest festival in connection with Lynam; Primitive Methodist Chapel was celebrated, when sermons were preached to good congregations by Mr. A. Spencer, of Oldham. At the afternoon service Mr. Snencer took for his text the words "0 that man would praise the Lord for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men," and in the evening he based ins discourse upon the words "For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." The services were continued on Monday evening, the chapel being crowded. The choir rendered a service of song entitled' Harvest Gleaning," the-con- nective readings being given by Mr. G. L. Welforli. Mr. T. Appleton acted as conductor. The collections realized £5 Bs.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

An influential meeting was held at Staines on Friday evening, in support of the local site for the annual meeting of the National Rifle Association. Goulding, ex-warder of Tullamore goal, was charged at Mitchelstown, on Friday, with committing perjury at the Mandeville inquest. He was was released on ball. On Friday the Mayor of Nottingham, Aldermarr Tunaey, unveiled a statue to the late Samuel Morley, which has been erected at the top of Market-st., Notting- ham, by public subscription. DESTRUCTIVE Fraz.—The weaving mills of Mr. Meek Rathfriland, near Newry, were entirely destroyed by fire on Friday morning. A large number of hands are thrown out of employment. The premises were not insured.

IMPORTANT CONFERENCE AT HAWARDEN CASTLE.— Yesterday, an important conference took place at Hawarden Castle. Lord Rosebery, Sir William Harcourt, and Mr. Lewis Harcourt arrived at the Castle in the evening, and Mr. Arnold Morley, the Chief Liberal Whip, journeyed to Hawarden rota Chester. RESIGNATION OF AN M.P.—Su John Simon, who has represented Dewsbury as a Liberal since 1868, on Friday wrote announcing his intention of resigning on the re-assembling of Parliament on account of ill-heal th . Mr. Mark Oldroyd, Mayor of Dewsbury, is spoken of as a probable Liberal candidate in succession to Sir John Simon.

ADVANCE IN THE PRICE or laox.—There was great excitement at the ironmasters' quarterly meeting at Birmingham on Thursday afternoon owing to the advance in the ironworkers' wages. A rise in all des- criptions of iron was expected, and at a private meeting of the principal members of the trade it was desired to advance marked bars 10s. a ton, and inferior qualities ss. a ton.

div.head: ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER IN SALFORD.
div.p: ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER IN SALFORD.

A shocking case of attempted wife murder occurred shortly after nine o'clock on Friday morning in Salford. A pensioner, named George Chandlett, murderously attacked his wife with a poker without apparent cause, and leaving her with her skull battered, almost dead, he made his escape. A horrible sight was presented when the police arrived, the woman lying in a pool of blood, and the furniture spattered. The poker was found broken, and the woman was removed to the hos- pital in a critical condition.

div.head: LONDON MURDERS.
div.p: THE LONDON MURDERS.
The police have under close observation in connection with the VVhitchapel murders an inmate of the East End Infirmary, who was admitted since the murder.
THE BELFAST SUSPECT.

At Belfast Police Court, on Friday, John Foster was charged on suspicion of being concerned in the White- chapel murders.—Constable Carland deposed that from information received he arrested the suspect in Mernel- street. He gave the name of William John Foster, said he was a watchmaker, and had been during the past week at Greenock. Glasgow' and Edinburgh. A clasp knife, three razors, and two knives were found on him, and a watch with the monogram " A.M.R."—He was remanded.

div.head: STRANGE STORY FROM LIVERPOOL.
div.p: STRANGE STORY FROM LIVERPOOL.

A strange story is transmitted -ff:C:in Liverpool. On Wednesday evening a young lady was walking alonU Shiel-road, not far from Shiel Park, when she was stopped by an elderly woman, who in an excited manner, urged her not to go into the park. She explained that a few minutes previously she had been resting on one of the seats in the park, when she was accosted by a respectable looking man, dressed in a black coat, light trousers, and a soft felt hat, who inquired if she knew if there werefanylloose women about the neighbourhood, and immediately afterwards he produced a knife with a long thin blade, and said that he intended to kill as many women in Liverpool as.ln London, adding that he would send the ears of the first victim to the editor of a Liverpool paper. The old woman stated that she was so terribly frightened that she hardly knew how she got away from the man.

div.head: EMPEROR WILLIAM IN ROME.
div.p: THE EMPEROR WILLIAM IN ROME.

The German Emperor arrived in Rome on Thursday afternoon, and was received by King Humbert with cordial greetings, while the crowd manifested the most pronounced enthusiasm along the line of route from the railway station to the Quirinal.

ROME, FRIDAY EVENING.—The German Emperor was received at the Vatican with great pomp and ceremony. His interview with the Pope, which took place in the latter's private study, lasted an hour and a half.

BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862. CHIEF OFFICES : BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 30th, 1888. „ Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- I ate. Mr. Fowke Is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his owu life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 , 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 us 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s ld, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid Up to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 us 91 in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECRETT, Secretary. DISTRICT Os-pica: MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SI7PERINI'ENDENT.
